lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 17: Giving and generosity, sowing generously and giving cheerfully**

Good morning, Greg. Paul is collecting an offering from the church in Corinth for poor believers in Jerusalem, and he uses a farmer’s picture to explain it. A farmer who throws one handful of seed shouldn’t expect a big harvest. Giving works the same way. Tony Evans calls this a spiritual axiom and notes it reaches past money: “We reap what we sow in all of life—not just where money is concerned.” He puts it bluntly: “Many Christians want a great harvest from God, but they have sown very few seeds for God.”

Then Paul gets to the heart. God isn’t after a grudging gift or one you were pressured into. “God loves a cheerful giver.” John Piper says that verse shows love is joy spilling over: “Love is the overflow of joy in God that meets the needs of others.” Cheer isn’t a mood you fake. It comes from enjoying God more than the money.

Verses 8–11 can be misread as “give so you get rich.” Read them closely. God supplies seed to the sower and enlarges the harvest “so that you can be generous on every occasion.” You’re blessed so you can keep giving, and the result is thanks to God (vv. 11–12). Billy Graham admitted, “Generosity doesn’t come naturally to most of us,” and reminded us, “We must never forget that everything we have has been given to us by God.” Proverbs adds the promise: whoever refreshes others will himself be refreshed.

Paul ends where all giving starts: “Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!” That gift is Jesus. A man who knows how much he’s been given can open his hands to his church, to people in need, and to his own family.

**2 Corinthians 9:6–15 (NIV)**
6 Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously. 7 Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. 8 And God is able to bless you abundantly, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work. 9 As it is written:

“They have freely scattered their gifts to the poor; their righteousness endures forever.”

10 Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and increase your store of seed and will enlarge the harvest of your righteousness. 11 You will be enriched in every way so that you can be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will result in thanksgiving to God.

12 This service that you perform is not only supplying the needs of the Lord’s people but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanks to God. 13 Because of the service by which you have proved yourselves, others will praise God for the obedience that accompanies your confession of the gospel of Christ, and for your generosity in sharing with them and with everyone else. 14 And in their prayers for you their hearts will go out to you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you. 15 Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!

**Proverbs 11:24–25 (NIV)**
24 One person gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds unduly, but comes to poverty.
25 A generous person will prosper; whoever refreshes others will be refreshed.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **2 Cor 9:6.** NIV: “whoever sows generously will also reap generously.” LSB: “he who sows with blessing will also reap with blessing.” Paul’s Greek literally says “on (the basis of) blessings” (*eulogia*). The NIV gives the sense, a big-hearted gift; the LSB keeps the word “blessing,” which ties back to v5, where Paul calls their gift a “blessing” rather than something squeezed out of them.
- **2 Cor 9:8.** NIV: “God is able to bless you abundantly.” LSB: “God is able to make every grace abound to you.” The Greek word is *charis*, grace. The LSB keeps it; the NIV renders what that grace looks like here. Either way, the point is that God supplies first, and the supply is for “every good work,” not for hoarding.
- **2 Cor 9:13.** NIV: “your generosity in sharing with them.” LSB: “the generosity of your fellowship toward them” (footnote: “Or sharing”). The word is *koinōnia*, the same word for fellowship. The LSB also footnotes “generosity” as “Or simplicity; without false motives” (*haplotēs*): a single-hearted, no-strings gift.
- **Prov 11:24–25.** NIV: “One person gives freely… A generous person will prosper; whoever refreshes others will be refreshed.” LSB: “There is one who scatters… The soul that blesses will be enriched, and he who waters will himself be watered.” The LSB keeps the Hebrew pictures (scattering seed, a “soul of blessing” that is literally “made fat,” watering a field). The NIV turns those pictures into plain English.

**Go deeper:** Grace Life’s podcast episode [“Living with Generosity”](https://media.podpoint.com/grace-life/living-with-generosity) (Chris Haralson, Aug 17, 2023) covers giving your time, talents and treasure. Piper’s message [“Delighting in God as the Fountain of Love”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/delighting-in-god-as-the-fountain-of-love) works through 2 Corinthians 8–9, and his Look at the Book lab [“God Gives to Create Cheerful Givers”](https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/god-gives-to-create-cheerful-givers) (Jan 6, 2018) walks verses 6–11. Also see Tony Evans, [“Reaping What You Sow”](https://go.tonyevans.org/blog/reaping-what-you-sow), and Billy Graham, [“Why Should We Be Generous Toward Others?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/why-should-we-be-generous-toward-others). BibleProject’s overviews of [2 Corinthians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/2-corinthians/) and [Proverbs](https://bibleproject.com/videos/proverbs/) show where both readings fit.

**Reflection question:** When you and Sanqueta give, is it planned and cheerful or last-minute and reluctant? And what are Jordyn, Elijah and Enoch learning about generosity from watching how their dad handles money, time and attention?

lessons.title: Sharing your faith: sent with good news

sources.label: Piper, All Authority in Heaven and Earth (Oct 8, 2015)
Tony Evans, What Matters to Jesus
Billy Graham, How can I witness for Christ?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 18: Sharing your faith: sent with good news**

Good morning, Greg. Matthew ends with the risen Jesus on a mountain in Galilee with his eleven disciples, and “some doubted” (v. 17). He doesn’t wait for perfect faith before giving them the job. He starts with who he is: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” Then he tells them to go and make disciples. John Piper says the courage to do that rests “on the rock solid foundation of the words — and the reality — ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.’” Because Jesus holds that authority, Piper says, the church’s mission “cannot fail.”

The goal isn’t just getting people to make a decision. It’s making disciples. Tony Evans calls Matthew 28:18–20 Jesus’ last words and describes discipleship as growing believers to maturity “so that they are then able to reproduce the process with someone else.” In his words, “Disciples are to turn around and make other disciples.” For a dad, the first disciples on your list sleep down the hall.

Romans 10 gives both the message and how it spreads. You’re saved by believing in your heart that God raised Jesus and declaring “Jesus is Lord” (v. 9), and “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (v. 13). Then Paul works backward: people can’t call on Jesus without believing, can’t believe without hearing, and can’t hear unless someone tells them (vv. 14–15). God reaches people through people. “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”

You don’t need a pulpit for this. Billy Graham’s practical advice: “Live a consistent Christ-centered life,” “be a friend and a good listener,” pray for openings, and “avoid arrogance and preachiness.” The results belong to God. Verse 16 admits not everyone believes. Our part is to tell people, and Jesus promises, “I am with you always.”

**Matthew 28:16–20 (NIV)**
16 Then the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had told them to go. 17 When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted. 18 Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. 19 Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, 20 and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”

**Romans 10:9–17 (NIV)**
9 If you declare with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. 10 For it is with your heart that you believe and are justified, and it is with your mouth that you profess your faith and are saved. 11 As Scripture says, “Anyone who believes in him will never be put to shame.” 12 For there is no difference between Jew and Gentile—the same Lord is Lord of all and richly blesses all who call on him, 13 for, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

14 How, then, can they call on the one they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the one of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone preaching to them? 15 And how can anyone preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”

16 But not all the Israelites accepted the good news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our message?” 17 Consequently, faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**

Paul didn’t have mothers specifically in mind, she says, but “few preach the gospel to our children if not us.” She adds, “The little moments moms sometimes wish away are God’s open doors to faithfully and joyfully preach the gospel.” A spilled cup, a bedtime fear or a sibling fight can turn into a conversation about Jesus.

**Lesson 19: A ready witness in ordinary life**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Jesus sent us out with good news. Today Peter and Paul show what that looks like on a normal Tuesday: at work, at the ballfield, across the fence from a neighbor. Peter was writing to believers who were being slandered for their faith, and he tells them, “Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have” (1 Pet 3:15).

How do you get ready? John Piper points out that in Greek there’s no separate verb for “be prepared.” It hangs right on the line before it: revere Christ as Lord in your heart. In his words, “Reverence the Lord Christ in your heart, and your fear will be replaced with hope.” Readiness doesn’t start with having every argument memorized. It starts with Jesus being bigger to you than whatever people might say or do.

And notice what people ask about: your hope. Piper says Peter “doesn’t say that they will ask about our faith. Or about our doctrine.” A calm, steady man under pressure makes people curious. He adds, “Very few people are deeply impressed with a lifestyle that only avoids bad behaviors.” What gets noticed is doing good, even to people who treat you badly, with joy.

Paul adds how to talk. “Make the most of every opportunity” literally means “buy up the opportunity,” as Piper puts it, and “life is a series of never to be repeated opportunities.” “Seasoned with salt,” he says, means speaking about Christ so it is “as appetizing as possible,” and the best way to get there is “to enjoy him yourself.” Paul also starts with prayer (v. 2–4): ask God to open the door before you walk through it.

You don’t need every answer. When someone asked Billy Graham what to do about a neighbor whose questions he couldn’t answer, Graham said to pray, explain the gospel simply, point him to the Bible, and “share with him what Christ means to you. You may not be able to answer all his questions, but your life will demonstrate Christ’s reality to him.” And do it the way Peter says: “with gentleness and respect.” Winning the argument and losing the person isn’t the goal.

**1 Peter 3:13–17 (NIV)**
13 Who is going to harm you if you are eager to do good? 14 But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. “Do not fear their threats; do not be frightened.” 15 But in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect, 16 keeping a clear conscience, so that those who speak maliciously against your good behavior in Christ may be ashamed of their slander. 17 For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.

**Colossians 4:2–6 (NIV)**
2 Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful. 3 And pray for us, too, that God may open a door for our message, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains. 4 Pray that I may proclaim it clearly, as I should. 5 Be wise in the way you act toward outsiders; make the most of every opportunity. 6 Let your conversation be always full of grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **1 Pet 3:14.** NIV: “Do not fear their threats; do not be frightened.” LSB: “do not fear their fear, and do not be troubled.” Peter is quoting Isaiah 8:12, and the Greek (*phobon autōn*, “their fear”) can mean the fear they try to cause in you or the things they themselves fear. The NIV picks the first sense and puts the other in its footnote (“Or *fear what they fear*”); the LSB keeps the literal, open wording.
- **1 Pet 3:15.** NIV: “in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer… the reason for the hope… with gentleness and respect.” LSB: “sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts, always being ready to make a defense… give an account for the hope… with gentleness and fear.” “Sanctify” (*hagiazō*, footnote “Set apart”) means treat him as holy; the NIV says the same idea as “revere.” “Defense” is *apologia*, a reasoned reply (where “apologetics” comes from), and the LSB footnote allows “an argument, an explanation.” The last word is *phobos*, “fear”: the NIV reads it as respect toward the person asking, while the LSB leaves it as “fear,” which many read as reverence toward God.
- **Col 4:5.** NIV: “make the most of every opportunity.” LSB: “redeeming the time.” The Greek pictures buying something up (*exagorazō*) and uses *kairos*, a fitting moment. Piper renders it literally as “Buy up the opportunity.”
- **Col 4:6.** NIV: “Let your conversation be always full of grace.” LSB: “Let your words always be with grace” (footnotes: “Lit *word*,” “Or *gracious*”). Same meaning; the LSB stays closer to the Greek.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s message [“Make a Case for Your Hope”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/make-a-case-for-your-hope) (Oct 19, 1980) on 1 Peter 3:13–16, his short article [“Why Would the World Ask About Your Hope?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/why-would-the-world-ask-about-your-hope) (Nov 3, 2015), and his message [“Walk in Wisdom Toward Those Outside”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/walk-in-wisdom-toward-those-outside) (May 29, 1988) on Colossians 4:2–6. Billy Graham’s answer on [a neighbor’s sincere questions](https://billygraham.org/answers/my-neighbor-asks-sincere-questions-about-my-faith-but-im-struggling-to-find-answers-where-can-i-find-resources-to-help-me) is a one-minute read. BibleProject’s overviews of [1 Peter](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-peter/) and [Colossians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/colossians/) show where these verses fit.

**Reflection question:** If a coworker at the VA, or Jordyn on a hard day, asked you, “How do you stay so steady?”, what would you say in two or three plain sentences about your hope in Jesus? Try saying it out loud once today.

**Lesson 20: Spiritual warfare: the full armor of God**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we talked about being a ready witness. Today Paul pulls back the curtain on what is going on behind a lot of hard days. The coworker who pushes your buttons, the tension at home, the pull toward an old habit: Paul says, “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Eph 6:12). There is a real enemy, and God doesn’t send you out to face him in a T-shirt.

Notice where the strength comes from. “Be strong in the Lord and in his mighty power” (v. 10). John Piper puts it simply: “So, it isn’t our strength.… It’s the Lord’s strength in you.” And look at the armor itself: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God. Piper says, “it’s all internal stuff.” You don’t buy this gear. You get it by staying close to Jesus and his word.

Paul says “stand” again and again (vv. 11, 13, 14). Piper, who once compared it to boxing, says, “When you’re in a battle and you’re standing, you’ve still got a chance to win.” He also warns that the devil “tailors his schemes.” What tempts a man at 25 isn’t what tempts him at 39 with a wife, three kids, a career, and a full school load. “Satan always has a new method for your new situation.” That is why the armor isn’t a one-time thing. You put it on every day.

Only one piece cuts: “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (v. 17). Jesus fought temptation in the wilderness with Scripture, and so can you. Then Paul ties it all to prayer (v. 18). Billy Graham said, “Through prayer, through the truth of God’s Word, through the Spirit, and through our fellowship with other believers we can resist the devil’s assaults.” And he added the best news of all about the enemy: “he is a defeated foe!” Jesus already won at the cross. We stand in his victory; we don’t fight for it.

**Ephesians 6:10–18 (NIV)**
10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in his mighty power. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you can take your stand against the devil’s schemes. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. 13 Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand. 14 Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness in place, 15 and with your feet fitted with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace. 16 In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. 17 Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. 18 And pray in the Spirit on all occasions with all kinds of prayers and requests. With this in mind, be alert and always keep on praying for all the Lord’s people.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Eph 6:12.** NIV: “the powers of this dark world.” LSB: “the world forces of this darkness.” The Greek word (*kosmokratoras*) literally means “world-rulers.” The NIV smooths it into plain English; the LSB keeps the sense that these powers try to rule over a dark world system.
- **Eph 6:14.** NIV: “with the belt of truth buckled around your waist.” LSB: “having girded your loins with truth.” Same picture. A soldier in a long tunic tucked it up into his belt so he could move and fight. The NIV gives the modern image; the LSB keeps the older, more literal idiom.
- **Eph 6:15.** NIV: “the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace.” LSB: “the preparation of the gospel of peace.” The Greek word (*hetoimasia*) can mean either readiness or preparation. Piper reads it as feet “ready to move with the gospel.”
- **Eph 6:17–18.** NIV starts a new sentence: “And pray in the Spirit on all occasions.” LSB keeps one sentence: “the word of God, praying at all times.” In Greek, “praying” is a participle that hangs on the call to stand and take up the armor, so prayer isn’t a seventh piece of gear but the way the whole armor is worn. The NIV breaks it up for easier reading.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s message [“Spiritual Warfare and Prayer”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/spiritual-warfare-and-prayer) (Nov 8, 1999) walks through Ephesians 6:10–20, and his message [“Ready to Move with the Gospel of Peace”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ready-to-move-with-the-gospel-of-peace) (May 15, 1988) looks closely at verse 15. Billy Graham’s short answer on [spiritual warfare](https://billygraham.org/answers/our-pastor-spoke-on-spiritual-warfare-talking-about-how-the-devil-and-god-are-at-war-with-each-other-is-this-true) is a one-minute read. BibleProject’s overview of [Ephesians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/ephesians/) shows where this passage fits.

**Reflection question:** Where is the enemy most likely to aim at you this week, as a man, a husband, and a father, and what one verse will you carry into that spot as your sword?

**Lesson 20: Spiritual warfare: the full armor of God**

Good morning. Paul ends his letter to the Ephesians by pulling back the curtain: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Eph 6:12). The short temper at bedtime, the lie that you’re failing your kids, the distance that creeps into a marriage: there is a real enemy behind more of it than we like to think, and God doesn’t send you out to face him unprotected.

Tilly Dillehay, a pastor’s wife and homeschooling mother of four, writes that in this war “the home is located in the heat of the battle, and we mothers are in combat roles.” She says, “Mothers are stewards of the home, superintendents of the precious time called childhood, where Satan hopes to do his worst work — and often sees worse defeat.” One of his oldest tricks is still the question he asked Eve: “Did God really say . . . ?” Her answer: “Waiting for truth to find us is not sufficient; we must actively resist his lies by feeding ourselves with what God has said.”

That is what the armor is. Gloria Furman says the belt of truth “encircles you with the confident protection of knowing who God is, what Christ has done for you, and who you are” in Christ. And the breastplate is Christ’s righteousness, not yours; she calls it “one-size-fits-all-who-believe.” On the days you feel you have nothing left, you aren’t standing in your own goodness. As John Piper says, “It’s the Lord’s strength in you.”

Only one piece cuts: “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (v. 17). And Paul ties it all to prayer (v. 18). Billy Graham said, “Through prayer, through the truth of God’s Word, through the Spirit, and through our fellowship with other believers we can resist the devil’s assaults.” He also reminded us that the devil “is a defeated foe!” Jesus already won at the cross. We stand in his victory.

**Ephesians 6:10–18 (NIV)**
10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in his mighty power. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you can take your stand against the devil’s schemes. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. 13 Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand. 14 Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness in place, 15 and with your feet fitted with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace. 16 In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. 17 Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. 18 And pray in the Spirit on all occasions with all kinds of prayers and requests. With this in mind, be alert and always keep on praying for all the Lord’s people.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Eph 6:12.** NIV: “the powers of this dark world.” LSB: “the world forces of this darkness.” The Greek word (*kosmokratoras*) literally means “world-rulers.” The NIV smooths it into plain English; the LSB keeps the sense that these powers try to rule over a dark world system.
- **Eph 6:14.** NIV: “with the belt of truth buckled around your waist.” LSB: “having girded your loins with truth.” Same picture. A soldier in a long tunic tucked it up into his belt so he could move and fight. The NIV gives the modern image; the LSB keeps the older, more literal idiom.
- **Eph 6:15.** NIV: “the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace.” LSB: “the preparation of the gospel of peace.” The Greek word (*hetoimasia*) can mean either readiness or preparation. Piper reads it as feet “ready to move with the gospel.”
- **Eph 6:17–18.** NIV starts a new sentence: “And pray in the Spirit on all occasions.” LSB keeps one sentence: “the word of God, praying at all times.” In Greek, “praying” is a participle that hangs on the call to stand and take up the armor, so prayer isn’t a seventh piece of gear but the way the whole armor is worn. The NIV breaks it up for easier reading.

**Go deeper:** Tilly Dillehay’s [“How Satan Undoes a Mom”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how-satan-undoes-a-mom) (Desiring God, Oct 19, 2021) names several of the enemy’s favorite attacks on mothers, and Gloria Furman’s [“A Pregnant Woman’s Defense Against the Schemes of the Devil”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-pregnant-womans-defense-against-the-schemes-of-the-devil) (May 26, 2012) walks through each piece of the armor. Piper’s message [“Spiritual Warfare and Prayer”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/spiritual-warfare-and-prayer) (Nov 8, 1999) and BibleProject’s overview of [Ephesians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/ephesians/) go further.

**Reflection question:** Which “Did God really say . . . ?” whisper do you hear most often as a woman, a wife, or a mother, and what verse will you answer it with this week?

**Lesson 21: The enemy is real, but greater is He who is in you**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we put on the armor. Today Peter tells us how the enemy hunts, and John tells us why we don’t have to be afraid of him. Peter doesn’t sugarcoat it: “Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour” (1 Pet 5:8). But John answers with one of the most freeing lines in the Bible: “the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world” (1 John 4:4).

What is the lion after? John Piper says, “The two great enemies of our souls are sin and Satan,” and the only way Satan can really hurt a believer is by pulling him into sin and keeping him from repenting. “Satan cannot condemn us or rob us of eternal life.” So Peter’s answer is simple: “Resist him, standing firm in the faith” (v. 9). Piper puts it this way: “The way to thwart the devil is to strengthen the very thing he is trying most to destroy — your faith.”

Notice the order, too. Before the lion shows up, Peter says to humble yourself and cast your anxiety on God (vv. 6–7). Marshall Segal points out that the devil “spends a lot of his time among the suffering,” looking for the tired and hurting. A man carrying stress alone is easy prey. “Humility refuses to treat God like an incompetent or unsympathetic boss, but comes to him, even in suffering, as a compassionate and invested Father.” Handing God the worry about work, money, school, or the kids isn’t weakness. It is how you stay alert.

And you don’t fight in your own power. Billy Graham said, “You have a power within you when you come to Christ that is greater than the devil and all the world around. And that power is the Holy Spirit.” As Segal says, “You are at war, but you are not alone.” Peter ends with a promise, not a pep talk: after a little while, “the God of all grace… will himself restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast” (v. 10).

**1 John 4:4 (NIV)**
4 You, dear children, are from God and have overcome them, because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.

**1 Peter 5:6–11 (NIV)**
6 Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, that he may lift you up in due time. 7 Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you. 8 Be alert and of sober mind. Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour. 9 Resist him, standing firm in the faith, because you know that the family of believers throughout the world is undergoing the same kind of sufferings. 10 And the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, after you have suffered a little while, will himself restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast. 11 To him be the power for ever and ever. Amen.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **1 John 4:4.** NIV: “the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.” LSB: “greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.” Same meaning. The LSB keeps the familiar older word order (the line many of us learned from the KJV) and capitalizes “He” to show it is God. NIV “dear children,” LSB “little children”: John’s tender word for the believers in his care.
- **1 Pet 5:7.** NIV: “Cast all your anxiety on him.” LSB: “casting all your anxiety on Him.” In Greek, “casting” is a participle tied to “humble yourselves” in verse 6. The LSB keeps that link: handing God your worries is how you humble yourself under his hand. The NIV makes it a separate command, which is still true but loses a little of the connection.
- **1 Pet 5:8.** NIV: “Your enemy the devil.” LSB: “Your adversary, the devil.” The Greek word (*antidikos*) is the word for an opponent in a lawsuit, an accuser. The LSB keeps that flavor; the NIV gives the general sense.
- **1 Pet 5:10.** NIV: “restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast.” LSB: “restore, strengthen, confirm, and ground you.” Peter uses four verbs; the LSB keeps all four, and the last one pictures a house set on a foundation.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s short devotional [“Satan’s Strategy and Your Defense”](https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/satans-strategy-and-your-defense) is a three-minute read on 1 Peter 5:8–9. Marshall Segal’s [“Satan Hunts Among the Hurting”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/satan-hunts-among-the-hurting) walks through verses 6–10. Billy Graham’s one-minute message [“Yes or No”](https://billygraham.org/minutes/yes-or-no) is on 1 John 4:4. BibleProject’s overviews of [1–3 John](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-3-john/) and [1 Peter](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-peter/) show where these verses fit.

**Reflection question:** What worry are you carrying by yourself right now that could make you easy prey, and what would it look like to cast it on God today and tell Sanqueta about it, so you can lead your family alert instead of worn down?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 22: Identity in Christ: a new creation**

Good morning, Greg. The last two days we looked at the enemy. Today we look at who you are, because a man who forgets who he is will fight the wrong battles. Paul says, “if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!” (2 Cor 5:17). And he says it about himself: “I have been crucified with Christ and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal 2:20).

Most of us know what Jesus did for us: our sins are forgiven. John Piper says we also need to know what happened to us. He says Paul stresses “what happened to us, what changed in us” as the key to living the Christian life. What died? Piper says the old self in its rebellion: “God killed my hostility to God.” What came alive? “The new self of the Christian is the God-loving, son-of-God-trusting, Christ-inhabited self.”

That changes how you see yourself. You are a veteran, a nurse, a manager, a student, a husband, and a dad, and those are good things. But none of them is the deepest thing about you. The deepest thing is that you are in Christ, and he lives in you. A new title, a grade, or a rough day at work can’t add to that or take it away.

Does that mean you won’t struggle? No. Billy Graham told a new believer, “You’re no longer the same person you once were; you have been given a new nature,” and in the same answer he said the old pull doesn’t vanish overnight. “The good news is, we don’t need to fight this battle alone!” And “the nearer we are to Him, the harder it is for temptations to touch us.” Notice, too, that Paul says new people get a new job: “We are therefore Christ’s ambassadors” (2 Cor 5:20). A new man in Christ represents his King at home first.

**2 Corinthians 5:14–21 (NIV)**
14 For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that one died for all, and therefore all died. 15 And he died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and was raised again. 16 So from now on we regard no one from a worldly point of view. Though we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer. 17 Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here! 18 All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: 19 that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ, not counting people’s sins against them. And he has committed to us the message of reconciliation. 20 We are therefore Christ’s ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us. We implore you on Christ’s behalf: Be reconciled to God. 21 God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

**Galatians 2:20 (NIV)**
20 I have been crucified with Christ and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I now live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **2 Cor 5:14.** NIV: “Christ’s love compels us.” LSB: “the love of Christ controls us.” The Greek verb (*synechō*) means to press in on, hold, or grip. Both translations are fair: Christ’s love both drives us and holds us.
- **2 Cor 5:17.** NIV: “the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!” LSB: “he is a new creation; the old things passed away; behold, new things have come.” Paul’s Greek is very compressed and has no verb: literally, “if anyone in Christ, new creation.” The LSB fills it in as a statement about the person (“he is”); the NIV fills it in as a statement about God’s new world breaking in (“has come”). Both are true, and the NIV footnote gives the other reading. The LSB also keeps Paul’s “behold,” a word that says, “Look at this!”
- **2 Cor 5:21.** NIV: “him who had no sin.” LSB: “Him who knew no sin.” The Greek says “knew.” Jesus never knew sin from the inside, by doing it. The NIV gives the meaning; the LSB keeps the word.
- **Gal 2:20.** NIV: “The life I now live in the body.” LSB: “the life which I now live in the flesh.” Paul’s word is *sarx*, “flesh,” but here it simply means his ordinary physical life, not the sinful nature, so the NIV says “body” to avoid confusion. NIV “gave himself for me”; LSB “gave Himself up for me,” which keeps the sense of handing himself over.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s [“My Flesh Was Crucified — So Why Do I Still Sin?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/my-flesh-was-crucified-so-why-do-i-still-sin) (Ask Pastor John, Mar 11, 2022) explains what died and what came alive when you trusted Christ. Billy Graham’s short answer on [temptation after coming to Christ](https://billygraham.org/answers/i-thought-that-when-i-gave-my-life-to-jesus-i-wouldnt-have-any-more-problems-with-temptation) is a one-minute read. BibleProject’s overviews of [2 Corinthians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/2-corinthians/) and [Galatians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/galatians/) show where these verses fit.

**Reflection question:** Which title or role (veteran, nurse, manager, student, provider) are you most tempted to lean on for your worth, and how would remembering “Christ lives in me” change the way you lead your wife and children this week?

**Lesson 23: Who you are in Christ, blessed with every spiritual blessing**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we saw that in Christ you are a new creation. Today Paul shows what that new man has been given. Ephesians 1:3–14 is one long sentence in Greek, as if Paul can’t stop to breathe: God “has blessed us in the heavenly realms with every spiritual blessing in Christ” (v. 3). Not some blessings. Every one.

Look at the list. You were chosen “before the creation of the world” (v. 4). You were adopted (v. 5). You have “redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (v. 7). You were “marked in him with a seal, the promised Holy Spirit” (v. 13). And notice the little phrase that keeps coming back: “in him,” “in Christ.” John Piper points out that Paul is thinking of us as “undeserving of these blessings”; God sees us in relation to Christ “so that we may have every blessing that heaven has to offer, though we don’t deserve them.”

Chris Bruno, writing for Desiring God, shows how the whole Trinity is at work here: the Father planned it, the Son purchased it, and the Spirit preserves it. He calls the Spirit our “salvation sealer,” like the sealant on a wooden deck, except “we don’t need to reapply the Spirit every three years.” In his words, “The Father, the Son, and the Spirit have conspired since eternity past to save you from your sins.”

Billy Graham used a picture every father understands: “When a child is born, he or she becomes part of a family.” A child doesn’t stop being yours because he has a bad day. “And when we come to Christ, we become members of a new family — the family of God.” That is your standing with God, and it is the same security you want Jordyn, Eli, and Enoch to feel with you.

Christians have long discussed how God’s choosing (vv. 4–5, 11) fits with our believing (v. 13). Reformed teachers like Piper stress God’s sovereign choice; many other Baptists, along with Methodists and others, stress God’s foreknowledge and our free response. All of them agree on what Paul celebrates here: salvation starts with God’s grace, not with our résumé.

**Ephesians 1:3–14 (NIV)**
3 Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in the heavenly realms with every spiritual blessing in Christ. 4 For he chose us in him before the creation of the world to be holy and blameless in his sight. In love 5 he predestined us for adoption to sonship through Jesus Christ, in accordance with his pleasure and will— 6 to the praise of his glorious grace, which he has freely given us in the One he loves. 7 In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, in accordance with the riches of God’s grace 8 that he lavished on us. With all wisdom and understanding, 9 he made known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in Christ, 10 to be put into effect when the times reach their fulfillment—to bring unity to all things in heaven and on earth under Christ. 11 In him we were also chosen, having been predestined according to the plan of him who works out everything in conformity with the purpose of his will, 12 in order that we, who were the first to put our hope in Christ, might be for the praise of his glory. 13 And you also were included in Christ when you heard the message of truth, the gospel of your salvation. When you believed, you were marked in him with a seal, the promised Holy Spirit, 14 who is a deposit guaranteeing our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God’s possession—to the praise of his glory.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Eph 1:4–5.** NIV: “to be holy and blameless in his sight. In love he predestined us.” LSB: “that we would be holy and blameless before Him in love, by predestining us.” Ancient Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so “in love” can go with verse 4 (we are made holy and blameless in love) or with verse 5 (God predestined us in love). Piper says both are true and concludes, “Just enjoy them both.”
- **Eph 1:5.** NIV: “adoption to sonship.” LSB: “adoption as sons.” Same Greek word (*huiothesia*), a legal term for taking someone in as a full son and heir. It includes daughters; Paul’s point is that every believer gets the full rights of an heir.
- **Eph 1:11.** NIV: “In him we were also chosen.” LSB: “In Him, we also have been made an inheritance.” The Greek verb (*eklērōthēmen*) comes from the word for a lot or portion. It can mean we were chosen (as if by lot) or that we became God’s own inheritance, his treasured portion. The NIV takes the first sense; the LSB the second.
- **Eph 1:14.** NIV: “a deposit guaranteeing our inheritance.” LSB: “given as a pledge of our inheritance.” The word (*arrabōn*) means a down payment, the first installment that guarantees the rest is coming. The Spirit in you now is God’s promise of everything still to come.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s message [“The Gospel Promises True Prosperity”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-gospel-promises-true-prosperity) (Sep 25, 2015) works slowly through Ephesians 1:3–6. Chris Bruno’s [“Planned. Purchased. Preserved.”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/planned-purchased-preserved) (Desiring God, Sep 16, 2018) is a short read on the Trinity in this passage. Billy Graham’s answer [“In Christ, we become members of the family of God”](https://billygraham.org/answers/in-christ-we-become-members-of-the-family-of-god) takes one minute. BibleProject’s overview of [Ephesians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/ephesians/) shows where this passage fits.

**Reflection question:** Which one of these blessings (chosen, adopted, forgiven, sealed) do you most need to believe about yourself this week, and how could you show your children that same kind of secure, steady love as their father?

**Lesson 24: Sanctification: growing in holiness**

Good morning, Greg. We’ve seen who you are in Christ. Now Paul talks about growing into it. He doesn’t leave God’s will vague: “It is God’s will that you should be sanctified” (1 Thess 4:3). Sanctification means being made holy, set apart for God, little by little becoming in practice what you already are in Christ. And Hebrews adds, “Make every effort… to be holy; without holiness no one will see the Lord” (Heb 12:14).

That verse can sound scary. Billy Graham explained it with a farmer coming in from the field, covered in mud, invited to dinner with the governor. We can’t clean ourselves up enough. “But when we come to Christ, God takes those rags away, and He clothes us instead with the perfect holiness of Christ.” Then he said, “Yes, without Christ’s holiness we’ll never see God—but with it we will!” We pursue holiness because we have been made holy, not to earn it.

Paul gets specific fast: sexual purity (vv. 3–6). John Piper preached this text and was plain about where many men are tempted today, including pornography. His strategy comes straight from verse 5, where pagans act this way because they “do not know God.” So, he says, “knowing God is the path to sexual purity,” and “We defeat the deceitful pleasures of lust with the superior pleasures of knowing God.” He adds that “Controlling your body in purity is a matter of honor,” honor toward your wife and toward other women.

Holiness isn’t dull. Scott Hubbard writes, “True holiness, however, knows nothing of blandness and cannot abide boredom.” It is “breathtakingly beautiful.” He quotes a prayer worth borrowing from Robert Murray M’Cheyne: “Lord, make me as holy as a pardoned sinner can be made.” And Paul says the God who calls you to this “gives you his Holy Spirit” (v. 8). As Piper puts it, “You are not left to yourself to win this war.”

**1 Thessalonians 4:1–8 (NIV)**
1 As for other matters, brothers and sisters, we instructed you how to live in order to please God, as in fact you are living. Now we ask you and urge you in the Lord Jesus to do this more and more. 2 For you know what instructions we gave you by the authority of the Lord Jesus. 3 It is God’s will that you should be sanctified: that you should avoid sexual immorality; 4 that each of you should learn to control your own body in a way that is holy and honorable, 5 not in passionate lust like the pagans, who do not know God; 6 and that in this matter no one should wrong or take advantage of a brother or sister. The Lord will punish all those who commit such sins, as we told you and warned you before. 7 For God did not call us to be impure, but to live a holy life. 8 Therefore, anyone who rejects this instruction does not reject a human being but God, the very God who gives you his Holy Spirit.

**Hebrews 12:14 (NIV)**
14 Make every effort to live in peace with everyone and to be holy; without holiness no one will see the Lord.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **1 Thess 4:1.** NIV: “how to live in order to please God.” LSB: “how you ought to walk and please God.” Paul’s verb is *peripateō*, “walk,” a common Bible picture for a whole way of life. The NIV gives the meaning; the LSB keeps the picture of daily steps.
- **1 Thess 4:3, 7.** NIV: “It is God’s will that you should be sanctified… to live a holy life.” LSB: “this is the will of God, your sanctification… in sanctification.” Paul uses the same noun (*hagiasmos*) in verses 3, 4, and 7. The LSB keeps it as “sanctification” each time so you can see the thread; the NIV varies the wording for smoother English.
- **1 Thess 4:4.** NIV: “learn to control your own body.” LSB: “know how to possess his own vessel.” The Greek word *skeuos* means “vessel.” Most take it as your own body (as the NIV does); some take it as a man’s wife. The LSB keeps the literal word and leaves the choice to the reader.
- **Heb 12:14.** NIV: “Make every effort… to be holy.” LSB: “Pursue… the sanctification.” The verb (*diōkō*) means to chase or run after, and the noun is the same *hagiasmos* from 1 Thessalonians. Holiness isn’t something you drift into; you pursue it.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s message [“This Is the Will of God for You”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/this-is-the-will-of-god-for-you) (Oct 13, 2002) is a direct, practical sermon on 1 Thessalonians 4:1–8. Scott Hubbard’s [“Does God Delight in Me?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/does-god-delight-in-me) is on why holiness pleases God. Billy Graham’s answer [“Is believing in Jesus enough for me to be saved?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/is-believing-in-jesus-enough-for-me-to-be-saved) explains Hebrews 12:14. BibleProject’s overviews of [1 Thessalonians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-thessalonians/) and [Hebrews](https://bibleproject.com/videos/hebrews/) show where these verses fit.

**Reflection question:** What is one area (your eyes, your phone, your temper, your words) where you need to pursue holiness this week, and what practical step will you take so your wife and children see a man growing more like Christ?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 25: The greatest commandment: love God and love your neighbor**

Good morning, Greg. Happy Thanksgiving. An expert in the law tried to trap Jesus with a question: “which is the greatest commandment in the Law?” (Matt 22:36). There were hundreds to choose from. Jesus gave two: love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself. “All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments” (v. 40).

Jesus answers by quoting Deuteronomy 6:5, part of the Shema (“Hear, O Israel”), which faithful Jews recited morning and evening, “when you lie down and when you get up” (Deut 6:7). To this day many observant Jewish families pray it daily and fix it to their doorframes in a small case called a mezuzah (v. 9). Jesus takes that familiar prayer and puts it at the center of everything.

John Piper says it plainly: “The greatest and most important thing you can do is love God—love GOD—with all your heart and soul and mind.” And “Everything else in the Old Testament in some sense depends on these two commandments.” Then he admits that the second one is overwhelming: “it seems to demand that I tear the skin off my body and wrap it around another person,” wanting for them everything you want for yourself. That takes “Something supernatural.” It takes God’s love filling you first.

Who is your neighbor? Billy Graham starts close to home: “Your neighbor is the person who is close to you. Your boyfriend, girlfriend, husband, wife, mother, father, person next door.” For you that means Sanqueta first, then Jordyn, Eli, and Enoch, then the people at work and church. And he points to the Good Samaritan, who stopped, bound up a stranger’s wounds, and paid for his care: “He didn’t just love him and leave him.”

Deuteronomy 6 gives fathers a simple plan for passing this on: talk about God’s words “when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (v. 7). For your family, that might be the drive to volleyball practice, the ride home from a ballgame, or the dinner table today.

**Matthew 22:34–40 (NIV)**
34 Hearing that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, the Pharisees got together. 35 One of them, an expert in the law, tested him with this question: 36 “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the Law?” 37 Jesus replied: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ 38 This is the first and greatest commandment. 39 And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ 40 All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”

**Deuteronomy 6:4–9 (NIV)**
4 Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. 5 Love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. 6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 8 Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 9 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Deut 6:4–5.** NIV: “The LORD our God, the LORD is one.” LSB: “Yahweh is our God, Yahweh is one!” The Hebrew here is God’s personal name, YHWH. Most English Bibles, including the NIV, follow an old Jewish custom and print it as “LORD” in small capitals; the LSB prints the name itself, “Yahweh,” throughout the Old Testament.
- **Deut 6:5.** NIV: “with all your strength.” LSB: “with all your might.” The Hebrew word (*me’od*) usually means “very” or “exceedingly,” so here it is something like “with all your muchness”: everything you have. Jesus quotes the verse with “mind” (Matt 22:37), drawing out that loving God includes how we think.
- **Deut 6:7.** NIV: “Impress them on your children.” LSB: “You shall teach them diligently to your sons.” The Hebrew verb (*shanan*) means to sharpen, and here it carries the idea of repeating something until it sticks. “Sons” (*banim*) is the common word for children, so the NIV says “children.”
- **Matt 22:38.** NIV: “the first and greatest commandment.” LSB: “the great and foremost commandment.” The Greek says “great and first.” The NIV reads “great” as “greatest,” since that’s the point of the question; the LSB keeps the plain wording.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s message [“Love Your Neighbor as Yourself, Part 1”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/love-your-neighbor-as-yourself-part-1) (Apr 30, 1995) is a careful walk through Matthew 22:34–40. Billy Graham’s [devotional on the Good Samaritan](https://billygraham.org/lp/75-day-devotional-day-53) answers “Who is my neighbor?” BibleProject’s overviews of [Matthew 14–28](https://bibleproject.com/videos/matthew-14-28/) and [Deuteronomy](https://bibleproject.com/videos/deuteronomy/) show where these passages fit.

**Reflection question:** As a husband and father, where could you “talk about” God’s words this week (in the car, at the table, at bedtime), and what is one concrete way you will love the neighbor closest to you, your wife, today?

**Lesson 25: The greatest commandment: love God and love your neighbor**

Good morning, and happy Thanksgiving. An expert in the law tried to trap Jesus with a question: “which is the greatest commandment in the Law?” (Matt 22:36). Jesus gave two: love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself. “All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments” (v. 40).

Jesus answers by quoting Deuteronomy 6:5, part of the Shema (“Hear, O Israel”), which faithful Jews recited morning and evening, “when you lie down and when you get up” (Deut 6:7). To this day many observant Jewish families pray it daily and fix it to their doorframes in a small case called a mezuzah (v. 9). Jesus takes that familiar prayer and puts it at the center of everything.

Jen Wilkin writes that many women’s gatherings focus on self-worth, but “Our primary problem as Christian women is not that we lack self-worth, not that we lack a sense of significance or purpose. It’s that we lack awe.” She notes that people who experience awe become less self-focused, and “In marveling at something greater than ourselves, we become more able to reach out to others.” That, she says, “begins to sound a lot like the greatest commandments.” Her plea to women teachers: “Don’t tell me who I am until you have caused me to gaze in awe at ‘I Am.’” Love for God comes first, and love for others grows out of it. As she puts it, “Awe yields self-forgetfulness.”

Who is your neighbor? Billy Graham starts close to home: “Your neighbor is the person who is close to you. Your boyfriend, girlfriend, husband, wife, mother, father, person next door.” He points to the Good Samaritan, who stopped and cared for a stranger: “He didn’t just love him and leave him.” John Piper admits loving others as yourself takes “Something supernatural.” It takes God’s love filling you first.

Deuteronomy 6 gives parents a simple plan for passing this on: talk about God’s words “when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (v. 7). That might be the drive to practice, bedtime, or the table today.

**Matthew 22:34–40 (NIV)**
34 Hearing that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, the Pharisees got together. 35 One of them, an expert in the law, tested him with this question: 36 “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the Law?” 37 Jesus replied: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ 38 This is the first and greatest commandment. 39 And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ 40 All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”

**Deuteronomy 6:4–9 (NIV)**
4 Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. 5 Love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength. 6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 8 Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 9 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Deut 6:4–5.** NIV: “The LORD our God, the LORD is one.” LSB: “Yahweh is our God, Yahweh is one!” The Hebrew here is God’s personal name, YHWH. Most English Bibles, including the NIV, follow an old Jewish custom and print it as “LORD” in small capitals; the LSB prints the name itself, “Yahweh,” throughout the Old Testament.
- **Deut 6:5.** NIV: “with all your strength.” LSB: “with all your might.” The Hebrew word (*me’od*) usually means “very” or “exceedingly,” so here it is something like “with all your muchness”: everything you have. Jesus quotes the verse with “mind” (Matt 22:37), drawing out that loving God includes how we think.
- **Deut 6:7.** NIV: “Impress them on your children.” LSB: “You shall teach them diligently to your sons.” The Hebrew verb (*shanan*) means to sharpen, and here it carries the idea of repeating something until it sticks. “Sons” (*banim*) is the common word for children, so the NIV says “children.”
- **Matt 22:38.** NIV: “the first and greatest commandment.” LSB: “the great and foremost commandment.” The Greek says “great and first.” The NIV reads “great” as “greatest,” since that’s the point of the question; the LSB keeps the plain wording.

**Go deeper:** Jen Wilkin’s [“Women, Trade Self-Worth for Awe and Wonder”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/women-trade-self-worth-for-awe-and-wonder) (Desiring God, Jul 14, 2016) is a short, bracing read. Piper’s message [“Love Your Neighbor as Yourself, Part 1”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/love-your-neighbor-as-yourself-part-1) (Apr 30, 1995) and Billy Graham’s [devotional on the Good Samaritan](https://billygraham.org/lp/75-day-devotional-day-53) go further. BibleProject’s overviews of [Matthew 14–28](https://bibleproject.com/videos/matthew-14-28/) and [Deuteronomy](https://bibleproject.com/videos/deuteronomy/) show where these passages fit.

**Reflection question:** What would it look like this week to start your day in awe of God before you turn to your husband, your children, and your work, and who is one “neighbor” close to you whom you will love in a concrete way today?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 26: Forgiving others as you have been forgiven**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday was about loving God and your neighbor. Today Jesus shows where that love gets tested most: forgiving people who wrong you. Peter thought he was being generous: “Up to seven times?” Jesus answered, “not seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matt 18:21–22). Billy Graham explained, “What Jesus meant by this expression was that we ought to forgive others without limit.”

Then Jesus told a story. A servant owed a king a debt he could never repay, and the king canceled it. That same servant walked out and choked a man who owed him a few months’ pay. John Piper says the point is not that we earn heaven by forgiving, but that “holding fast to an unforgiving spirit proves that we do not trust Christ.” In his words, “If we trust him, we will not be able to take forgiveness from his hand for our million dollar debt and withhold it from our ten dollar debtor.”

Where do you get the power? Paul says, “forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you” (Eph 4:32). Piper puts it this way: “God’s forgiveness is underneath ours and creates it and supports it.” Billy Graham adds, “No, they may not deserve it—but neither did we when God forgave us.” And holding on costs you: unforgiven hurt, he warned, becomes “like a festering wound in our minds and souls.”

What does forgiveness look like in practice? Piper borrows an old definition from the Puritan Thomas Watson: we forgive “When we strive against all thoughts of revenge; when we will not do our enemies mischief, but wish well to them, grieve at their calamities, pray for them, seek reconciliation with them.” That applies at work, with family after a long holiday weekend, and at home. Your kids learn forgiveness by watching how fast Dad says, “I’m sorry,” and how fully he says, “I forgive you.”

One more thing Billy Graham was careful to say: forgiving someone doesn’t always mean everything goes back to the way it was. Even after Jacob and Esau reconciled, he noted, “it’s hard to have the same relationship we once had.” Forgiveness cancels the debt and lets go of revenge. Trust is rebuilt over time, and forgiving never means staying in harm’s way.

**Matthew 18:21–35 (NIV)**
21 Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother or sister who sins against me? Up to seven times?” 22 Jesus answered, “I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times. 23 “Therefore, the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants. 24 As he began the settlement, a man who owed him ten thousand bags of gold was brought to him. 25 Since he was not able to pay, the master ordered that he and his wife and his children and all that he had be sold to repay the debt. 26 “At this the servant fell on his knees before him. ‘Be patient with me,’ he begged, ‘and I will pay back everything.’ 27 The servant’s master took pity on him, canceled the debt and let him go. 28 “But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred silver coins. He grabbed him and began to choke him. ‘Pay back what you owe me!’ he demanded. 29 “His fellow servant fell to his knees and begged him, ‘Be patient with me, and I will pay it back.’ 30 “But he refused. Instead, he went off and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay the debt. 31 When the other servants saw what had happened, they were outraged and went and told their master everything that had happened. 32 “Then the master called the servant in. ‘You wicked servant,’ he said, ‘I canceled all that debt of yours because you begged me to. 33 Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?’ 34 In anger his master handed him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should pay back all he owed. 35 “This is how my heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother or sister from your heart.”

**Ephesians 4:31–32 (NIV)**
31 Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, brawling and slander, along with every form of malice. 32 Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Matt 18:22.** NIV: “seventy-seven times.” LSB: “seventy times seven.” The Greek can be read either way. “Seventy-seven” echoes Genesis 4:24, where Lamech boasted of taking revenge seventy-seven times; Jesus turns that boast upside down. Either way the point is the same: stop counting.
- **Matt 18:24, 28.** NIV: “ten thousand bags of gold” and “a hundred silver coins.” LSB: “ten thousand talents” and “one hundred denarii.” The LSB keeps the original money words. A denarius was about a day’s pay, so the second debt was a few months’ wages; a single talent was worth roughly twenty years of a laborer’s wages, so ten thousand talents was a debt no one could ever repay. That is the gap between what we owe God and what others owe us.
- **Matt 18:23–35.** NIV: “servants.” LSB: “slaves.” The Greek word (*doulos*) can mean either. The LSB uses “slave” to stress that the man owed his master everything.
- **Eph 4:32.** NIV: “forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.” LSB: “graciously forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has graciously forgiven you.” Paul’s verb (*charizomai*) comes from the word for grace (*charis*). The LSB adds “graciously” to bring that out: forgiveness is grace passed along.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s message [“As We Forgive Our Debtors”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/as-we-forgive-our-debtors) (Mar 20, 1994) walks through Matthew 18 and gives Watson’s full definition. Billy Graham’s short answers on [forgiving without limit](https://billygraham.org/answers/how-many-times-does-god-expect-us-to-forgive-someone-who-hurts-us) and on [whether forgiving means forgetting](https://billygraham.org/answers/if-i-forgive-someone-does-that-mean-i-have-to-forget-the-hurt-they-caused-and-act-like-everythings-back-to-normal) are one-minute reads. BibleProject’s overviews of [Matthew 14–28](https://bibleproject.com/videos/matthew-14-28/) and [Ephesians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/ephesians/) show where these passages fit.

**Reflection question:** Is there anyone (a coworker, a family member, or someone in your own home) you are still holding a debt over, and what would it look like this week to cancel it before God and, as a husband and father, show your family what forgiveness looks like?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 27: Spiritual gifts and one body in Christ**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday was about forgiving others the way God forgave you. Today Paul shows what forgiven people are put into: a body. “Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it” (1 Cor 12:27). God doesn’t save you to sit alone. He places you in his church and gives you something to do there.

Every Christian has at least one gift. Paul says, “Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Cor 12:7). John Piper puts it simply: “To be a member of the body of Christ is to have a role in the body.” That role may be “not flashy, not prominent, but essential.” Piper even points out that God sometimes uses weakness itself, saying “the gift that some people have in the body of Christ is to be weak and needy so that others may have opportunity to show them special care.”

The trap Paul warns about is comparing. Some in Corinth felt useless because they were not like others; some felt they did not need anyone. Billy Graham said, “We don’t all have the same gift, and we shouldn’t envy someone who has different gifts from us.” How do you find yours? Pray, serve, and listen. He suggested asking, “What can you do that others find difficult, or don’t want to do? What do others say about your abilities?”

Your gifts are not only for Sunday. Billy Graham wrote, “Are you a parent? Ask God to help you raise your children wisely and teach them about God and His love for them.” The leadership, mercy, and teaching you use at work and with patients are ways God can serve others through you, and your home is the first place your family sees them. His advice is good for any man who feels ordinary: “Don’t worry about the gifts you don’t have, but ask God to use you right where you are—and He will.”

A brief note: Bible-believing Christians disagree about whether some gifts on Paul’s list, like tongues and prophecy, still work the same way today. Pentecostal and charismatic churches emphasize them; many Baptist churches are more cautious. But that debate is not Paul’s main point here. His point is that every believer has been given something by the Spirit, and every part is needed.

**1 Corinthians 12:4–27 (NIV)**
4 There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit distributes them. 5 There are different kinds of service, but the same Lord. 6 There are different kinds of working, but in all of them and in everyone it is the same God at work. 7 Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good. 8 To one there is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge by means of the same Spirit, 9 to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, 10 to another miraculous powers, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in different kinds of tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. 11 All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, and he distributes them to each one, just as he determines. 12 Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ. 13 For we were all baptized by one Spirit so as to form one body—whether Jews or Gentiles, slave or free—and we were all given the one Spirit to drink. 14 Even so the body is not made up of one part but of many. 15 Now if the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” it would not for that reason stop being part of the body. 16 And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” it would not for that reason stop being part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But in fact God has placed the parts in the body, every one of them, just as he wanted them to be. 19 If they were all one part, where would the body be? 20 As it is, there are many parts, but one body. 21 The eye cannot say to the hand, “I don’t need you!” And the head cannot say to the feet, “I don’t need you!” 22 On the contrary, those parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, 23 and the parts that we think are less honorable we treat with special honor. And the parts that are unpresentable are treated with special modesty, 24 while our presentable parts need no special treatment. But God has put the body together, giving greater honor to the parts that lacked it, 25 so that there should be no division in the body, but that its parts should have equal concern for each other. 26 If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it. 27 Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.

**Romans 12:3–8 (NIV)**
3 For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgment, in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you. 4 For just as each of us has one body with many members, and these members do not all have the same function, 5 so in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others. 6 We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. If your gift is prophesying, then prophesy in accordance with your faith; 7 if it is serving, then serve; if it is teaching, then teach; 8 if it is to encourage, then give encouragement; if it is giving, then give generously; if it is to lead, do it diligently; if it is to show mercy, do it cheerfully.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **1 Cor 12:5.** NIV: “different kinds of service.” LSB: “varieties of ministries.” The Greek word (*diakonia*) means service or ministry. The LSB’s “ministries” is a reminder that ministry is not only the pastor’s job; every act of service done for Christ’s body counts.
- **1 Cor 12:7.** NIV: “for the common good.” LSB: “for what is profitable.” The Greek word means what benefits or helps. The NIV stresses who the gift is for (everyone); the LSB stresses what it does (real benefit). Either way, your gift is not for you.
- **1 Cor 12:27.** NIV: “each one of you is a part of it.” LSB: “individually members of it.” The Greek word (*melos*) means a limb or part of a body. The LSB keeps the older word “members” used all through the chapter, which is where our phrase “church member” comes from. Paul does not mean a name on a roll but a working part of a living body.
- **Rom 12:3.** NIV: “in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you.” LSB: “as God has allotted to each a measure of faith.” The LSB keeps Paul’s word “measure.” Both mean that whatever faith and gifting you have, God gave it, so there is no room to look down on anyone.
- **Rom 12:8.** NIV: “if it is to encourage.” LSB: “he who exhorts.” The Greek verb (*parakaleō*) can mean to encourage, comfort, or urge. The NIV picks the gentler side; the LSB picks the side that calls someone to action. The gift includes both.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s short Ask Pastor John episode [“What If I Don’t Have a Spiritual Gift?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/what-if-i-dont-have-a-spiritual-gift) walks through 1 Corinthians 12 and Romans 12. Billy Graham’s answers [“Do I Have Any Spiritual Gifts?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/how-can-i-find-out-if-i-have-any-spiritual-gifts) and [“God has given everyone gifts with which to serve Him”](https://billygraham.org/answers/god-has-given-everyone-gifts-with-which-to-serve-him) are one-minute reads. BibleProject’s overviews of [1 Corinthians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-corinthians/) and [Romans 5–16](https://bibleproject.com/videos/romans-5-16/) show where these chapters fit.

**Reflection question:** What gift has God given you that others have noticed, and how could you use it this week to build up your church family and, as a husband and father, help Sanqueta and the kids find and use theirs?

Billy Graham wrote, “Are you a parent? Ask God to help you raise your children wisely and teach them about God and His love for them.” And for the days you feel ordinary: “Don’t worry about the gifts you don’t have, but ask God to use you right where you are—and He will.”

A brief note: Bible-believing Christians disagree about whether some gifts on Paul’s list, like tongues and prophecy, still work the same way today. Pentecostal and charismatic churches emphasize them; many Baptist churches are more cautious. But that debate is not Paul’s main point here. His point is that every believer has been given something by the Spirit, and every part is needed.

**1 Corinthians 12:4–27 (NIV)**
4 There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit distributes them. 5 There are different kinds of service, but the same Lord. 6 There are different kinds of working, but in all of them and in everyone it is the same God at work. 7 Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good. 8 To one there is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge by means of the same Spirit, 9 to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, 10 to another miraculous powers, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in different kinds of tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. 11 All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, and he distributes them to each one, just as he determines. 12 Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ. 13 For we were all baptized by one Spirit so as to form one body—whether Jews or Gentiles, slave or free—and we were all given the one Spirit to drink. 14 Even so the body is not made up of one part but of many. 15 Now if the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” it would not for that reason stop being part of the body. 16 And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” it would not for that reason stop being part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But in fact God has placed the parts in the body, every one of them, just as he wanted them to be. 19 If they were all one part, where would the body be? 20 As it is, there are many parts, but one body. 21 The eye cannot say to the hand, “I don’t need you!” And the head cannot say to the feet, “I don’t need you!” 22 On the contrary, those parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, 23 and the parts that we think are less honorable we treat with special honor. And the parts that are unpresentable are treated with special modesty, 24 while our presentable parts need no special treatment. But God has put the body together, giving greater honor to the parts that lacked it, 25 so that there should be no division in the body, but that its parts should have equal concern for each other. 26 If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it. 27 Now you are the body of Christ, and each one of you is a part of it.

**Romans 12:3–8 (NIV)**
3 For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgment, in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you. 4 For just as each of us has one body with many members, and these members do not all have the same function, 5 so in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others. 6 We have different gifts, according to the grace given to each of us. If your gift is prophesying, then prophesy in accordance with your faith; 7 if it is serving, then serve; if it is teaching, then teach; 8 if it is to encourage, then give encouragement; if it is giving, then give generously; if it is to lead, do it diligently; if it is to show mercy, do it cheerfully.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **1 Cor 12:5.** NIV: “different kinds of service.” LSB: “varieties of ministries.” The Greek word (*diakonia*) means service or ministry. The LSB’s “ministries” is a reminder that ministry is not only the pastor’s job; every act of service done for Christ’s body counts.
- **1 Cor 12:7.** NIV: “for the common good.” LSB: “for what is profitable.” The Greek word means what benefits or helps. The NIV stresses who the gift is for (everyone); the LSB stresses what it does (real benefit). Either way, your gift is not for you.
- **1 Cor 12:27.** NIV: “each one of you is a part of it.” LSB: “individually members of it.” The Greek word (*melos*) means a limb or part of a body. The LSB keeps the older word “members” used all through the chapter, which is where our phrase “church member” comes from. Paul does not mean a name on a roll but a working part of a living body.
- **Rom 12:3.** NIV: “in accordance with the faith God has distributed to each of you.” LSB: “as God has allotted to each a measure of faith.” The LSB keeps Paul’s word “measure.” Both mean that whatever faith and gifting you have, God gave it, so there is no room to look down on anyone.
- **Rom 12:8.** NIV: “if it is to encourage.” LSB: “he who exhorts.” The Greek verb (*parakaleō*) can mean to encourage, comfort, or urge. The NIV picks the gentler side; the LSB picks the side that calls someone to action. The gift includes both.

**Go deeper:** Erin Davis’s articles [“Don’t Rob Us of You”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/articles/dont-rob-us/) and [“We Have Gifts. Let Us Use Them!”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/articles/we-have-gifts-let-us-use-them/) on Revive Our Hearts are short and practical. Piper’s Ask Pastor John episode [“What If I Don’t Have a Spiritual Gift?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/what-if-i-dont-have-a-spiritual-gift) and Billy Graham’s [“Do I Have Any Spiritual Gifts?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/how-can-i-find-out-if-i-have-any-spiritual-gifts) go further. BibleProject’s overviews of [1 Corinthians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-corinthians/) and [Romans 5–16](https://bibleproject.com/videos/romans-5-16/) show where these chapters fit.

**Reflection question:** What gift has God given you that you have been hiding or comparing away, and how could you use it this week to serve your church family and, as a wife and mother, build up your husband and children?
