**Lesson 28: Suffering, hope, and the God who is near**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday was about the gifts God gives his people for the good of the body. Today is about what that body walks through together: suffering. Paul does not pretend it is small. He says the whole creation is “groaning,” and so are we (Rom 8:22–23). But he also says, “our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom 8:18).

Billy Graham was honest: “There are no easy answers to the question of the purpose of suffering and evil.” He did not blame God for it; suffering came into the world through sin. But he said God is not distant from it. “God never asks us to understand; we need only trust Him in the same way that we expect our earthly children to trust our love.” Any father knows that kind of trust. Your kids don’t understand every no, but they trust you.

God is near in the hardest moments. When you don’t even know what to pray, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans” (Rom 8:26). And then comes the promise: “in all things God works for the good of those who love him” (Rom 8:28). John Piper says the promise is for those who love God, and explains, “When you love God, God is central in your affections, not his gifts.” For those God has called, “all things work for good all the time.”

Peter adds that trials test faith the way fire tests gold (1 Pet 1:6–7). You see suffering up close in your work: patients in deep pain, families under strain. Billy Graham wrote, “The way we react to suffering will determine whether life’s most tragic experiences bring bitterness and despair or become sources of blessing.” And he gave this picture: “Peace comes when we realize we are able to see only a few threads in the great tapestry of life and of God’s plan.” Your hope is not that pain will skip your house. It is “a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Pet 1:3).

**Romans 8:18–28 (NIV)**
18 I consider that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us. 19 For the creation waits in eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed. 20 For the creation was subjected to frustration, not by its own choice, but by the will of the one who subjected it, in hope 21 that the creation itself will be liberated from its bondage to decay and brought into the freedom and glory of the children of God. 22 We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time. 23 Not only so, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption to sonship, the redemption of our bodies. 24 For in this hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what they already have? 25 But if we hope for what we do not yet have, we wait for it patiently. 26 In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans. 27 And he who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for God’s people in accordance with the will of God. 28 And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose.

**1 Peter 1:3–9 (NIV)**
3 Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! In his great mercy he has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, 4 and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade. This inheritance is kept in heaven for you, 5 who through faith are shielded by God’s power until the coming of the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time. 6 In all this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in all kinds of trials. 7 These have come so that the proven genuineness of your faith—of greater worth than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory and honor when Jesus Christ is revealed. 8 Though you have not seen him, you love him; and even though you do not see him now, you believe in him and are filled with an inexpressible and glorious joy, 9 for you are receiving the end result of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Rom 8:28.** NIV: “in all things God works for the good of those who love him.” LSB: “for those who love God all things work together for good.” Some early Greek manuscripts name God as the one doing the work; others do not. The NIV follows the first and makes it explicit; the LSB follows the traditional wording. Either way, the verse ends with “his purpose,” so God is the one weaving it together. Things do not work out on their own.
- **Rom 8:20.** NIV: “frustration.” LSB: “futility.” The Greek word means emptiness or pointlessness, the same idea as “meaningless” in Ecclesiastes. Creation is not yet what it was made to be, and it is waiting for its repair.
- **Rom 8:26.** NIV: “wordless groans.” LSB: “groanings too deep for words.” The LSB brings out that the Spirit prays for you when your grief is too deep for you to put into words.
- **1 Pet 1:6.** NIV: “you may have had to suffer grief.” LSB: “if necessary, you have been grieved.” The LSB is more literal here. Peter’s phrase means trials come only as God sees they are needed; none are wasted or random.
- **1 Pet 1:7.** NIV: “the proven genuineness of your faith.” LSB: “the proof of your faith.” The Greek word was used for testing metal to show it is real. Trials do not create faith; they show it is genuine, like gold coming out of the fire.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s sermon [“All Things for Good, Part 1”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/all-things-for-good-part-1) explains who Romans 8:28 is for. Billy Graham’s short answers [“Why does God allow suffering in the world?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/why-does-god-allow-suffering-in-the-world) and [“How Can ‘All Things Work Together’ as the Bible Says?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/how-can-all-things-work-together-as-the-bible-says) are quick reads. BibleProject’s overviews of [Romans 5–16](https://bibleproject.com/videos/romans-5-16/) and [1 Peter](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-peter/) show where these passages fit.

**Reflection question:** What hardship are you carrying right now, and how could you show your wife and kids this week, as a man, husband, and father, what it looks like to trust God’s love when you cannot see the whole tapestry?

**Lesson 29: The blessed hope: the resurrection and the Lord’s return**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday was about suffering and the God who is near in it. Today Paul lifts your eyes to how the story ends. The Christians in Thessalonica were burying loved ones and wondering if they had missed out. Paul answered, “we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope” (1 Thess 4:13).

Notice that Paul does not say don’t grieve. Ryan Chase, a pastor who buried one of his twin sons, writes at Desiring God that “Those who believe in the resurrection of Jesus are decidedly not to grieve in whatever way feels right to us, nor are we to grieve like those who have no hope.” He quotes John Piper’s counsel: “Occasionally, weep deeply over the life you hoped would be. Grieve the losses. Then wash your face. Trust God. And embrace the life you have.” Grief and hope can sit in the same heart.

The hope is specific. “For the Lord himself will come down from heaven… and the dead in Christ will rise first” (1 Thess 4:16). Billy Graham wrote, “When Christ comes again — as He repeatedly promised to do — He will come through the heavens with glory and power, accompanied by a host of angels.” Paul says our bodies will be changed “in a flash, in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Cor 15:52), and death itself will be “swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor 15:54). Billy Graham put it plainly: “Our hope is instilled in us by the resurrection of Christ.”

This hope is meant to change Monday morning. Paul ends, “Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Cor 15:58). Billy Graham asked the question every man has to answer: “The real issue, however, is this: Are you ready for that day?” His counsel was to trust Christ, and “Then learn to walk with Him every day.” Your faithful work, your patient fathering, and the prayers you pray over your kids are not wasted.

A brief note: Christians differ on the order of end-time events. Many Baptist and evangelical churches teach that believers will be “caught up” (1 Thess 4:17) before a time of tribulation; the word “rapture” comes from the Latin translation of that phrase. Others, including many Presbyterian, Lutheran, and Catholic Christians, read it as part of a single, visible return of Christ at the end. Every one of these traditions agrees on what Paul is clear about: Jesus is coming back bodily, the dead in Christ will rise, and we will be with him forever.

**1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 (NIV)**
13 Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope. 14 For we believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him. 15 According to the Lord’s word, we tell you that we who are still alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not precede those who have fallen asleep. 16 For the Lord himself will come down from heaven, with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first. 17 After that, we who are still alive and are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord forever. 18 Therefore encourage one another with these words.

**1 Corinthians 15:50–58 (NIV)**
50 I declare to you, brothers and sisters, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. 51 Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed— 52 in a flash, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. 53 For the perishable must clothe itself with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. 54 When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” 55 “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” 56 The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. 57 But thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. 58 Therefore, my dear brothers and sisters, stand firm. Let nothing move you. Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **1 Thess 4:13.** NIV: “those who sleep in death.” LSB: “those who are asleep.” Paul’s word is simply “sleep.” The NIV adds “in death” so no one misses that he means believers who have died; the LSB keeps the picture. Sleep is temporary. You wake up from it.
- **1 Thess 4:18.** NIV: “encourage one another.” LSB: “comfort one another.” The Greek verb (*parakaleō*) can mean either. At a graveside, Paul’s words are both comfort and courage.
- **1 Cor 15:50–54.** NIV: “perishable” and “imperishable.” LSB: “corruptible” and “incorruptible.” The Greek word means decay. Our bodies now wear out and break down; the resurrection body will never decay.
- **1 Cor 15:58.** NIV: “stand firm. Let nothing move you. Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord.” LSB: “be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord.” The verb behind “abounding” means to overflow. The NIV turns it into a command to give your all; the LSB keeps the picture of a life running over with work for the Lord.

**Go deeper:** Billy Graham’s [“Christ’s second coming will be glorious, for all to see”](https://billygraham.org/answers/christs-second-coming-will-be-glorious-for-all-to-see) and his devotion [“The Hope of Resurrection”](https://billygraham.org/devotions/the-hope-of-resurrection) are short reads. Ryan Chase’s article [“We Can’t Grieve However We Want”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/we-cant-grieve-however-we-want) is a father’s honest look at grief and hope. BibleProject’s overviews of [1 Thessalonians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-thessalonians/) and [1 Corinthians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-corinthians/) show where these passages fit.

**Reflection question:** If Jesus returned this week, what would he find you giving yourself fully to, and what is one way you could help your wife and kids live with their eyes on that day as a man, husband, and father?

This hope is meant to shape an ordinary Tuesday. Paul ends, “Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Cor 15:58). The meals, the bedtime prayers, the patient words to a tired child, the care you give others: none of it is wasted.

Others, including many Presbyterian, Lutheran, and Catholic Christians, read it as part of a single, visible return of Christ at the end. Every one of these traditions agrees on what Paul is clear about: Jesus is coming back bodily, the dead in Christ will rise, and we will be with him forever.

13 Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope. 14 For we believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him. 15 According to the Lord’s word, we tell you that we who are still alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not precede those who have fallen asleep. 16 For the Lord himself will come down from heaven, with a loud command, with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet call of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first. 17 After that, we who are still alive and are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will be with the Lord forever. 18 Therefore encourage one another with these words.

**1 Corinthians 15:50–58 (NIV)**
50 I declare to you, brothers and sisters, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. 51 Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed— 52 in a flash, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed. 53 For the perishable must clothe itself with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. 54 When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality, then the saying that is written will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” 55 “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” 56 The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. 57 But thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. 58 Therefore, my dear brothers and sisters, stand firm. Let nothing move you. Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.

- **1 Thess 4:18.** NIV: “encourage one another.” LSB: “comfort one another.” The Greek verb (*parakaleō*) can mean either. At a graveside, Paul’s words are both comfort and courage.
- **1 Cor 15:50–54.** NIV: “perishable” and “imperishable.” LSB: “corruptible” and “incorruptible.” The Greek word means decay. Our bodies now wear out and break down; the resurrection body will never decay.
- **1 Cor 15:58.** NIV: “stand firm. Let nothing move you. Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord.” LSB: “be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord.” The verb behind “abounding” means to overflow. The NIV turns it into a command to give your all; the LSB keeps the picture of a life running over with work for the Lord.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s Revive Our Hearts episode [“Expecting Christ’s Return”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/expecting-christs-return/) (Sept 28, 2023) is a warm, practical listen. **Reflection question:** How would eagerly waiting for Jesus’ return change the way you spend this week as a woman, wife, and mother, and what is one way you could help your children look forward to that day?

**Lesson 30: The fear of the Lord, and a life of thanksgiving**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday was about the blessed hope of Christ’s return. Today closes the foundations section with two habits that hold everything else together: fearing God and thanking him. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov 9:10), and “give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus” (1 Thess 5:18).

What does it mean for a Christian to fear God? John Piper says, “The fear of the Lord is a pervasive and important topic,” and warns that we can get casual: “It would be insane to think we can just stroll up to the Creator of the universe and have a cavalier spirit.” But in Christ the fear changes. “There is terror outside of Christ, and there is a different kind of trembling inside of Christ.” He sums it up from Hebrews 12: “We are safe. We have a kingdom that cannot be shaken. But our God is a consuming fire. You don’t come near him without reverence and awe.”

Piper adds that “fear functions as a preservative.” It keeps a man from drifting into pride and self-sufficiency. Yet it is not slavish fear: “God doesn’t want us to cower like slaves in the household where the children should be enjoying sweet peace in their Father’s care.” A father wants his kids to respect him and also to run to him. That is the fear of the Lord.

Fear and gratitude belong together. The same passage Piper cites says, “let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Heb 12:28). Billy Graham was careful about what Paul means by thanks in all circumstances: “we aren’t called to be thankful for things that are evil. But you can be thankful that God has promised to be with you, even when life isn’t the way you wish it were.” His counsel was simple: “Then thank Him every day that He is with you, and ahead of you is Heaven.” A thankful father sets the weather in his home.

**Proverbs 9:10 (NIV)**
10 The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.

**1 Thessalonians 5:16–18 (NIV)**
16 Rejoice always, 17 pray continually, 18 give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Prov 9:10.** NIV: “The fear of the Lord.” LSB: “The fear of Yahweh.” The Hebrew text uses God’s personal covenant name, YHWH. Most English Bibles, including the NIV, follow the old Jewish and Christian custom of writing it as “the Lord” (shown in small capitals in print). The LSB spells the name out. It is a reminder that the fear of the Lord is reverence for a personal God who has bound himself to his people, not dread of an unknown power.
- **1 Thess 5:17.** NIV: “pray continually.” LSB: “pray without ceasing.” The Greek word means without interruption, like something that keeps coming back. Paul does not mean saying words every second; he means a life that keeps turning back to God all day long.
- **1 Thess 5:18.** NIV: “give thanks in all circumstances.” LSB: “in everything give thanks.” The Greek is simply “in everything.” The NIV spells out that this includes hard situations. Notice the small word in both: it is thanks *in* everything, not *for* every evil thing.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s Ask Pastor John episode [“What Does It Mean for the Christian to Fear God?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/what-does-it-mean-for-the-christian-to-fear-god) is a clear, short answer. Billy Graham’s [“Why Should I Be Thankful Even When Bad Things Happen?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/why-should-i-be-thankful-even-when-bad-things-happen) is a one-minute read. BibleProject’s overviews of [Proverbs](https://bibleproject.com/videos/proverbs/) and [1 Thessalonians](https://bibleproject.com/videos/1-thessalonians/) show where these verses fit.

**Reflection question:** Where has your reverence for God grown casual, and what is one way you could lead your family in thanking God this week as a man, husband, and father, even for the things you are still waiting on?

**Lesson 31: Genesis: in the beginning, God creates**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday closed the foundations. Today the long walk through all 66 books begins, right where the Bible begins: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Gen 1:1). Before there was anything, there was God. Everything else, from the stars to your kids’ laughter, exists because he spoke.

Billy Graham put it simply: “It didn’t just happen, nor was it an accident; it was created by a deliberate and purposeful act on the part of God.” And he marveled at how: “God spoke—and it happened!” Over and over in Genesis 1, God says, and it is so. The same God who spoke light into darkness speaks to you through his Word every morning.

Notice how often God looks at what he made and calls it good. John Piper says, “I take this to mean that God was delighted with his work. When he looked at it, it gave him pleasure.” Why? Because “in creation he sees the reflection of his own glory.” He even says creation “is an expression of the overflow of that life and joy that the Father and the Son have in each other.” God did not create because he was lonely. He created because his joy overflowed.

Then comes the high point: “So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Gen 1:27). Every person you meet at work, every patient, your wife, and each of your children bears God’s image. And on the seventh day God rested, not because he was tired, but to bless a rhythm of work and rest for his people (Gen 2:2–3). Billy Graham pointed to the bigger story Genesis starts: “The greatest truth of all, however, is that God loves us, and He sent His Son into the world to save us.”

A brief note: Bible-believing Christians hold different views on how long the six days were. Many Baptist churches teach six ordinary days and a young earth; others, like many Presbyterians and Anglicans, see the days as long ages or as a literary framework. Billy Graham’s counsel is wise: “Since Christians hold various views, it is important to keep an attitude of humility and charity toward others in these complicated areas. One fact is absolutely clear from the Bible—God is the Creator!”

**Genesis 1:1–2:3 (NIV)**
1 In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. 2 Now the earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters. 3 And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. 4 God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the darkness. 5 God called the light “day,” and the darkness he called “night.” And there was evening, and there was morning—the first day. 6 And God said, “Let there be a vault between the waters to separate water from water.” 7 So God made the vault and separated the water under the vault from the water above it. And it was so. 8 God called the vault “sky.” And there was evening, and there was morning—the second day. 9 And God said, “Let the water under the sky be gathered to one place, and let dry ground appear.” And it was so. 10 God called the dry ground “land,” and the gathered waters he called “seas.” And God saw that it was good. 11 Then God said, “Let the land produce vegetation: seed-bearing plants and trees on the land that bear fruit with seed in it, according to their various kinds.” And it was so. 12 The land produced vegetation: plants bearing seed according to their kinds and trees bearing fruit with seed in it according to their kinds. And God saw that it was good. 13 And there was evening, and there was morning—the third day. 14 And God said, “Let there be lights in the vault of the sky to separate the day from the night, and let them serve as signs to mark sacred times, and days and years, 15 and let them be lights in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth.” And it was so. 16 God made two great lights—the greater light to govern the day and the lesser light to govern the night. He also made the stars. 17 God set them in the vault of the sky to give light on the earth, 18 to govern the day and the night, and to separate light from darkness. And God saw that it was good. 19 And there was evening, and there was morning—the fourth day. 20 And God said, “Let the water teem with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the vault of the sky.” 21 So God created the great creatures of the sea and every living thing with which the water teems and that moves about in it, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. 22 God blessed them and said, “Be fruitful and increase in number and fill the water in the seas, and let the birds increase on the earth.” 23 And there was evening, and there was morning—the fifth day. 24 And God said, “Let the land produce living creatures according to their kinds: the livestock, the creatures that move along the ground, and the wild animals, each according to its kind.” And it was so. 25 God made the wild animals according to their kinds, the livestock according to their kinds, and all the creatures that move along the ground according to their kinds. And God saw that it was good. 26 Then God said, “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.” 27 So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them. 28 God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky and over every living creature that moves on the ground.” 29 Then God said, “I give you every seed-bearing plant on the face of the whole earth and every tree that has fruit with seed in it. They will be yours for food. 30 And to all the beasts of the earth and all the birds in the sky and all the creatures that move along the ground—everything that has the breath of life in it—I give every green plant for food.” And it was so. 31 God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning—the sixth day. 2:1 Thus the heavens and the earth were completed in all their vast array. 2:2 By the seventh day God had finished the work he had been doing; so on the seventh day he rested from all his work. 2:3 Then God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all the work of creating that he had done.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Gen 1:5.** NIV: “the first day.” LSB: “one day.” The Hebrew literally says “one day” here, then “a second day,” “a third day,” and so on. The LSB keeps that wording; the NIV smooths it into normal English counting.
- **Gen 1:6–8.** NIV: “vault.” LSB: “expanse.” The Hebrew word (*raqia*) describes something spread out or stretched out, like the sky as it looks from the ground. The NIV pictures it as a dome; the LSB keeps the more general idea.
- **Gen 1:26–27.** NIV: “mankind.” LSB: “man.” The Hebrew word is *adam*, which means humanity as a whole and later becomes the first man’s name. The NIV uses “mankind” to make clear it includes everyone; the LSB keeps the one word that links us to Adam. Both then say plainly, “male and female he created them.”
- **Gen 1:26, 28.** NIV: “rule.” LSB: “have dominion.” Same Hebrew verb. Our rule over creation is a king’s stewardship under God, not permission to waste it.
- **Gen 1:31.** NIV: “it was very good.” LSB: “behold, it was very good.” The Hebrew has a word that means “look!” The LSB keeps it, as if God stops and invites us to see what he sees.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Genesis 1–11 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-1-11/) is the best seven-minute map of where this walk is heading. Piper’s sermon [“The Pleasure of God in His Creation”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-pleasure-of-god-in-his-creation) explains why God delights in what he made. Billy Graham’s answers [“Where Did the World Come From?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/where-did-the-world-come-from) and [on the six days](https://billygraham.org/answers/how-can-the-bible-be-correct-about-the-world-being-created-in-six-days) are one-minute reads.

**Reflection question:** How would treating each person in your home as an image-bearer of God change the way you lead, speak, and rest this week as a man, husband, and father?

The NIV uses “mankind” to make clear it includes everyone; the LSB keeps the one word that links us to Adam. Both then say plainly, “male and female he created them.”
- **Gen 1:26, 28.** NIV: “rule.” LSB: “have dominion.” Same Hebrew verb. Our rule over creation is a king’s stewardship under God, not permission to waste it.
- **Gen 1:31.** NIV: “it was very good.” LSB: “behold, it was very good.” The Hebrew has a word that means “look!” The LSB keeps it, as if God stops and invites us to see what he sees.

God Created”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/weekend/and-god-created/) with Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, Dannah Gresh, and Erin Davis is a joyful listen, and Nancy’s [“God’s Grand Story”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/gods-grand-story/) (Sept 11, 2019) shows how Genesis 1 anchors hard seasons. **Lesson 32: Genesis: the fall, and the first promise of a Savior**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God made everything good. Today, one chapter later, it all comes crashing down. A serpent speaks, a command is doubted, fruit is eaten, and the world is broken. But before the chapter ends, God makes a promise. Genesis 3 explains why the world hurts, and it also shows the first light of the gospel.

Billy Graham wrote that Adam “walked with God and had fellowship with Him. He was intended to live as a king, ruling by the will of God.” And “Upon this man, God bestowed a most precious gift; God gave to man the freedom of choice.” Notice where Adam is when temptation comes: his wife “gave some to her husband, who was with her” (Gen 3:6). He was standing right there and said nothing. Then, when God called, “Where are you?” (3:9), Adam blamed “The woman you put here with me” (3:12). Silence, then blame: that is the first husband’s failure, and every man since knows the pull of both.

Who was the serpent? John Piper says, “He is already evil, already a deceiver, already a murderer when he appears in the garden of God.” But God speaks the first word of hope to him as a curse: the woman’s offspring “will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (3:15). Piper explains, “That decisive blow was struck by the perfect offspring of the woman, Jesus Christ, when he died on the cross.” Greg Morse at Desiring God adds that death “merely bruised his heel because it was impossible for death to hold him.”

Then look at verse 21: “The Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them.” Fig leaves could not cover their shame; God covered them himself, and something died to do it. That points forward to Christ. Billy Graham said it well: “it is what we choose to do with our freedom that determines whether or not we find peace with God and with ourselves.” A godly man does not stand silent when his home is under attack, and when he fails, he does not hide or blame. He runs to the God who covers.

**Genesis 3:1–24 (NIV)**
1 Now the serpent was more crafty than any of the wild animals the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden’?” 2 The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees in the garden, 3 but God did say, ‘You must not eat fruit from the tree that is in the middle of the garden, and you must not touch it, or you will die.’” 4 “You will not certainly die,” the serpent said to the woman. 5 “For God knows that when you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” 6 When the woman saw that the fruit of the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eye, and also desirable for gaining wisdom, she took some and ate it. She also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it. 7 Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they realized they were naked; so they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves. 8 Then the man and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God as he was walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and they hid from the Lord God among the trees of the garden. 9 But the Lord God called to the man, “Where are you?” 10 He answered, “I heard you in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid.” 11 And he said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” 12 The man said, “The woman you put here with me—she gave me some fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” 13 Then the Lord God said to the woman, “What is this you have done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” 14 So the Lord God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, “Cursed are you above all livestock and all wild animals! You will crawl on your belly and you will eat dust all the days of your life. 15 And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” 16 To the woman he said, “I will make your pains in childbearing very severe; with painful labor you will give birth to children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.” 17 To Adam he said, “Because you listened to your wife and ate fruit from the tree about which I commanded you, ‘You must not eat from it,’ “Cursed is the ground because of you; through painful toil you will eat food from it all the days of your life. 18 It will produce thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. 19 By the sweat of your brow you will eat your food until you return to the ground, since from it you were taken; for dust you are and to dust you will return.” 20 Adam named his wife Eve, because she would become the mother of all the living. 21 The Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them. 22 And the Lord God said, “The man has now become like one of us, knowing good and evil. He must not be allowed to reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life and eat, and live forever.” 23 So the Lord God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken. 24 After he drove the man out, he placed on the east side of the Garden of Eden cherubim and a flaming sword flashing back and forth to guard the way to the tree of life.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Gen 3:15.** NIV: “between your offspring and hers; he will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” LSB: “between your seed and her seed; He shall bruise you on the head, And you shall bruise him on the heel.” The Hebrew word for offspring is literally “seed,” and the LSB keeps it, which helps you follow the promised Seed through the rest of the Bible (see Gal 3:16). Hebrew uses the same verb for both blows; the NIV uses two different verbs to show the difference between a crushing blow to the head and a wound to the heel.
- **Gen 3:1.** NIV: “Did God really say…?” LSB: “Indeed, has God said…?” Both catch the serpent’s tone. His first move is not to deny God outright but to make God’s word sound doubtful and stingy.
- **Gen 3:16.** NIV: “I will make your pains in childbearing very severe.” LSB: “I will greatly multiply Your pain and conception.” The Hebrew literally says “your pain and your conception.” Most scholars read this as a way of saying “pain in childbearing,” which is how the NIV renders it. The LSB keeps the literal wording.
- **Gen 3:6.** NIV: “She also gave some to her husband, who was with her.” LSB: “and she gave also to her husband with her.” Both make the same point: Adam was there. He was not off somewhere else; he stood by silently while the serpent spoke.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s sermon [“The Fall of Satan and the Victory of Christ”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-fall-of-satan-and-the-victory-of-christ) (Aug 19, 2007) traces the serpent from Genesis 3 to the cross. Greg Morse’s [“God of Bloodstained Hands”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-of-bloodstained-hands) follows the promised Seed through the Old Testament. Billy Graham’s short answer on [the great fall](https://billygraham.org/answers/if-adam-and-eve-were-perfect-then-why-did-they-bring-the-great-fall) and BibleProject’s [Genesis 1–11 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-1-11/) round it out.

**Reflection question:** Where are you tempted to stay silent like Adam or to shift blame when you fail, and what would it look like this week to step up and lead your wife and kids toward God as a man, husband, and father?

**Lesson 33: Genesis: Noah, the flood, and God’s covenant**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday sin entered the world, and God promised a Savior. Today you see how far sin spread, “the earth was corrupt in God’s sight and was full of violence” (Gen 6:11), and how God kept his promise alive through one man and his family.

Billy Graham called the flood “not a natural catastrophe but a moral tsunami.” In a world like that, “Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, and he walked faithfully with God” (6:9). Billy Graham noted, “Noah was perhaps the most unlikely seaman. He knew nothing about sailing the high seas, and he certainly was at a loss as to how to build a boat. But he believed God.” He also wrote, “People laughed and mocked Noah, but through his obedience and faith in God, he was the first person in the Bible to be called righteous.” The chapter ends simply: “Noah did everything just as God commanded him” (6:22).

Notice who goes into the ark with him: “you and your sons and your wife and your sons’ wives with you” (6:18). Noah’s faith and obedience became shelter for his whole household. A father’s quiet, steady obedience still matters that much.

John Piper preached on this covenant at the start of Advent and drew out two truths. First, the flood did not fix the human heart: “God’s assessment of our moral condition is not improved by the flood.” Even Noah sinned afterward. Second, “Judgment is real and horrible, but it will not be the last word.” God set his bow in the clouds and promised never again to destroy the earth by a flood (9:11–13). Piper ends where the story is headed: “God still hates sin. We are still sinful. But God will never surrender his purpose to fill the earth with his glory. The final remedy is Jesus Christ.” Every rainbow your kids point out is a chance to tell them God keeps his promises.

**Genesis 6:9–22 (NIV)**
9 This is the account of Noah and his family. Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time, and he walked faithfully with God. 10 Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth. 11 Now the earth was corrupt in God’s sight and was full of violence. 12 God saw how corrupt the earth had become, for all the people on earth had corrupted their ways. 13 So God said to Noah, “I am going to put an end to all people, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. I am surely going to destroy both them and the earth. 14 So make yourself an ark of cypress wood; make rooms in it and coat it with pitch inside and out. 15 This is how you are to build it: The ark is to be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide and thirty cubits high. 16 Make a roof for it, leaving below the roof an opening one cubit high all around. Put a door in the side of the ark and make lower, middle and upper decks. 17 I am going to bring floodwaters on the earth to destroy all life under the heavens, every creature that has the breath of life in it. Everything on earth will perish. 18 But I will establish my covenant with you, and you will enter the ark—you and your sons and your wife and your sons’ wives with you. 19 You are to bring into the ark two of all living creatures, male and female, to keep them alive with you. 20 Two of every kind of bird, of every kind of animal and of every kind of creature that moves along the ground will come to you to be kept alive. 21 You are to take every kind of food that is to be eaten and store it away as food for you and for them.” 22 Noah did everything just as God commanded him.

**Genesis 9:8–17 (NIV)**
8 Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him: 9 “I now establish my covenant with you and with your descendants after you 10 and with every living creature that was with you—the birds, the livestock and all the wild animals, all those that came out of the ark with you—every living creature on earth. 11 I establish my covenant with you: Never again will all life be destroyed by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth.” 12 And God said, “This is the sign of the covenant I am making between me and you and every living creature with you, a covenant for all generations to come: 13 I have set my rainbow in the clouds, and it will be the sign of the covenant between me and the earth. 14 Whenever I bring clouds over the earth and the rainbow appears in the clouds, 15 I will remember my covenant between me and you and all living creatures of every kind. Never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all life. 16 Whenever the rainbow appears in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and all living creatures of every kind on the earth.” 17 So God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant I have established between me and all life on the earth.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Gen 6:9.** NIV: “This is the account of Noah.” LSB: “These are the generations of Noah.” The Hebrew word (*toledot*) is a heading that appears again and again in Genesis to start a new section. The LSB keeps the older wording so you can spot the pattern.
- **Gen 6:9.** NIV: “he walked faithfully with God.” LSB: “Noah walked with God.” The Hebrew simply says “walked with God,” the same phrase used of Enoch (Gen 5:24). The NIV adds “faithfully” to bring out what that walk meant.
- **Gen 6:14.** NIV: “cypress wood.” LSB: “gopher wood.” The Hebrew word appears only here, and no one knows for sure what tree it means. The LSB keeps the Hebrew word; the NIV gives its best guess.
- **Gen 9:9.** NIV: “your descendants.” LSB: “your seed.” Same Hebrew word as Genesis 3:15. The LSB keeps “seed,” so you can see God carrying his promise forward through Noah’s family.
- **Gen 9:13.** NIV: “my rainbow.” LSB: “My bow.” The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for a bow, the kind a warrior uses. Many teachers see a picture here of God hanging up his weapon in the sky after the judgment: a sign of peace.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s Advent sermon [“God’s Covenant with Noah”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-with-noah) (Nov 27, 1983) is a fitting read as December begins. Billy Graham’s short answers [“Why Did God Choose Noah to Build the Ark?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/why-did-god-choose-noah-to-build-the-ark) and [“What Does God Promise With a Rainbow?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/what-does-god-promise-with-a-rainbow) are quick reads. BibleProject’s [Genesis 1–11 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-1-11/) shows how the flood fits the bigger story.

**Reflection question:** What is God asking you to keep building in obedience, even if others don’t understand it, so that your wife and children are sheltered by your faith as a man, husband, and father?

- **Gen 9:13.** NIV: “my rainbow.” LSB: “My bow.” The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for a bow, the kind a warrior uses. Many teachers see a picture here of God hanging up his weapon in the sky after the judgment: a sign of peace.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s Revive Our Hearts series “Noah and the Flood: The Gospel in the Old Testament” begins with [“A Glimmer of Hope”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/glimmer-hope-3/) (Aug 3, 2015). Piper’s Advent sermon [“God’s Covenant with Noah”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gods-covenant-with-noah) and Billy Graham’s [“Why Did God Choose Noah to Build the Ark?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/why-did-god-choose-noah-to-build-the-ark) go further. BibleProject’s [Genesis 1–11 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-1-11/) shows how the flood fits the bigger story.

**Reflection question:** Like Noah’s wife, where is God asking you to trust him through a long season you didn’t choose, and how could you help your husband and children remember this week, as a woman, wife, and mother, that God keeps his promises?

**Lesson 34: Genesis: Abraham, called and counted righteous**

Good morning, Greg. After the flood, people still rebelled, and at Babel they tried to make a name for themselves. Genesis 12 is God’s answer: he starts his rescue plan with one man and says, “I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing” (12:2).

God’s call to Abram came with no map: “Go … to the land I will show you” (12:1). John Piper said, “Abraham left a secure family and home in Ur of the Chaldees.” He applied it to every believer: “So they come like Abraham, knowing God’s call, but not the details. And so it will be with every major act of obedience you perform.” Notice what Abram did when he arrived: “he built an altar there to the Lord” (12:7). Everywhere he moved his family, worship came first.

Years later, still childless, Abram brought his honest worry to God (15:2–3). God took him outside and told him to count the stars, and “Abram believed the Lord, and he credited it to him as righteousness” (15:6). Piper put it plainly: “Abraham found grace in the eyes of the Lord, through faith alone.” He warned against the opposite: “If you work for your justification, what you are doing is trying to get God to owe you something.” Abram did not earn a right standing with God; he trusted God’s promise, and God counted him righteous. That is the same way you and your children are made right with God today, through faith in Christ.

Piper said, “Saving faith changes the way you live.” Leaving home and living in tents made no sense to Abram’s neighbors. “That’s the way the life of faith is: it doesn’t make sense without God. But with God, it is utterly reasonable.”

**Genesis 12:1–9 (NIV)**
1 The Lord had said to Abram, “Go from your country, your people and your father’s household to the land I will show you. 2 “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing. 3 I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you.” 4 So Abram went, as the Lord had told him; and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he set out from Harran. 5 He took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, all the possessions they had accumulated and the people they had acquired in Harran, and they set out for the land of Canaan, and they arrived there. 6 Abram traveled through the land as far as the site of the great tree of Moreh at Shechem. At that time the Canaanites were in the land. 7 The Lord appeared to Abram and said, “To your offspring I will give this land.” So he built an altar there to the Lord, who had appeared to him. 8 From there he went on toward the hills east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to the Lord and called on the name of the Lord. 9 Then Abram set out and continued toward the Negev.

**Genesis 15:1–6 (NIV)**
1 After this, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.” 2 But Abram said, “Sovereign Lord, what can you give me since I remain childless and the one who will inherit my estate is Eliezer of Damascus?” 3 And Abram said, “You have given me no children; so a servant in my household will be my heir.” 4 Then the word of the Lord came to him: “This man will not be your heir, but a son who is your own flesh and blood will be your heir.” 5 He took him outside and said, “Look up at the sky and count the stars—if indeed you can count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your offspring be.” 6 Abram believed the Lord, and he credited it to him as righteousness.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Gen 12:1 and throughout.** NIV: “The Lord.” LSB: “Yahweh.” The Hebrew text uses God’s personal name here. Most English Bibles, including the NIV, follow an old Jewish custom and print it as “Lord” in small capitals. The LSB spells out the name so you see that God is introducing himself personally to Abram.
- **Gen 12:3.** NIV: “all peoples on earth.” LSB: “all the families of the earth.” The Hebrew word means families or clans. The LSB keeps that household picture: God’s blessing is aimed at families everywhere, including yours.
- **Gen 12:7 and 15:5.** NIV: “your offspring.” LSB: “your seed.” Same Hebrew word as Genesis 3:15 and 9:9. Paul builds on this singular word in Galatians 3:16 to point to Christ, so the LSB keeps “seed.”
- **Gen 15:1.** NIV: “I am your shield, your very great reward.” LSB: “I am a shield to you; Your reward shall be very great.” The Hebrew can be read either way. The NIV stresses that God himself is Abram’s reward; the LSB stresses that the reward God gives will be great. Both are true.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s sermons [“The Faith of Noah, Abraham, and Sarah”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-faith-of-noah-abraham-and-sarah) and [“God Credits Faith as Righteousness”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/god-credits-faith-as-righteousness) go further, the second walking through how Paul uses Genesis 15:6 in Romans 4. BibleProject’s [Genesis 12–50 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-12-50/) shows where Abraham fits in the whole story.

**Reflection question:** Where is God calling you to take the next step of obedience before you see the details, and how can you, as a man, husband, and father, keep worship first for your family the way Abram built an altar wherever he went?

**Lesson 35: Genesis: Abraham tested, and the Lord will provide**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God called Abram and counted his faith as righteousness. Today that faith is tested in the hardest way a father could imagine: “Take your son, your only son, whom you love—Isaac” (22:2).

Look at how Abraham answered: “Early the next morning Abraham got up” (22:3). He did not argue or delay. He even told his servants, “We will worship and then we will come back to you” (22:5). Hebrews 11:19 says Abraham reasoned that God could even raise the dead. Then Isaac asked the question every reader feels: “where is the lamb?” Abraham answered, “God himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son” (22:8).

John Piper points out that in Genesis 22 the word translated “provide” is the Hebrew word for “see.” Abraham was saying, in effect, God will see to it. Piper explains, “I think the deepest answer is that God never simply sees without acting,” and “Wherever God is looking, God is acting.”

God stopped Abraham’s hand and provided a ram “instead of his son” (22:13). Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth calls this a picture of “the day when God would one day sacrifice His only Son, the Lamb of God, who would die in our place.” Abraham did not have to give up his son. God did.

**Genesis 22:1–18 (NIV)**
1 Some time later God tested Abraham. He said to him, “Abraham!” “Here I am,” he replied. 2 Then God said, “Take your son, your only son, whom you love—Isaac—and go to the region of Moriah. Sacrifice him there as a burnt offering on a mountain I will show you.” 3 Early the next morning Abraham got up and loaded his donkey. He took with him two of his servants and his son Isaac. When he had cut enough wood for the burnt offering, he set out for the place God had told him about. 4 On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance. 5 He said to his servants, “Stay here with the donkey while I and the boy go over there. We will worship and then we will come back to you.” 6 Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac, and he himself carried the fire and the knife. As the two of them went on together, 7 Isaac spoke up and said to his father Abraham, “Father?” “Yes, my son?” Abraham replied. “The fire and wood are here,” Isaac said, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” 8 Abraham answered, “God himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” And the two of them went on together. 9 When they reached the place God had told him about, Abraham built an altar there and arranged the wood on it. He bound his son Isaac and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood. 10 Then he reached out his hand and took the knife to slay his son. 11 But the angel of the Lord called out to him from heaven, “Abraham! Abraham!” “Here I am,” he replied. 12 “Do not lay a hand on the boy,” he said. “Do not do anything to him. Now I know that you fear God, because you have not withheld from me your son, your only son.” 13 Abraham looked up and there in a thicket he saw a ram caught by its horns. He went over and took the ram and sacrificed it as a burnt offering instead of his son. 14 So Abraham called that place The Lord Will Provide. And to this day it is said, “On the mountain of the Lord it will be provided.” 15 The angel of the Lord called to Abraham from heaven a second time 16 and said, “I swear by myself, declares the Lord, that because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son, 17 I will surely bless you and make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will take possession of the cities of their enemies, 18 and through your offspring all nations on earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed me.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Gen 22:2, 12, 16.** NIV: “your only son.” LSB: “your only one.” The Hebrew word means “only one” or “unique one.” Isaac was the one son of the promise. The same idea stands behind John 3:16, where God gave “his one and only Son.”
- **Gen 22:8.** NIV: “God himself will provide the lamb.” LSB: “God will provide for Himself the lamb.” The Hebrew literally says God “will see for himself” the lamb. The LSB keeps “for Himself”: the lamb belongs to God, and God supplies it.
- **Gen 22:14.** NIV: “The Lord Will Provide.” LSB: “Yahweh Will Provide.” The LSB prints God’s personal name. In Hebrew the place name is built on the verb “to see,” the same word as verse 8. Older Bibles kept it as “Jehovah-jireh.”
- **Gen 22:17–18.** NIV: “your descendants … your offspring.” LSB: “your seed … your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies.” The Hebrew word “seed” is singular, and so is “his.” The LSB keeps that wording; the NIV smooths it to “their enemies.” Paul reads the singular “seed” as pointing to Christ (Gal 3:16).

**Go deeper:** Piper’s short article [“The Providence of God”](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-providence-of-god) unpacks the “see to it” meaning of Genesis 22. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“His Name Is Lamb of God”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/his-name-is-lamb-of-god/) traces the lamb from Genesis 22 through Passover to Jesus. BibleProject’s [Genesis 12–50 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-12-50/) shows how Abraham’s test fits the bigger story.

**Reflection question:** What are you holding tightly, even a good gift like your children, that God may be asking you to trust him with, and how can you, as a man, husband, and father, show your family this week that the Lord will provide?

**Lesson 36: Genesis: Jacob wrestles, and Joseph the dreamer**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Abraham trusted that the Lord would provide. Today you meet his grandson Jacob, a man who spent years grabbing for blessing by his own schemes, and then Jacob’s son Joseph.

Jacob was afraid. His brother Esau was coming with four hundred men. Alone at night, “a man wrestled with him till daybreak” (32:24). Jacob held on: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (32:26). Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth writes that Jacob “was a man who wanted it his way. He manipulated his way through every problem, until one night when he got alone with God.” Jon Bloom of Desiring God sums up the change: “Jacob began the night believing his greatest need was to escape from Esau. He ended the night believing his greatest need was to trust in the blessing of God’s promise.”

God gave him a new name, Israel, and a limp he carried the rest of his life (32:28, 31). Bloom says, “It is a great mercy to be brought to the point where you’re desperate enough to insist on what you need the most.” Strong men often learn to lean on God only after he weakens them.

Then Genesis turns to Joseph. Jacob “loved Joseph more than any of his other sons” and gave him an ornate robe (37:3), and the brothers “hated him” (37:4). Jacob had grown up in a home torn by a parent’s favoritism, and he repeated it. A father’s favoritism can wound a whole family. Still, God was at work. Billy Graham wrote, “Joseph would never have been used by God had he not been sold into slavery by brothers who hated him,” and “God may sometimes seem slow in coming to help us, but He never comes too late.”

**Genesis 32:22–32 (NIV)**
22 That night Jacob got up and took his two wives, his two female servants and his eleven sons and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. 23 After he had sent them across the stream, he sent over all his possessions. 24 So Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him till daybreak. 25 When the man saw that he could not overpower him, he touched the socket of Jacob’s hip so that his hip was wrenched as he wrestled with the man. 26 Then the man said, “Let me go, for it is daybreak.” But Jacob replied, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” 27 The man asked him, “What is your name?” “Jacob,” he answered. 28 Then the man said, “Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with humans and have overcome.” 29 Jacob said, “Please tell me your name.” But he replied, “Why do you ask my name?” Then he blessed him there. 30 So Jacob called the place Peniel, saying, “It is because I saw God face to face, and yet my life was spared.” 31 The sun rose above him as he passed Peniel, and he was limping because of his hip. 32 Therefore to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon attached to the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob’s hip was touched near the tendon.

**Genesis 37:1–11 (NIV)**
1 Jacob lived in the land where his father had stayed, the land of Canaan. 2 This is the account of Jacob’s family line. **Lesson 37: Genesis: Joseph forgives — God meant it for good**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday you met Joseph, the favored son whose brothers hated him. They sold him into slavery. Years later, through prison and long waiting, God raised him to rule over Egypt, and famine drove the same brothers to his door.

Joseph had the power to pay them back. Instead he wept, said, “Come close to me,” and told them, “it was not you who sent me here, but God” (45:4, 8). After their father died, the brothers were afraid again. Joseph answered, “Am I in the place of God? You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good” (50:19–20).

John Piper points out what that verse says and what it doesn’t: “Notice it does not say that God used their evil for good after they meant it for evil. It says that in the very act of evil, there were two different designs.” He shows how it points to Jesus: “God’s saving victory for his people often comes through sin and suffering.” Jesus was sold, betrayed, and crucified by sinful men, and in that very act God was saving his people.

Billy Graham drew a line straight to the home: “Because of Joseph’s demonstration of forgiveness, he was blessed of God. If we cannot find it in our hearts to forgive within our own family, we will never exhibit this attribute of Christ with others and know God’s blessings.” He is also realistic: “It is not always possible to mend a broken relationship.” But “we can demonstrate it by how we react.” A father who forgives quickly teaches his children what the gospel looks like.

**Genesis 45:1–15 (NIV)**
1 Then Joseph could no longer control himself before all his attendants, and he cried out, “Have everyone leave my presence!” So there was no one with Joseph when he made himself known to his brothers. 2 And he wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and Pharaoh’s household heard about it. 3 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Is my father still living?” But his brothers were not able to answer him, because they were terrified at his presence. 4 Then Joseph said to his brothers, “Come close to me.” When they had done so, he said, “I am your brother Joseph, the one you sold into Egypt! 5 And now, do not be distressed and do not be angry with yourselves for selling me here, because it was to save lives that God sent me ahead of you. 6 For two years now there has been famine in the land, and for the next five years there will be no plowing and reaping. 7 But God sent me ahead of you to preserve for you a remnant on earth and to save your lives by a great deliverance. 8 “So then, it was not you who sent me here, but God. He made me father to Pharaoh, lord of his entire household and ruler of all Egypt. 9 Now hurry back to my father and say to him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says: God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me; don’t delay. 10 You shall live in the region of Goshen and be near me—you, your children and grandchildren, your flocks and herds, and all you have. 11 I will provide for you there, because five years of famine are still to come. Otherwise you and your household and all who belong to you will become destitute.’ 12 “You can see for yourselves, and so can my brother Benjamin, that it is really I who am speaking to you. 13 Tell my father about all the honor accorded me in Egypt and about everything you have seen. And bring my father down here quickly.” 14 Then he threw his arms around his brother Benjamin and wept, and Benjamin embraced him, weeping. 15 And he kissed all his brothers and wept over them. Afterward his brothers talked with him.

**Genesis 50:15–21 (NIV)**
15 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?” 16 So they sent word to Joseph, saying, “Your father left these instructions before he died: 17 ‘This is what you are to say to Joseph: I ask you to forgive your brothers the sins and the wrongs they committed in treating you so badly.’ Now please forgive the sins of the servants of the God of your father.” When their message came to him, Joseph wept. 18 His brothers then came and threw themselves down before him. “We are your slaves,” they said. 19 But Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Am I in the place of God? 20 You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives. 21 So then, don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.” And he reassured them and spoke kindly to them.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Gen 45:7.** NIV: “to save your lives by a great deliverance.” LSB: “to keep you alive for a great remnant of survivors.” The Hebrew word can mean an escape or the group who escape. The NIV stresses the rescue; the LSB stresses the people who are rescued.
- **Gen 50:20.** NIV: “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.” LSB: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” The Hebrew uses the same verb, “meant” or “planned,” for the brothers and for God, and the word for “harm” is the ordinary word for evil. The LSB keeps both features, so you see two plans in one event: theirs evil, God’s good.
- **Gen 50:21.** NIV: “he reassured them and spoke kindly to them.” LSB: “he comforted them and spoke to their heart.” “Spoke to their heart” is a Hebrew way of saying he spoke tenderly. Joseph didn’t just stop being angry; he reached for their hearts.

**Go deeper:** Piper’s sermon [“The Sale of Joseph and the Son of God”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-sale-of-joseph-and-the-son-of-god) traces the whole Joseph story to Christ. Billy Graham’s [“Why Is Forgiving Others So Important?”](https://billygraham.org/answers/why-is-forgiving-others-important) is a two-minute read. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Providential Purposes”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/seeking-him/providential-purposes/) is a short listen. BibleProject’s [Genesis 12–50 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-12-50/) shows how Genesis ends with God’s promise still on track.

**Reflection question:** Who in your family or past do you still need to forgive, and how can you, as a man, husband, and father, show your children this week what it looks like to say, “God meant it for good”?

**Lesson 38: Exodus: a people oppressed, and a deliverer born**

Good morning, Greg. Genesis ended with Joseph’s family safe in Egypt. Exodus opens about four hundred years later. Israel has grown into a great people, just as God promised Abraham, but “a new king, to whom Joseph meant nothing, came to power in Egypt” (1:8), and fear turned into slavery and then murder.

Two health workers stood in the gap. The midwives Shiphrah and Puah “feared God and did not do what the king of Egypt had told them to do; they let the boys live” (1:17). John Piper notes, “And God blessed them for doing what was right and disobeying the king.” As a nurse, you know what it means to hold life in your hands. Fearing God more than any boss or system is still the calling.

Then Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile. Piper says, “In the very darkest season of the worst child-killing, Moses was born.” Moses’ mother hid him, then placed him in a basket in the very river meant to kill him. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth says, “The preservation of Moses’ life didn’t just happen. God was superintending it.” Pharaoh’s own daughter rescued the boy and paid his mother to nurse him. Nancy’s verdict: “Coincidence? I don’t think so. Providence.”

Nancy also says this story shows why we need godly men: “Don’t we need men like that today? Men of courage, conviction, servants of God, men who know God, husbands, dads.” And Piper points past Moses to Jesus: “Moses delivered the people who were being oppressed. Jesus delivers oppressed and oppressor.”

**Exodus 1:8–22 (NIV)**
8 Then a new king, to whom Joseph meant nothing, came to power in Egypt. 9 “Look,” he said to his people, “the Israelites have become far too numerous for us. 10 Come, we must deal shrewdly with them or they will become even more numerous and, if war breaks out, will join our enemies, fight against us and leave the country.” 11 So they put slave masters over them to oppress them with forced labor, and they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. 12 But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread; so the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites 13 and worked them ruthlessly. 14 They made their lives bitter with harsh labor in brick and mortar and with all kinds of work in the fields; in all their harsh labor the Egyptians worked them ruthlessly. 15 The king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, whose names were Shiphrah and Puah, 16 “When you are helping the Hebrew women during childbirth on the delivery stool, if you see that the baby is a boy, kill him; but if it is a girl, let her live.” 17 The midwives, however, feared God and did not do what the king of Egypt had told them to do; they let the boys live. 18 Then the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and asked them, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” 19 The midwives answered Pharaoh, “Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women; they are vigorous and give birth before the midwives arrive.” 20 So God was kind to the midwives and the people increased and became even more numerous. 21 And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families of their own. 22 Then Pharaoh gave this order to all his people: “Every Hebrew boy that is born you must throw into the Nile, but let every girl live.”

**Exodus 2:1–10 (NIV)**
1 Now a man of the tribe of Levi married a Levite woman, 2 and she became pregnant and gave birth to a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him for three months. 3 But when she could hide him no longer, she got a papyrus basket for him and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in it and put it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile. 4 His sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him. 5 Then Pharaoh’s daughter went down to the Nile to bathe, and her attendants were walking along the riverbank. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her female slave to get it. 6 She opened it and saw the baby. He was crying, and she felt sorry for him. “This is one of the Hebrew babies,” she said. 7 Then his sister asked Pharaoh’s daughter, “Shall I go and get one of the Hebrew women to nurse the baby for you?” 8 “Yes, go,” she answered. So the girl went and got the baby’s mother. 9 Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this baby and nurse him for me, and I will pay you.” So the woman took the baby and nursed him. 10 When the child grew older, she took him to Pharaoh’s daughter and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, “I drew him out of the water.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 1:8.** NIV: “to whom Joseph meant nothing.” LSB: “who did not know Joseph.” The Hebrew says “did not know.” The NIV explains what that meant: the new king had no regard for Joseph or the debt Egypt owed him.
- **Exod 1:21.** NIV: “he gave them families of their own.” LSB: “He made households for them.” The Hebrew word is “houses,” which often means families. God gave the midwives the very thing they had protected for others.
- **Exod 2:2.** NIV: “a fine child.” LSB: “beautiful.” The Hebrew word is simply “good,” the same word as “God saw that it was good” in Genesis 1. Stephen says in Acts 7:20 that Moses was “no ordinary child.”
- **Exod 2:3, 5.** NIV: “a papyrus basket.” LSB: “an ark of papyrus reeds.” The Hebrew word is the same one used for Noah’s ark, and it appears only in these two stories. The LSB keeps “ark” so you can see the link: God again saves his chosen one through the waters in a sealed vessel.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Parenting under Providence”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/parenting-under-providence/) walks through all five women in Exodus 1–2. Piper’s sermon [“Abortion, Race, Gender, and Christ”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/abortion-race-gender-and-christ) works through Pharaoh’s plan and ends with Christ the greater Deliverer. BibleProject’s [Exodus 1–18 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-1-18/) sets the scene for the whole book.

**Lesson 38: Exodus: a people oppressed, and a deliverer born**

Good morning. Genesis ended with Joseph’s family safe in Egypt. Exodus opens about four hundred years later. Israel has grown into a great people, just as God promised, but “a new king, to whom Joseph meant nothing, came to power in Egypt” (1:8), and fear turned into slavery and then murder.

God’s rescue began with women. The midwives Shiphrah and Puah “feared God and did not do what the king of Egypt had told them to do; they let the boys live” (1:17). Then a Levite mother hid her son for three months. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth says, “She exercises faith, which delivers her from fear.” She also notes how carefully this mother worked: she sealed the basket, placed it where Pharaoh’s daughter would come, and set the baby’s sister to watch. “There was intentionality.”

A Revive Our Hearts devotional says, “This woman put her baby in a basket and placed him in the very river intended for his death.” And “She didn’t know that at the time; she only knew she would trust the Lord.” Pharaoh’s own daughter rescued the boy and even paid his mother to nurse him. Nancy says, “The preservation of Moses’ life didn’t just happen. God was superintending it.”

Nancy encourages mothers: “Now, let me remind you that God may work in your children’s lives in ways that are different than you might expect.” And “Pharaoh was plotting for the extermination of God’s people, but God was planning for their emancipation.” John Piper adds, “In the very darkest season of the worst child-killing, Moses was born.”

**Exodus 1:8–22 (NIV)**
8 Then a new king, to whom Joseph meant nothing, came to power in Egypt. 9 “Look,” he said to his people, “the Israelites have become far too numerous for us. 10 Come, we must deal shrewdly with them or they will become even more numerous and, if war breaks out, will join our enemies, fight against us and leave the country.” 11 So they put slave masters over them to oppress them with forced labor, and they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. 12 But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread; so the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites 13 and worked them ruthlessly. 14 They made their lives bitter with harsh labor in brick and mortar and with all kinds of work in the fields; in all their harsh labor the Egyptians worked them ruthlessly. 15 The king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, whose names were Shiphrah and Puah, 16 “When you are helping the Hebrew women during childbirth on the delivery stool, if you see that the baby is a boy, kill him; but if it is a girl, let her live.” 17 The midwives, however, feared God and did not do what the king of Egypt had told them to do; they let the boys live. 18 Then the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and asked them, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” 19 The midwives answered Pharaoh, “Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women; they are vigorous and give birth before the midwives arrive.” 20 So God was kind to the midwives and the people increased and became even more numerous. 21 And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families of their own. 22 Then Pharaoh gave this order to all his people: “Every Hebrew boy that is born you must throw into the Nile, but let every girl live.”

**Exodus 2:1–10 (NIV)**
1 Now a man of the tribe of Levi married a Levite woman, 2 and she became pregnant and gave birth to a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him for three months. 3 But when she could hide him no longer, she got a papyrus basket for him and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in it and put it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile. 4 His sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him. 5 Then Pharaoh’s daughter went down to the Nile to bathe, and her attendants were walking along the riverbank. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her female slave to get it. 6 She opened it and saw the baby. He was crying, and she felt sorry for him. “This is one of the Hebrew babies,” she said. 7 Then his sister asked Pharaoh’s daughter, “Shall I go and get one of the Hebrew women to nurse the baby for you?” 8 “Yes, go,” she answered. So the girl went and got the baby’s mother. 9 Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this baby and nurse him for me, and I will pay you.” So the woman took the baby and nursed him. 10 When the child grew older, she took him to Pharaoh’s daughter and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, “I drew him out of the water.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Exod 1:8.** NIV: “to whom Joseph meant nothing.” LSB: “who did not know Joseph.” The Hebrew says “did not know.” The NIV explains what that meant: the new king had no regard for Joseph or the debt Egypt owed him.
- **Exod 1:21.** NIV: “he gave them families of their own.” LSB: “He made households for them.” The Hebrew word is “houses,” which often means families. God gave the midwives the very thing they had protected for others.
- **Exod 2:2.** NIV: “a fine child.” LSB: “beautiful.” The Hebrew word is simply “good,” the same word as “God saw that it was good” in Genesis 1. Stephen says in Acts 7:20 that Moses was “no ordinary child.”
- **Exod 2:3, 5.** NIV: “a papyrus basket.” LSB: “an ark of papyrus reeds.” The Hebrew word is the same one used for Noah’s ark, and it appears only in these two stories. The LSB keeps “ark” so you can see the link: God again saves his chosen one through the waters in a sealed vessel.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Parenting under Providence”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/parenting-under-providence/) walks through all five women in Exodus 1–2. The short devotional [“Put It in a Basket”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/devotional/daily-reflections/put-it-in-a-basket/) is a one-minute read. Piper’s sermon [“Abortion, Race, Gender, and Christ”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/abortion-race-gender-and-christ) ends with Christ the greater Deliverer. BibleProject’s [Exodus 1–18 overview](https://bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-1-18/) sets the scene.

**Reflection question:** What do you need to “put in a basket” and trust God with today, and how can you, as a woman, wife, and mother, combine careful effort with quiet faith for your husband and children?
