**Lesson 98: Job: I know that my Redeemer lives**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard a crushed heart curse the day of its birth. Today Job wants his words cut into rock forever, because he has come to a sentence he will not let go: “I know that my redeemer lives, and that in the end he will stand on the earth. And after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God; I myself will see him with my own eyes—I, and not another. How my heart yearns within me!” (19:23–27).

John Piper said that earlier Job had only asked, “If a man dies, shall he live again?” “Here he’s no longer asking the question, he’s making the affirmation.” Job “rises to the level that he has a redeemer — God is not ultimately an enemy, but he is his redeemer — and this disease will not have the last word.” In another message Piper said, “Job is finally sure that beyond the grave he will meet God as a Redeemer and not an angry Judge.” That confidence does not end all of Job’s questions. In chapter 23 his complaint is still bitter: “If only I knew where to find him.” “I would state my case before him.” He cannot perceive God in front or behind, on the left or the right, and yet he says, “But he knows the way that I take; when he has tested me, I will come forth as gold.” He is terrified of the majesty he cannot see, and he will not be silenced (23:1–17). Faith here is not a calm that never aches. It is a yearning: I will see God, and my Redeemer lives.

A man, a husband, and a father may have to say both things in the same week: I cannot find him, and I know that my Redeemer lives. Hold the second sentence when the first is still true.

**Job 19:23–27 (NIV)**
23 “Oh, that my words were recorded, that they were written on a scroll, 24 that they were inscribed with an iron tool on lead, or engraved in rock forever! 25 I know that my redeemer lives, and that in the end he will stand on the earth. 26 And after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God; 27 I myself will see him with my own eyes—I, and not another. How my heart yearns within me!

**Job 23:1–17 (NIV)**
1 Then Job replied: 2 “Even today my complaint is bitter; his hand is heavy in spite of my groaning. 3 If only I knew where to find him; if only I could go to his dwelling! 4 I would state my case before him and fill my mouth with arguments. 5 I would find out what he would answer me, and consider what he would say to me. 6 Would he vigorously oppose me? No, he would not press charges against me. 7 There the upright can establish their innocence before him, and there I would be delivered forever from my judge. 8 “But if I go to the east, he is not there; if I go to the west, I do not find him. 9 When he is at work in the north, I do not see him; when he turns to the south, I catch no glimpse of him. 10 But he knows the way that I take; when he has tested me, I will come forth as gold. 11 My feet have closely followed his steps; I have kept to his way without turning aside. 12 I have not departed from the commands of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my daily bread. 13 “But he stands alone, and who can oppose him? He does whatever he pleases. 14 He carries out his decree against me, and many such plans he still has in store. 15 That is why I am terrified before him; when I think of all this, I fear him. 16 God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me. 17 Yet I am not silenced by the darkness, by the thick darkness that covers my face.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Job 19:25.** NIV: “I know that my redeemer lives, and that in the end he will stand on the earth.” LSB: “As for me, I know that my Redeemer lives, And at the last He will rise up over the dust of this world.” The LSB’s “Redeemer” and “rise up over the dust” make the hope sharper: the one who will stand at the end is not a maybe. He is Job’s Redeemer.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s message [“Job: When the Righteous Suffer, Part 2”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-2) at Desiring God (2008) opens Job 19:25–27 as affirmation, not only a question. His sermon [“Job: Wrestling with Suffering”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-wrestling-with-suffering) traces the same hope: Job will meet God as Redeemer, not as an angry Judge.

**Reflection question:** Job said, “I know that my redeemer lives,” and also, “If only I knew where to find him.” As a man, husband, and father, where is your complaint still bitter, and how will you hold onto the Redeemer who lives and will stand on the earth?

lessons.title: Job: then the Lord answered Job out of the storm

sources.label: John Piper, Job: The Revelation of God in Suffering (Desiring God, 1985)

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 99: Job: then the Lord answered Job out of the storm**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Job confessed, “I know that my redeemer lives,” even while he still could not find God. Today the LORD answers him. “Then the LORD spoke to Job out of the storm. He said: ‘Who is this that obscures my plans with words without knowledge? Brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer me.’” Then the questions come, one after another: Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundation? Who marked off its dimensions? Who shut up the sea behind doors when it burst forth from the womb? “Have you ever given orders to the morning, or shown the dawn its place, that it might take the earth by the edges and shake the wicked out of it?” “Have you journeyed to the springs of the sea or walked in the recesses of the deep? Have the gates of death been shown to you?” “Have you comprehended the vast expanses of the earth? Tell me, if you know all this.” Job is a real sufferer, and he is also a finite man being shown the size of the world he does not run.

John Piper said someone might think God is criticizing Elihu in 38:2, “but that is not the case. He is speaking to Job and criticizing Job.” “We know this because in 42:3 when God is through speaking, Job quotes these words from 38:2 and applies them to himself.” After more of the Lord’s questions, “The LORD said to Job: ‘Will the one who contends with the Almighty correct him? Let him who accuses God answer him!’” Job answers, “I am unworthy—how can I reply to you? I put my hand over my mouth. I spoke once, but I have no answer— twice, but I will say no more.” Piper put the point sharply: “a finite creature who has no wisdom to run this world and is utterly ignorant of 99.999% of its processes has no business instructing his Maker and Ruler how to run the world, even condemning God for the way he runs it.” BibleProject says, “In a surprising turn, God visits Job in a powerful storm and responds to his prayers. A whirlwind of rhetorical questions exposes Job’s lack of understanding.” What God asked of Job “is trust in his wisdom and character.”

A man, a husband, and a father will meet days that cannot be explained. The Lord’s questions are not cruelty. They are a mercy that puts you back in your place, with your hand over your mouth, and with a God big enough to be trusted in the storm.

**Job 38:1–18 (NIV)**
1 Then the LORD spoke to Job out of the storm. He said: 2 “Who is this that obscures my plans with words without knowledge? 3 Brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer me. 4 “Where were you when I laid the earth’s foundation? Tell me, if you understand. 5 Who marked off its dimensions? Surely you know! Who stretched a measuring line across it? 6 On what were its footings set, or who laid its cornerstone— 7 while the morning stars sang together and all the angels shouted for joy? 8 “Who shut up the sea behind doors when it burst forth from the womb, 9 when I made the clouds its garment and wrapped it in thick darkness, 10 when I fixed limits for it and set its doors and bars in place, 11 when I said, ‘This far you may come and no farther; here is where your proud waves halt’? 12 “Have you ever given orders to the morning, or shown the dawn its place, 13 that it might take the earth by the edges and shake the wicked out of it? 14 The earth takes shape like clay under a seal; its features stand out like those of a garment. 15 The wicked are denied their light, and their upraised arm is broken. 16 “Have you journeyed to the springs of the sea or walked in the recesses of the deep? 17 Have the gates of death been shown to you? Have you seen the gates of the deepest darkness? 18 Have you comprehended the vast expanses of the earth? Tell me, if you know all this.

**Job 40:1–5 (NIV)**
1 The LORD said to Job: 2 “Will the one who contends with the Almighty correct him? Let him who accuses God answer him!” 3 Then Job answered the LORD: 4 “I am unworthy—how can I reply to you? I put my hand over my mouth. 5 I spoke once, but I have no answer— twice, but I will say no more.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Job 38:1.** NIV: “Then the LORD spoke to Job out of the storm.” LSB: “Then Yahweh answered Job out of the whirlwind and said.” The LSB’s “answered” and “whirlwind” make this a reply from inside the storm, not only a speech about it.
- **Job 40:4.** NIV: “I am unworthy—how can I reply to you? I put my hand over my mouth.” LSB: “Behold, I am insignificant; what can I respond to You? I place my hand over my mouth.” Both stop Job’s mouth. The LSB’s “insignificant” underlines how small he is before the Maker he has been questioning.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s message [“Job: The Revelation of God in Suffering”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-the-revelation-of-god-in-suffering) at Desiring God (July 28, 1985) opens Job 38–41 as God’s answer from the whirlwind, and as Job’s place as a finite creature. BibleProject’s [Book of Job guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-job/) describes that storm as “a whirlwind of rhetorical questions” that calls Job to trust God’s wisdom and character.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been instructing your Maker how to run the world? What would it look like, today, to put your hand over your mouth and trust his wisdom in the storm?

lessons.title: Job: repentance, restoration, and praying for your friends

sources.label: John Piper, Job: Reversal in Suffering (Desiring God)
Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, Fallen on the Rock (Revive Our Hearts)

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 100: Job: repentance, restoration, and praying for your friends**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD answered Job out of the storm, and Job put his hand over his mouth. Today Job speaks again, and then he prays for his friends. “I know that you can do all things; no purpose of yours can be thwarted.” He takes the Lord’s charge onto himself: “You asked, ‘Who is this that obscures my plans without knowledge?’ Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know.” “My ears had heard of you but now my eyes have seen you. Therefore I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” This is not Job polishing his record. It is a man who has seen the Lord, and who cannot stand on his own righteousness anymore.

Then the LORD turns to Eliphaz and the two friends: “I am angry with you and your two friends, because you have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has.” John Piper noted that God had accused Job of darkening counsel without knowledge, “so he doesn’t mean that everything Job said had been right. But when it comes to the basic dispute between Job and these three friends, he was in the right.” The friends must go to Job with a sacrifice. “My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly.” Piper said Job “is now being asked to love his enemies and pray for those who abused him.” “He is being asked to bless those who cursed him and not to return evil for evil.” “And he is still a very sick man! God has not yet reversed his misery.” Then the line the book has been waiting for: “After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes and gave him twice as much as he had before.” BibleProject says, “Job demanded a full explanation from God, and what God asked Job for is trust in his wisdom and character. And so Job responds with humility and repentance.”

As a man, husband, and father, you may be asked to pray for people who have wounded you before you see any reversal. Job’s restoration comes on the far side of repentance — and on the far side of intercession.

**Job 42:1–17 (NIV)**
1 Then Job replied to the LORD: 2 “I know that you can do all things; no purpose of yours can be thwarted. 3 You asked, ‘Who is this that obscures my plans without knowledge?’ Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know. 4 “You said, ‘Listen now, and I will speak; I will question you, and you shall answer me.’ 5 My ears had heard of you but now my eyes have seen you. 6 Therefore I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” 7 After the LORD had said these things to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “I am angry with you and your two friends, because you have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has. 8 So now take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly. You have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has.” 9 So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite did what the LORD told them; and the LORD accepted Job’s prayer. 10 After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes and gave him twice as much as he had before. 11 All his brothers and sisters and everyone who had known him before came and ate with him in his house. They comforted and consoled him over all the trouble the LORD had brought on him, and each one gave him a piece of silver and a gold ring. 12 The LORD blessed the latter part of Job’s life more than the former part. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen and a thousand donkeys. 13 And he also had seven sons and three daughters. 14 The first daughter he named Jemimah, the second Keziah and the third Keren-Happuch. 15 Nowhere in all the land were there found women as beautiful as Job’s daughters, and their father granted them an inheritance along with their brothers. 16 After this, Job lived a hundred and forty years; he saw his children and their children to the fourth generation. 17 And so Job died, an old man and full of years.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Job 42:6.** NIV: “Therefore I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” LSB: “Therefore I reject myself, And I repent in dust and ashes.” The turn is the same: Job is done defending himself, and he repents.
- **Job 42:10.** NIV: “After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes and gave him twice as much as he had before.” LSB: “And Yahweh restored the fortunes of Job when he prayed for his friends, and Yahweh increased all that Job had twofold.” The LSB ties the restoration to the moment of the prayer.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Fallen on the Rock”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/fallen-rock/) at Revive Our Hearts lingers over Job 42:5–6: a man who has seen God, with “no more self-righteousness,” pleading for mercy. John Piper’s message [“Job: Reversal in Suffering”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-reversal-in-suffering) traces the friends’ need to go to Job, and Job’s call to pray for those who abused him while he is still sick. BibleProject’s [Book of Job guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-job/) frames the ending as humility, repentance, and trust.

lessons.title: Job: repentance, restoration, and praying for your friends

sources.label: Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, Fallen on the Rock (Revive Our Hearts)
John Piper, Job: Reversal in Suffering (Desiring God)

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 100: Job: repentance, restoration, and praying for your friends**

Good morning. Yesterday the LORD answered Job out of the storm, and Job put his hand over his mouth. Today Job speaks again, and then he prays for his friends. “I know that you can do all things; no purpose of yours can be thwarted.” He takes the Lord’s charge onto himself: “You asked, ‘Who is this that obscures my plans without knowledge?’ Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know.” “My ears had heard of you but now my eyes have seen you. Therefore I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, teaching Job 42:5–6, lingered over Job’s words: “Oh God, I had heard of you with the hearing of my ear, but now my eye has seen you. And now I abhor myself. And I repent in dust and ashes.” Then she said, “No more self-righteousness, rather a broken man pleading with God for mercy.” This is not Job polishing his record. It is a man who has seen the Lord, and who cannot stand on his own righteousness anymore.

Then the LORD turns to Eliphaz and the two friends: “I am angry with you and your two friends, because you have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has.” John Piper noted that God had accused Job of darkening counsel without knowledge, “so he doesn’t mean that everything Job said had been right. But when it comes to the basic dispute between Job and these three friends, he was in the right.” The friends must go to Job with a sacrifice. “My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly.” Piper said Job “is now being asked to love his enemies and pray for those who abused him.” “He is being asked to bless those who cursed him and not to return evil for evil.” “And he is still a very sick man! God has not yet reversed his misery.” Then the line the book has been waiting for: “After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes and gave him twice as much as he had before.” BibleProject says, “Job demanded a full explanation from God, and what God asked Job for is trust in his wisdom and character. And so Job responds with humility and repentance.”

As a woman, wife, and mother, you may be asked to pray for people who have wounded you before you see any reversal. Job’s restoration comes on the far side of repentance — and on the far side of intercession.

**Job 42:1–17 (NIV)**
1 Then Job replied to the LORD: 2 “I know that you can do all things; no purpose of yours can be thwarted. 3 You asked, ‘Who is this that obscures my plans without knowledge?’ Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know. 4 “You said, ‘Listen now, and I will speak; I will question you, and you shall answer me.’ 5 My ears had heard of you but now my eyes have seen you. 6 Therefore I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” 7 After the LORD had said these things to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “I am angry with you and your two friends, because you have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has. 8 So now take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly. You have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has.” 9 So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite did what the LORD told them; and the LORD accepted Job’s prayer. 10 After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes and gave him twice as much as he had before. 11 All his brothers and sisters and everyone who had known him before came and ate with him in his house. They comforted and consoled him over all the trouble the LORD had brought on him, and each one gave him a piece of silver and a gold ring. 12 The LORD blessed the latter part of Job’s life more than the former part. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen and a thousand donkeys. 13 And he also had seven sons and three daughters. 14 The first daughter he named Jemimah, the second Keziah and the third Keren-Happuch. 15 Nowhere in all the land were there found women as beautiful as Job’s daughters, and their father granted them an inheritance along with their brothers. 16 After this, Job lived a hundred and forty years; he saw his children and their children to the fourth generation. 17 And so Job died, an old man and full of years.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Job 42:6.** NIV: “Therefore I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes.” LSB: “Therefore I reject myself, And I repent in dust and ashes.” The turn is the same: Job is done defending himself, and he repents.
- **Job 42:10.** NIV: “After Job had prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes and gave him twice as much as he had before.” LSB: “And Yahweh restored the fortunes of Job when he prayed for his friends, and Yahweh increased all that Job had twofold.” The LSB ties the restoration to the moment of the prayer.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Fallen on the Rock”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/fallen-rock/) at Revive Our Hearts lingers over Job 42:5–6: a man who has seen God, with “no more self-righteousness,” pleading for mercy. John Piper’s message [“Job: Reversal in Suffering”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-reversal-in-suffering) traces the friends’ need to go to Job, and Job’s call to pray for those who abused him while he is still sick. BibleProject’s [Book of Job guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-job/) frames the ending as humility, repentance, and trust.

**Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and mother, whom do you need to pray for before you have been “paid back”? What would repentance in dust and ashes look like in your house this week?

lessons.title: Psalms: two ways, and the Lord's Anointed

sources.label: John Piper, Meditate on the Word of the Lord Day and Night (Desiring God)

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 101: Psalms: two ways, and the Lord's Anointed**

Good morning, Greg. We have just watched Job put his hand over his mouth, repent, and pray for his friends. Today we open the book of Psalms, the prayer book of God’s people. Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 stand at the front door. “Blessed is the one who does not walk in step with the wicked or stand in the way that sinners take or sit in the company of mockers, but whose delight is in the law of the LORD, and who meditates on his law day and night.” That person is “like a tree planted by streams of water.” The wicked “are like chaff that the wind blows away.” “For the LORD watches over the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked leads to destruction.” Then Psalm 2 asks, “Why do the nations conspire and the peoples plot in vain?” The kings of the earth rise up “against the LORD and against his anointed.” The One enthroned in heaven laughs, and he says of the Son, “You are my son; today I have become your father. Ask me, and I will make the nations your inheritance.” The psalm ends with a warning and a welcome: “Kiss his son, or he will be angry.” “Blessed are all who take refuge in him.”

BibleProject says, “Psalm 1 starts by celebrating the person who is ‘blessed’ because they meditate on the Torah, prayerfully reading and obeying it.” “The book of Psalms is being offered as a new Torah that will teach God’s people about the lifelong practice of prayer.” “Psalm 2 is a poetic reflection on God’s promise to King David.” From David’s line would come “a messianic (that is, ‘anointed’) King, who would establish God’s Kingdom over the world.” “The psalm concludes by saying that all those to take refuge in this messianic king will be ‘blessed,’ the same word used in the opening of Psalm 1.” “Together, these two poems tell us that the book of Psalms is designed to be the prayer book of God’s people, who are striving to be faithful to the commands of the Torah and hoping and waiting for the messianic kingdom.” John Piper said, “The central point of this psalm is made in verse 2.” “The person who delights in God’s law so much that he meditates on it day and night is delivered from the ways of the wicked and sinners and scoffers, and is made fruitful and durable and prosperous.” Why begin here? “The Psalter is the prayer book of the Bible.” “I begin Prayer Week with Psalm 1 because the Bible begins its prayer book with Psalm 1.”

As a man, husband, and father, two ways are set before you, and a King is set before you. Delight in the law of the LORD. Take refuge in his Anointed. That is how a life of prayer starts.

**Psalm 1:1–6 (NIV)**
1 Blessed is the one who does not walk in step with the wicked or stand in the way that sinners take or sit in the company of mockers, 2 but whose delight is in the law of the LORD, and who meditates on his law day and night. 3 That person is like a tree planted by streams of water, which yields its fruit in season and whose leaf does not wither— whatever they do prospers. 4 Not so the wicked! They are like chaff that the wind blows away. 5 Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. 6 For the LORD watches over the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked leads to destruction.

**Psalm 2:1–12 (NIV)**
1 Why do the nations conspire and the peoples plot in vain? 2 The kings of the earth rise up and the rulers band together against the LORD and against his anointed, saying, 3 “Let us break their chains and throw off their shackles.” 4 The One enthroned in heaven laughs; the Lord scoffs at them. 5 He rebukes them in his anger and terrifies them in his wrath, saying, 6 “I have installed my king on Zion, my holy mountain.” 7 I will proclaim the LORD’s decree: He said to me, “You are my son; today I have become your father. 8 Ask me, and I will make the nations your inheritance, the ends of the earth your possession. 9 You will break them with a rod of iron; you will dash them to pieces like pottery.” 10 Therefore, you kings, be wise; be warned, you rulers of the earth. 11 Serve the LORD with fear and celebrate his rule with trembling. 12 Kiss his son, or he will be angry and your way will lead to your destruction, for his wrath can flare up in a moment. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Psalms guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-psalms/) reads Psalms 1–2 as the doorway to the Psalter: a prayer book for people who meditate on God’s teaching and take refuge in the messianic King. John Piper’s message [“Meditate on the Word of the Lord Day and Night”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/meditate-on-the-word-of-the-lord-day-and-night) takes Psalm 1:2 as the center, and begins a prayer week here because “the Psalter is the prayer book of the Bible.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, which “way” is shaping your house right now — the counsel of the wicked, or delight in the law of the LORD? How will you take refuge in the Lord’s Anointed this week?

lessons.title: Psalms: the heavens declare, and the Lord is my shepherd

sources.label: John Piper, Restful Words for Labor Day (Desiring God)

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 102: Psalms: the heavens declare, and the Lord is my shepherd**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the Psalter opened with two ways, and with the Lord’s Anointed. Today the heavens preach, and the Shepherd keeps. “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands. Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge.” “The law of the LORD is perfect, refreshing the soul.” “The precepts of the LORD are right, giving joy to the heart.” “The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever.” The psalm turns into a prayer: “But who can discern their own errors? Forgive my hidden faults.” “Keep your servant also from willful sins; may they not rule over me.” “May these words of my mouth and this meditation of my heart be pleasing in your sight, LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer.” Then the best-known shepherd song in the Bible: “The LORD is my shepherd, I lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures, he leads me beside quiet waters, he refreshes my soul.” “Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.” “Surely your goodness and love will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.”

John Piper said that in a hard season this psalm itself became the place of rest: “the psalm itself was green pasture, the psalm itself was still water, the psalm itself restored my soul.” “Day by day, I lived by it, I ate it, I drank it in, and sure enough, in every situation it came true: The Lord was my shepherd, I did not want.” He also learned, from David, that “it is good not to talk very long about God without talking to God.” Notice the turn in the valley: the psalm moves from “he” to “you.” “We are more prone to talk about God when we are in the green pasture and more prone to cry out to God when we enter some fearful ravine.” Psalm 19 does the same kind of work: the heavens speak, the law of the LORD refreshes, and then the singer asks to be kept and forgiven. Theology becomes prayer.

As a man, husband, and father, let the skies and the Word tell you the glory of God today — and then speak back to the Shepherd who is with you in the valley. You lack nothing in his care.

**Psalm 19:1–14 (NIV)**
1 The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands. 2 Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge. 3 They have no speech, they use no words; no sound is heard from them. 4 Yet their voice goes out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world. In the heavens God has pitched a tent for the sun. 5 It is like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, like a champion rejoicing to run his course. 6 It rises at one end of the heavens and makes its circuit to the other; nothing is deprived of its warmth. 7 The law of the LORD is perfect, refreshing the soul. The statutes of the LORD are trustworthy, making wise the simple. 8 The precepts of the LORD are right, giving joy to the heart. The commands of the LORD are radiant, giving light to the eyes. 9 The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever. The decrees of the LORD are firm, and all of them are righteous. 10 They are more precious than gold, than much pure gold; they are sweeter than honey, than honey from the honeycomb. 11 By them your servant is warned; in keeping them there is great reward. 12 But who can discern their own errors? Forgive my hidden faults. 13 Keep your servant also from willful sins; may they not rule over me. Then I will be blameless, innocent of great transgression. 14 May these words of my mouth and this meditation of my heart be pleasing in your sight, LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer.

**Psalm 23:1–6 (NIV)**
1 The LORD is my shepherd, I lack nothing. 2 He makes me lie down in green pastures, he leads me beside quiet waters, 3 he refreshes my soul. He guides me along the right paths for his name’s sake. 4 Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. 5 You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. 6 Surely your goodness and love will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Psalm 23:1.** NIV: “The LORD is my shepherd, I lack nothing.” LSB: “Yahweh is my shepherd, I shall not want.” The promise is the same: under this Shepherd, you are not left in need.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s message [“Restful Words for Labor Day”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/restful-words-for-labor-day) lingers over Psalm 23 as green pasture and still water, and as a psalm that teaches us not to talk very long about God without talking to God. BibleProject’s [Book of Psalms guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-psalms/) helps set these prayers inside the Psalter as the prayer book of God’s people.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where is the darkest valley right now, and how will you talk to the Shepherd there — not only talk about him? What hidden fault do you need to bring to your Rock and Redeemer?

lessons.title: Psalms: the Lord is my light, and the joy of forgiveness
lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 103: Psalms: the Lord is my light, and the joy of forgiveness**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the heavens declared God’s glory, and the LORD was our shepherd. Today the psalms teach us to seek his face, and to confess so that we can be glad. “The LORD is my light and my salvation— whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life— of whom shall I be afraid?” David’s one request is not small: “One thing I ask from the LORD, this only do I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and to seek him in his temple.” “My heart says of you, ‘Seek his face!’ Your face, LORD, I will seek.” “Wait for the LORD; be strong and take heart and wait for the LORD.” Then Psalm 32 opens with a different kind of blessing: “Blessed is the one whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the one whose sin the LORD does not count against them and in whose spirit is no deceit.” When David kept silent, his bones wasted away. “Then I acknowledged my sin to you and did not cover up my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD.’ And you forgave the guilt of my sin.” “You are my hiding place.” “Rejoice in the LORD and be glad, you righteous; sing, all you who are upright in heart!”

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 104: Psalms: God is our refuge, and my soul thirsts for you**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD was our light, and forgiveness made a glad heart. Today we learn to take refuge, and to thirst. “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble.” “Therefore we will not fear, though the earth give way and the mountains fall into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam and the mountains quake with their surging.” “There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God.” “The LORD Almighty is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.” “He says, ‘Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.’” Psalm 63 is more intimate, and just as urgent: “You, God, are my God, earnestly I seek you; I thirst for you, my whole being longs for you, in a dry and parched land where there is no water.” David remembers God’s love as “better than life,” and he says, “I will praise you as long as I live, and in your name I will lift up my hands.” “On my bed I remember you; I think of you through the watches of the night. Because you are my help, I sing in the shadow of your wings. I cling to you; your right hand upholds me.”

These two psalms belong together in a fearful world. Psalm 46 looks at collapsing mountains and still says, “We will not fear,” because God is an ever-present help, and because he will be exalted in the earth. “Be still, and know that I am God” is not a call to numbness. It is a call to stop, and to know who is God when the ground gives way. Psalm 63 shows what that knowledge becomes in a dry land: thirst, praise, memory in the night, and a person clinging to God. The prayer book does not only teach us what to say in public trouble. It teaches us how to seek God on the bed, in the watches of the night, when the land feels parched.

As a man, husband, and father, the earth may feel like it is giving way in your house, or it may only feel dry. Either way, God is a refuge, and he is the One your soul can thirst for. Be still, and seek him.

**Psalm 46:1–11 (NIV)**
1 God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble. 2 Therefore we will not fear, though the earth give way and the mountains fall into the heart of the sea, 3 though its waters roar and foam and the mountains quake with their surging. 4 There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells. 5 God is within her, she will not fall; God will help her at break of day. 6 Nations are in uproar, kingdoms fall; he lifts his voice, the earth melts. 7 The LORD Almighty is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. 8 Come and see what the LORD has done, the desolations he has brought on the earth. 9 He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth. He breaks the bow and shatters the spear; he burns the shields with fire. 10 He says, “Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” 11 The LORD Almighty is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.

**Psalm 63:1–11 (NIV)**
1 You, God, are my God, earnestly I seek you; I thirst for you, my whole being longs for you, in a dry and parched land where there is no water. 2 I have seen you in the sanctuary and beheld your power and your glory. 3 Because your love is better than life, my lips will glorify you. 4 I will praise you as long as I live, and in your name I will lift up my hands. 5 I will be fully satisfied as with the richest of foods; with singing lips my mouth will praise you. 6 On my bed I remember you; I think of you through the watches of the night. 7 Because you are my help, I sing in the shadow of your wings. 8 I cling to you; your right hand upholds me. 9 Those who want to kill me will be destroyed; they will go down to the depths of the earth. 10 They will be given over to the sword and become food for jackals. 11 But the king will rejoice in God; all who swear by God will glory in him, while the mouths of liars will be silenced.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Psalms guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-psalms/) frames the Psalter as the prayer book of God’s people. Psalm 46 gives words for a world that feels like it is giving way (“Be still, and know that I am God”), and Psalm 63 gives words for a dry land: “earnestly I seek you; I thirst for you.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where does the ground feel like it is giving way, or the land feel dry? What would it look like tonight to be still, to remember God on your bed, and to cling to him?

lessons.title: Psalms: when the wicked prosper, and teach us to number our days
lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 105: Psalms: when the wicked prosper, and teach us to number our days**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God was our refuge, and a dry soul learned to thirst for him. Today Asaph tells the truth about a faith that almost slipped, and Moses teaches us to number our days. “Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. But as for me, my feet had almost slipped; I had nearly lost my foothold. For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” They looked, to him, healthy and “always free of care.” “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure and have washed my hands in innocence.” “All day long I have been afflicted, and every morning brings new punishments.” The turn comes when he enters God’s sanctuary: “then I understood their final destiny.” “Those who are far from you will perish.” Then the confession that holds the psalm together: “Yet I am always with you; you hold me by my right hand.” “Whom have I in heaven but you? And earth has nothing I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” “But as for me, it is good to be near God.” Moses prays next, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout all generations. Before the mountains were born or you brought forth the whole world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God. You turn people back to dust, saying, ‘Return to dust, you mortals.’ A thousand years in your sight are like a day that has just gone by, or like a watch in the night.” “Our days may come to seventy years, or eighty, if our strength endures; yet the best of them are but trouble and sorrow, for they quickly pass, and we fly away.” So he asks, “Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” “Satisfy us in the morning with your unfailing love, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days.” “May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us— yes, establish the work of our hands.”

The prayer book does not hide envy or weariness. Asaph almost slipped when he measured God’s goodness by the ease of the wicked. The sanctuary gave him a longer view: their prosperity is not the last word, and God himself is the portion that remains when flesh and heart fail. Moses looks at the same God from the other side of time: he is our dwelling place in every generation, and our years are short. The wise heart is not the heart that envies, and it is not the heart that pretends it will live forever. It is the heart that stays near God, numbers its days, and asks him to establish the work of our hands.

As a man, husband, and father, you will see people who seem to prosper without God, and you will feel how short a life is. Let Asaph’s turn, and Moses’ prayer, teach you to want God as your portion, and to ask him for a heart of wisdom while it is still morning.

**Psalm 73:1–28 (NIV)**
1 Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. 2 But as for me, my feet had almost slipped; I had nearly lost my foothold. 3 For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. 4 They have no struggles; their bodies are healthy and strong. 5 They are free from common human burdens; they are not plagued by human ills. 6 Therefore pride is their necklace; they clothe themselves with violence. 7 From their callous hearts comes iniquity; their evil imaginations have no limits. 8 They scoff, and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression. 9 Their mouths lay claim to heaven, and their tongues take possession of the earth. 10 Therefore their people turn to them and drink up waters in abundance. 11 They say, “How would God know? Does the Most High know anything?” 12 This is what the wicked are like— always free of care, they go on amassing wealth. 13 Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure and have washed my hands in innocence. 14 All day long I have been afflicted, and every morning brings new punishments. 15 If I had spoken out like that, I would have betrayed your children. 16 When I tried to understand all this, it troubled me deeply 17 till I entered the sanctuary of God; then I understood their final destiny. 18 Surely you place them on slippery ground; you cast them down to ruin. 19 How suddenly are they destroyed, completely swept away by terrors! 20 They are like a dream when one awakes; when you arise, Lord, you will despise them as fantasies. 21 When my heart was grieved and my spirit embittered, 22 I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before you. 23 Yet I am always with you; you hold me by my right hand. 24 You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will take me into glory. 25 Whom have I in heaven but you? And earth has nothing I desire besides you. 26 My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. 27 Those who are far from you will perish; you destroy all who are unfaithful to you. 28 But as for me, it is good to be near God. I have made the Sovereign LORD my refuge; I will tell of all your deeds.

**Psalm 90:1–17 (NIV)**
1 Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout all generations. 2 Before the mountains were born or you brought forth the whole world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God. 3 You turn people back to dust, saying, “Return to dust, you mortals.” 4 A thousand years in your sight are like a day that has just gone by, or like a watch in the night. 5 Yet you sweep people away in the sleep of death— they are like the new grass of the morning: 6 In the morning it springs up new, but by evening it is dry and withered. 7 We are consumed by your anger and terrified by your indignation. 8 You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence. 9 All our days pass away under your wrath; we finish our years with a moan. 10 Our days may come to seventy years, or eighty, if our strength endures; yet the best of them are but trouble and sorrow, for they quickly pass, and we fly away. 11 If only we knew the power of your anger! Your wrath is as great as the fear that is your due. 12 Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom. 13 Relent, LORD! How long will it be? Have compassion on your servants. 14 Satisfy us in the morning with your unfailing love, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days. 15 Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, for as many years as we have seen trouble. 16 May your deeds be shown to your servants, your splendor to their children. 17 May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us— yes, establish the work of our hands.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Psalms guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-psalms/) presents the Psalter as the prayer book of God’s people, honest enough for doubt and envy, and wise enough to end in trust. Psalm 73 turns in the sanctuary from envy of the wicked to “God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” Psalm 90 asks God to teach us to number our days and to establish the work of our hands.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, whose prosperity has made your foot almost slip, and what would it mean to say, “Earth has nothing I desire besides you”? How will you number your days this week, and ask God to establish the work of your hands?

Does the Most High know anything?” 12 This is what the wicked are like— always free of care, they go on amassing wealth. 13 Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure and have washed my hands in innocence. 14 All day long I have been afflicted, and every morning brings new punishments. 15 If I had spoken out like that, I would have betrayed your children. 16 When I tried to understand all this, it troubled me deeply 17 till I entered the sanctuary of God; then I understood their final destiny. 18 Surely you place them on slippery ground; you cast them down to ruin. 19 How suddenly are they destroyed, completely swept away by terrors! 20 They are like a dream when one awakes; when you arise, Lord, you will despise them as fantasies. 21 When my heart was grieved and my spirit embittered, 22 I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before you. 23 Yet I am always with you; you hold me by my right hand. 24 You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will take me into glory. 25 Whom have I in heaven but you? And earth has nothing I desire besides you. 26 My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. 27 Those who are far from you will perish; you destroy all who are unfaithful to you. 28 But as for me, it is good to be near God. 1 Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout all generations. 2 Before the mountains were born or you brought forth the whole world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God. 3 You turn people back to dust, saying, “Return to dust, you mortals.” 4 A thousand years in your sight are like a day that has just gone by, or like a watch in the night. 5 Yet you sweep people away in the sleep of death— they are like the new grass of the morning: 6 In the morning it springs up new, but by evening it is dry and withered. 7 We are consumed by your anger and terrified by your indignation. 8 You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence. 9 All our days pass away under your wrath; we finish our years with a moan. 10 Our days may come to seventy years, or eighty, if our strength endures; yet the best of them are but trouble and sorrow, for they quickly pass, and we fly away. 11 If only we knew the power of your anger! Your wrath is as great as the fear that is your due. 12 Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom. 13 Relent, LORD! How long will it be? Have compassion on your servants. 14 Satisfy us in the morning with your unfailing love, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days. 15 Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, for as many years as we have seen trouble. 16 May your deeds be shown to your servants, your splendor to their children. 17 May the favor of the Lord our God rest on us; establish the work of our hands for us— yes, establish the work of our hands.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Psalms guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-psalms/) presents the Psalter as the prayer book of God’s people, honest enough for doubt and envy, and wise enough to end in trust. **Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and mother, whose prosperity has made your foot almost slip, and what would it mean to say, “Earth has nothing I desire besides you”? How will you number your days this week, and ask God to establish the work of your hands?

**Lesson 106: Psalms: bless the Lord, O my soul; my help comes from the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Asaph almost slipped when he envied the wicked, and Moses taught us to number our days. Today the psalms teach a soul to remember, and a traveler to look for help in the right place. “Praise the LORD, my soul; all my inmost being, praise his holy name. Praise the LORD, my soul, and forget not all his benefits— who forgives all your sins and heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit and crowns you with love and compassion, who satisfies your desires with good things so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.” “The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love.” “he does not treat us as our sins deserve or repay us according to our iniquities. For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his love for those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.” “As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him; for he knows how we are formed, he remembers that we are dust.” The psalm ends where it began: “Praise the LORD, all his works everywhere in his dominion. Praise the LORD, my soul.” John Piper said, “What does it mean to bless the Lord? It means to speak well of his greatness and goodness.” “Blessing the Lord means speaking or singing about the goodness and greatness of the Lord.” And that speech “must come from the soul.” “Blessing God with the mouth without the soul would be hypocrisy.” David, Piper said, “is preaching to himself that it not happen.” “Come, soul, look at the greatness and goodness of God. Join my mouth, and let us bless the Lord with our whole being.” Piper asked what this psalm calls us to do for our children, our spouses, our churches, and our own souls. “The answer is: Bless the Lord.” He even dared to say that “there is perhaps nothing that you can do for your children to help them fear God and keep covenant with God and obey God that will be more effective than your own blessing the Lord continually in their presence.”

Psalm 121 then lifts the eyes. “I lift up my eyes to the mountains— where does my help come from? My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.” The hills are not the Helper. The Maker of the hills is. “He will not let your foot slip— he who watches over you will not slumber; indeed, he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.” “The LORD will keep you from all harm— he will watch over your life; the LORD will watch over your coming and going both now and forevermore.”

As a man, husband, and father, forget not all his benefits, and do not look to the hills for what only the Maker can give. Praise the LORD from the soul, and take your help from the One who does not sleep.

**Psalm 103:1–22 (NIV)**
1 Praise the LORD, my soul; all my inmost being, praise his holy name. 2 Praise the LORD, my soul, and forget not all his benefits— 3 who forgives all your sins and heals all your diseases, 4 who redeems your life from the pit and crowns you with love and compassion, 5 who satisfies your desires with good things so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s. 6 The LORD works righteousness and justice for all the oppressed. 7 He made known his ways to Moses, his deeds to the people of Israel: 8 The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love. 9 He will not always accuse, nor will he harbor his anger forever; 10 he does not treat us as our sins deserve or repay us according to our iniquities. 11 For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his love for those who fear him; 12 as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us. 13 As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him; 14 for he knows how we are formed, he remembers that we are dust. 15 The life of mortals is like grass, they flourish like a flower of the field; 16 the wind blows over it and it is gone, and its place remembers it no more. 17 But from everlasting to everlasting the LORD’s love is with those who fear him, and his righteousness with their children’s children— 18 with those who keep his covenant and remember to obey his precepts. 19 The LORD has established his throne in heaven, and his kingdom rules over all. 20 Praise the LORD, you his angels, you mighty ones who do his bidding, who obey his word. 21 Praise the LORD, all his heavenly hosts, you his servants who do his will. 22 Praise the LORD, all his works everywhere in his dominion. Praise the LORD, my soul.

**Psalm 121:1–8 (NIV)**
1 I lift up my eyes to the mountains— where does my help come from? 2 My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. 3 He will not let your foot slip— he who watches over you will not slumber; 4 indeed, he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. 5 The LORD watches over you— the LORD is your shade at your right hand; 6 the sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night. 7 The LORD will keep you from all harm— he will watch over your life; 8 the LORD will watch over your coming and going both now and forevermore.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Psalm 103:1.** NIV: “Praise the LORD, my soul; all my inmost being, praise his holy name.” LSB: “Bless Yahweh, O my soul, And all that is within me, bless His holy name.” The turn is the same: the whole inner life is called to speak well of the LORD. The LSB’s “Bless” matches the older English many sermons use for this psalm.
- **Psalm 121:2.** NIV: “My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.” LSB: “My help comes from Yahweh, Who made heaven and earth.” The Helper is not the hills. He is the One who made them.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s message [“Bless the Lord, O My Soul”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/bless-the-lord-o-my-soul) at Desiring God (June 15, 2008) opens Psalm 103 as a call to speak well of God’s greatness and goodness from the soul, especially in the hearing of a household. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Encouragement for Black Friday”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/encouragement-black-friday/) at Revive Our Hearts lingers over the same psalm as a way to counsel your own heart: take yourself by the scruff of the neck, and forget not all his benefits.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, what benefits have you been in danger of forgetting, and where have you been lifting your eyes for help? How will you praise the LORD from the soul in the hearing of your house today?

**Lesson 107: Psalms: searched and known, and let everything that has breath praise the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we were told to praise the LORD from the soul, and to take our help from the Maker of heaven and earth. Today the Psalter comes near to its end by telling us we are searched and known — and then it ends with breath itself praising the LORD. “You have searched me, LORD, and you know me. You know when I sit and when I rise; you perceive my thoughts from afar.” “Before a word is on my tongue you, LORD, know it completely.” “Where can I go from your Spirit? Where can I flee from your presence?” “If I say, ‘Surely the darkness will hide me and the light become night around me,’ even the darkness will not be dark to you; the night will shine like the day, for darkness is as light to you.” This knowing is not cold. “For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well.” “Your eyes saw my unformed body; all the days ordained for me were written in your book before one of them came to be.” John Piper, asked whether God can read our thoughts, said, “The short answer is yes,” and then lingered over the implications. He read Psalm 139:2, 4, and 23, and then said, “God is the great heart-knower, the great mind-knower.” There is no unsearched corner in you. That is why the psalm can also refuse the wicked with a holy severity (verses 19–22), and still end not in self-confidence, but in a request: “Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.”

Then the last psalm in the book is almost only praise. “Praise the LORD. Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens.” “Praise him for his acts of power; praise him for his surpassing greatness.” Trumpet, harp, lyre, timbrel, dancing, strings, pipe, and cymbals — and then the wide invitation: “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.” If he has searched you and known you, and if you still have breath, the right use of that breath is praise.

As a man, husband, and father, you are already known. You do not have to hide in the dark, and you cannot. Ask him to search you, and then use your breath to praise him.

**Psalm 139:1–24 (NIV)**
1 You have searched me, LORD, and you know me. 2 You know when I sit and when I rise; you perceive my thoughts from afar. 3 You discern my going out and my lying down; you are familiar with all my ways. 4 Before a word is on my tongue you, LORD, know it completely. 5 You hem me in behind and before, and you lay your hand upon me. 6 Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain. 7 Where can I go from your Spirit? Where can I flee from your presence? 8 If I go up to the heavens, you are there; if I make my bed in the depths, you are there. 9 If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle on the far side of the sea, 10 even there your hand will guide me, your right hand will hold me fast. 11 If I say, “Surely the darkness will hide me and the light become night around me,” 12 even the darkness will not be dark to you; the night will shine like the day, for darkness is as light to you. 13 For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother’s womb. 14 I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well. 15 My frame was not hidden from you when I was made in the secret place, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth. 16 Your eyes saw my unformed body; all the days ordained for me were written in your book before one of them came to be. 17 How precious to me are your thoughts, God! How vast is the sum of them! 18 Were I to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand— when I awake, I am still with you. 19 If only you, God, would slay the wicked! Away from me, you who are bloodthirsty! 20 They speak of you with evil intent; your adversaries misuse your name. 21 Do I not hate those who hate you, LORD, and abhor those who are in rebellion against you? 22 I have nothing but hatred for them; I count them my enemies. 23 Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. 24 See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.

**Psalm 150:1–6 (NIV)**
1 Praise the LORD. Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens. 2 Praise him for his acts of power; praise him for his surpassing greatness. 3 Praise him with the sounding of the trumpet, praise him with the harp and lyre, 4 praise him with timbrel and dancing, praise him with the strings and pipe, 5 praise him with the clash of cymbals, praise him with resounding cymbals. 6 Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Psalm 139:1.** NIV: “You have searched me, LORD, and you know me.” LSB: “O Yahweh, You have searched me and known me.” The knowing is complete, and it is personal.
- **Psalm 150:6.** NIV: “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.” LSB: “Let everything that has breath praise Yah. Praise Yah!” The book of Psalms ends in a shout of praise.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Teach Me the Fear of the Lord”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/teach-me-fear-lord/) at Revive Our Hearts reads Psalm 139 as the fear of the LORD: God is here, he sees, he knows the heart from which our words come. John Piper’s interview [“Does God Read Every Thought?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/does-god-read-every-thought) (March 24, 2023) takes up Psalm 139:2, 4, and 23 and calls God “the great heart-knower, the great mind-knower.” BibleProject’s [Book of Psalms guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-psalms/) helps set Psalm 150 as the book’s closing praise.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been hoping the darkness would hide you? What would it look like today to pray, “Search me, God,” and then to let everything that has breath in your house praise the LORD?

Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens. 2 Praise him for his acts of power; praise him for his surpassing greatness. 3 Praise him with the sounding of the trumpet, praise him with the harp and lyre, 4 praise him with timbrel and dancing, praise him with the strings and pipe, 5 praise him with the clash of cymbals, praise him with resounding cymbals. 6 Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.

**Lesson 108: Proverbs: the beginning of wisdom, and trust in the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. We have just closed the book of Psalms with search-me prayer and with breath spent in praise. Today a new book opens: the proverbs of Solomon, “for gaining wisdom and instruction; for understanding words of insight.” The doorway sentence is not a trick for getting ahead. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction.” A father then speaks: “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction and do not forsake your mother’s teaching.” And he warns, “My son, if sinful men entice you, do not give in to them.” “my son, do not go along with them, do not set foot on their paths;” Chapter 3 presses the same beginning into trust: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight. Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and shun evil.” Even the Lord’s discipline belongs to this path: “My son, do not despise the LORD’s discipline, and do not resent his rebuke, because the LORD disciplines those he loves, as a father the son he delights in.”

BibleProject says the introduction of Proverbs is linked to Solomon, who asked God for wisdom to lead Israel well, and that by reading this book “you will gain wisdom.” The Hebrew word, they note, “refers primarily to practical knowledge,” “skill” or “applied knowledge” for “living well in God’s good world.” And the book’s foundation is the fear of the LORD. “The word fear is not about terror. Rather, it refers to a sense of reverence and awe before God, which makes clear our small place in the universe.” “It’s a moral mindset that recognizes that we are not God and don’t get to make up what’s right and wrong for ourselves.” “The fear of the Lord is a posture of humility before God, embracing his definition of good and evil even when it’s difficult or inconvenient.” The first main section, they add, is “10 speeches from a father to a son.” “The father tells the son that he should listen to wisdom and cultivate the fear of the Lord.”

As a man, husband, and father, knowledge does not begin with being clever. It begins with the fear of the LORD. Do not lean on your own understanding. Submit to him in all your ways, and do not set foot on the path of those who entice you.

**Proverbs 1:1–19 (NIV)**
1 The proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel: 2 for gaining wisdom and instruction; for understanding words of insight; 3 for receiving instruction in prudent behavior, doing what is right and just and fair; 4 for giving prudence to those who are simple, knowledge and discretion to the young— 5 let the wise listen and add to their learning, and let the discerning get guidance— 6 for understanding proverbs and parables, the sayings and riddles of the wise. 7 The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction. 8 Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction and do not forsake your mother’s teaching. 9 They are a garland to grace your head and a chain to adorn your neck. 10 My son, if sinful men entice you, do not give in to them. 11 If they say, “Come along with us; let’s lie in wait for innocent blood, let’s ambush some harmless soul; 12 let’s swallow them alive, like the grave, and whole, like those who go down to the pit; 13 we will get all sorts of valuable things and fill our houses with plunder; 14 cast lots with us; we will all share the loot”— 15 my son, do not go along with them, do not set foot on their paths; 16 for their feet rush into evil, they are swift to shed blood. 17 How useless to spread a net where every bird can see it! 18 These men lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush only themselves! 19 Such are the paths of all who go after ill-gotten gain; it takes away the life of those who get it.

**Proverbs 3:1–12 (NIV)**
1 My son, do not forget my teaching, but keep my commands in your heart, 2 for they will prolong your life many years and bring you peace and prosperity. 3 Let love and faithfulness never leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart. 4 Then you will win favor and a good name in the sight of God and man. 5 Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; 6 in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight. 7 Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and shun evil. 8 This will bring health to your body and nourishment to your bones. 9 Honor the LORD with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops; 10 then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine. 11 My son, do not despise the LORD’s discipline, and do not resent his rebuke, 12 because the LORD disciplines those he loves, as a father the son he delights in.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Proverbs 1:7.** NIV: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction.” LSB: “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; Ignorant fools despise wisdom and discipline.”
- **Proverbs 3:6.** NIV: “in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.” LSB: “In all your ways acknowledge Him, And He will make your paths straight.” The LSB’s “acknowledge” and the NIV’s “submit” both refuse a life that only nods at God and then leans on its own understanding.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Proverbs guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-proverbs/) opens the book at Solomon’s wisdom and at “the fear of the Lord,” not as terror, but as humility before God: we are not God, and we do not get to make up what is right and wrong. The first nine chapters are a father’s speeches, training a son to listen and to cultivate that fear.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been leaning on your own understanding this week? What would it look like to fear the LORD, submit to him in all your ways, and refuse a path that entices you?

**Lesson 109: Proverbs: guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday wisdom began with the fear of the LORD, and with a son who would not lean on his own understanding. Today a father keeps speaking: “Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction; pay attention and gain understanding.” “The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom. Though it cost all you have, get understanding.” He tells his son to pay attention to his words, and then he comes to the spring of a life: “Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.” The next lines are not a different subject. “Let your eyes look straight ahead; fix your gaze directly before you. Give careful thought to the paths for your feet and be steadfast in all your ways. Do not turn to the right or the left; keep your foot from evil.” The heart is guarded by what you gaze at and by where you set your feet.

BibleProject notes that Proverbs 1–9 is not yet the short sayings. It is a father training a son to listen to wisdom and to cultivate the fear of the LORD. “This will require a life of virtue, integrity, and generosity.” “The father warns the son about folly and evil, about shortsighted, selfish decisions and pride.” Guarding the heart is that training in one sentence. Everything you do flows from it — your words, your work, your marriage, your hidden wants. So the father says, “Above all else.” If the spring is poisoned, the paths will not stay straight, no matter how carefully you try to manage the outside of a life.

As a man, husband, and father, above all else, guard your heart. Give careful thought to the paths for your feet. Do not turn to the right or the left. Everything you do flows from what you keep there.

**Proverbs 4:1–27 (NIV)**
1 Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction; pay attention and gain understanding. 2 I give you sound learning, so do not forsake my teaching. 3 For I too was a son to my father, still tender, and cherished by my mother. 4 Then he taught me, and he said to me, “Take hold of my words with all your heart; keep my commands, and you will live. 5 Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget my words or turn away from them. 6 Do not forsake wisdom, and she will protect you; love her, and she will watch over you. 7 The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom. Though it cost all you have, get understanding. 8 Cherish her, and she will exalt you; embrace her, and she will honor you. 9 She will give you a garland to grace your head and present you with a glorious crown.” 10 Listen, my son, accept what I say, and the years of your life will be many. 11 I instruct you in the way of wisdom and lead you along straight paths. 12 When you walk, your steps will not be hampered; when you run, you will not stumble. 13 Hold on to instruction, do not let it go; guard it well, for it is your life. 14 Do not set foot on the path of the wicked or walk in the way of evildoers. 15 Avoid it, do not travel on it; turn from it and go on your way. 16 For they cannot rest until they do evil; they are robbed of sleep till they make someone stumble. 17 They eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence. 18 The path of the righteous is like the morning sun, shining ever brighter till the full light of day. 19 But the way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know what makes them stumble. 20 My son, pay attention to what I say; turn your ear to my words. 21 Do not let them out of your sight, keep them within your heart; 22 for they are life to those who find them and health to one’s whole body. 23 Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it. 24 Keep your mouth free of perversity; keep corrupt talk far from your lips. 25 Let your eyes look straight ahead; fix your gaze directly before you. 26 Give careful thought to the paths for your feet and be steadfast in all your ways. 27 Do not turn to the right or the left; keep your foot from evil.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Proverbs 4:23.** NIV: “Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.” LSB: “Guard your heart with all diligence, For from it flow the springs of life.” The heart is not a side issue. It is the spring.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Proverbs guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-proverbs/) frames Proverbs 1–9 as a father’s training in wisdom, virtue, and the fear of the LORD, including warnings about folly, shortsighted decisions, and pride. Proverbs 4:23 sits in that training: the heart is the spring, and everything you do flows from it.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, what has been flowing from your heart into your house this week? What will you gaze at, and what path will you refuse, in order to guard that spring?

**Lesson 110: Proverbs: diligence, and the mouth of the righteous**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday a father said, “Above all else, guard your heart.” Today the book turns from those long speeches toward the short sayings, and it starts with work and with the mouth. “Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest.” “How long will you lie there, you sluggard? When will you get up from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest— and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man.” Then the collected sayings begin: “A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son brings grief to his mother.” “Lazy hands make for poverty, but diligent hands bring wealth.” “He who gathers crops in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son.” Diligence is not only about work. It is about the mouth as well. “The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.” “Hatred stirs up conflict, but love covers over all wrongs.” “The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool invites ruin.”

BibleProject says that in chapters 10–29 “we finally come to the collections of proverbs,” “hundreds of ancient sayings that apply wisdom and the fear of the Lord to every life topic you can imagine, including family, work, community life, friendship,” and more. “These proverbs are short and easy to memorize.” “This section of the book is meant to become like a reference work to which you return time after time for the rest of your life.” The ant is one of those pictures you can carry: a small creature, with no commander standing over it, still stores in summer. Diligent hands, and a righteous mouth, are how the fear of the LORD looks in a Tuesday afternoon.

As a man, husband, and father, consider the ant, and consider your mouth. A little more slumber can look harmless. The book says poverty and ruin come like a thief, and that the mouth of the righteous can be a fountain of life.

**Proverbs 6:6–11 (NIV)**
6 Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! 7 It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, 8 yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest. 9 How long will you lie there, you sluggard? When will you get up from your sleep? 10 A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest— 11 and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man.

**Proverbs 10:1–14 (NIV)**
1 The proverbs of Solomon: A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son brings grief to his mother. 2 Ill-gotten treasures have no lasting value, but righteousness delivers from death. 3 The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked. 4 Lazy hands make for poverty, but diligent hands bring wealth. 5 He who gathers crops in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son. 6 Blessings crown the head of the righteous, but violence overwhelms the mouth of the wicked. 7 The name of the righteous is used in blessings, but the name of the wicked will rot. 8 The wise in heart accept commands, but a chattering fool comes to ruin. 9 Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but whoever takes crooked paths will be found out. 10 Whoever winks maliciously causes grief, and a chattering fool comes to ruin. 11 The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. 12 Hatred stirs up conflict, but love covers over all wrongs. 13 Wisdom is found on the lips of the discerning, but a rod is for the back of one who has no sense. 14 The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool invites ruin.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Proverbs guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-proverbs/) describes chapters 10–29 as the collected sayings, a reference work for the rest of your life, applying the fear of the LORD to work, family, and the mouth. “Go to the ant” is one of those pictures you can carry into an ordinary day.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where has “a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands” taken root in your work or your words? What would diligence, and a fountain-of-life mouth, look like in your house today?

Yesterday a father said, “Above all else, guard your heart.” Today the book turns from those long speeches toward the short sayings, and it starts with work and with the mouth. “Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise! It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in summer and gathers its food at harvest.” “How long will you lie there, you sluggard? When will you get up from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest— and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed man.” Then the collected sayings begin: “A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son brings grief to his mother.” “Lazy hands make for poverty, but diligent hands bring wealth.” “He who gathers crops in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son.” Diligence is not only about work. It is about the mouth as well. “The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.” “Hatred stirs up conflict, but love covers over all wrongs.” “The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool invites ruin.”

BibleProject says that in chapters 10–29 “we finally come to the collections of proverbs,” “hundreds of ancient sayings that apply wisdom and the fear of the Lord to every life topic you can imagine, including family, work, community life, friendship,” and more. “These proverbs are short and easy to memorize.” “This section of the book is meant to become like a reference work to which you return time after time for the rest of your life.” The ant is one of those pictures you can carry: a small creature, with no commander standing over it, still stores in summer. Diligent hands, and a righteous mouth, are how the fear of the LORD looks in a Tuesday afternoon.

As a woman, wife, and mother, consider the ant, and consider your mouth. A little more slumber can look harmless. The book says poverty and ruin come like a thief, and that the mouth of the righteous can be a fountain of life.
