**Lesson 135: Ezekiel: shepherds who feed themselves, and the true Shepherd**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD took no pleasure in the death of anyone, and called his people to repent and live. Today he speaks against the shepherds who will not tend the flock, and promises to shepherd them himself. “Woe to you shepherds of Israel who only take care of yourselves! Should not shepherds take care of the flock?” They have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured. They have not brought back the strays or searched for the lost. “So they were scattered because there was no shepherd, and when they were scattered they became food for all the wild animals.” Then the promise: “For this is what the Sovereign LORD says: I myself will search for my sheep and look after them.” “I myself will tend my sheep and have them lie down, declares the Sovereign LORD. I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bind up the injured and strengthen the weak, but the sleek and the strong I will destroy. I will shepherd the flock with justice.” BibleProject says God “promises Israel that he will raise up a ‘new David,’ a future messianic king who will be the kind of leader that Israel always needed but never had (ch. 34).” The true Shepherd is not like the shepherds who feed themselves. He comes himself. As a man, husband, and father, do not be a shepherd who only takes care of yourself — not in your house, not among the people God has given you. And do not despair if you have been scattered. The LORD himself searches for his sheep.

**Ezekiel 34:1–16 (NIV)**
1 The word of the LORD came to me: 2 “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel; prophesy and say to them: ‘This is what the Sovereign LORD says: Woe to you shepherds of Israel who only take care of yourselves! Should not shepherds take care of the flock? 3 You eat the curds, clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the choice animals, but you do not take care of the flock. 4 You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured. You have not brought back the strays or searched for the lost. You have ruled them harshly and brutally. 5 So they were scattered because there was no shepherd, and when they were scattered they became food for all the wild animals. 6 My sheep wandered over all the mountains and on every high hill. They were scattered over the whole earth, and no one searched or looked for them. 7 “‘Therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD: 8 As surely as I live, declares the Sovereign LORD, because my flock lacks a shepherd and so has been plundered and has become food for all the wild animals, and because my shepherds did not search for my flock but cared for themselves rather than for my flock, 9 therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD: 10 This is what the Sovereign LORD says: I am against the shepherds and will hold them accountable for my flock. I will remove them from tending the flock so that the shepherds can no longer feed themselves. I will rescue my flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them. 11 “‘For this is what the Sovereign LORD says: I myself will search for my sheep and look after them. 12 As a shepherd looks after his scattered flock when he is with them, so will I look after my sheep. I will rescue them from all the places where they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness. 13 I will bring them out from the nations and gather them from the countries, and I will bring them into their own land. I will pasture them on the mountains of Israel, in the ravines and in all the settlements in the land. 14 I will tend them in a good pasture, and the mountain heights of Israel will be their grazing land. There they will lie down in good grazing land, and there they will feed in a rich pasture on the mountains of Israel. 15 I myself will tend my sheep and have them lie down, declares the Sovereign LORD. 16 I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bind up the injured and strengthen the weak, but the sleek and the strong I will destroy. I will shepherd the flock with justice.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Ezekiel 34:11.** NIV: “I myself will search for my sheep and look after them.” LSB: “I Myself will seek My sheep and care for them.” The true Shepherd does not send a substitute. He comes himself.

**Go deeper:** BibleProject’s [Book of Ezekiel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-ezekiel/) says God “promises Israel that he will raise up a ‘new David,’ a future messianic king who will be the kind of leader that Israel always needed but never had (ch. 34).” The true Shepherd is not like the shepherds who only take care of themselves.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been tending yourself and leaving the weak, the injured, or the stray untended? And where do you need to trust that the LORD himself will search for his sheep — including you?

**Lesson 136: Ezekiel: a new heart, and dry bones live**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD promised to search for his sheep himself. Today he gives the reason he will act, and then stands the prophet in a valley of dry bones. “It is not for your sake, people of Israel, that I am going to do these things, but for the sake of my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations where you have gone.” “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit in you and move you to follow my decrees and be careful to keep my laws.” “I want you to know that I am not doing this for your sake, declares the Sovereign LORD.” Then the hand of the LORD sets Ezekiel in a valley full of bones, very dry. “Son of man, can these bones live?” “Sovereign LORD, you alone know.” The prophet speaks the word, and there is a rattling; the bones come together, and breath enters them, and they stand on their feet, a vast army. “Son of man, these bones are the people of Israel. They say, ‘Our bones are dried up and our hope is gone; we are cut off.’” “I will put my Spirit in you and you will live.” BibleProject says God “is going to remove Israel’s hard hearts and send his Spirit into his people to give them new, soft hearts that will love and obey their God.” The valley of bones is “an image of Israel’s spiritual state.” “God then tells Ezekiel that his Spirit will come and bring them back to life.” John Piper has long heard Ezekiel 36 as God acting for his holy name, not first for ours. The new heart and the living bones are his work, for his name. As a man, husband, and father, you cannot give yourself the new heart that chapter 18 commanded, and you cannot make dry bones live. Ask the LORD, who acts for his holy name, to put his Spirit in you — and to stand in the valley where hope has dried up, and say, “Sovereign LORD, you alone know.”

**Ezekiel 36:22–32 (NIV)**
22 “Therefore say to the Israelites, ‘This is what the Sovereign LORD says: It is not for your sake, people of Israel, that I am going to do these things, but for the sake of my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations where you have gone. 23 I will show the holiness of my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, the name you have profaned among them. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, declares the Sovereign LORD, when I am proved holy through you before their eyes. 24 “‘For I will take you out of the nations; I will gather you from all the countries and bring you back into your own land. 25 I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean; I will cleanse you from all your impurities and from all your idols. 26 I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. 27 And I will put my Spirit in you and move you to follow my decrees and be careful to keep my laws. 28 Then you will live in the land I gave your ancestors; you will be my people, and I will be your God. 29 I will save you from all your uncleanness. I will call for the grain and make it plentiful and will not bring famine upon you. 30 I will increase the fruit of the trees and the crops of the field, so that you will no longer suffer disgrace among the nations because of famine. 31 Then you will remember your evil ways and wicked deeds, and you will loathe yourselves for your sins and detestable practices. 32 I want you to know that I am not doing this for your sake, declares the Sovereign LORD. Be ashamed and disgraced for your conduct, people of Israel!

**Ezekiel 37:1–14 (NIV)**
1 The hand of the LORD was on me, and he brought me out by the Spirit of the LORD and set me in the middle of a valley; it was full of bones. 2 He led me back and forth among them, and I saw a great many bones on the floor of the valley, bones that were very dry. 3 He asked me, “Son of man, can these bones live?” I said, “Sovereign LORD, you alone know.” 4 Then he said to me, “Prophesy to these bones and say to them, ‘Dry bones, hear the word of the LORD! 5 This is what the Sovereign LORD says to these bones: I will make breath enter you, and you will come to life. 6 I will attach tendons to you and make flesh come upon you and cover you with skin; I will put breath in you, and you will come to life. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’” 7 So I prophesied as I was commanded. And as I was prophesying, there was a noise, a rattling sound, and the bones came together, bone to bone. 8 I looked, and tendons and flesh appeared on them and skin covered them, but there was no breath in them. 9 Then he said to me, “Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and say to it, ‘This is what the Sovereign LORD says: Come, breath, from the four winds and breathe into these slain, that they may live.’” 10 So I prophesied as he commanded me, and breath entered them; they came to life and stood up on their feet—a vast army. 11 Then he said to me: “Son of man, these bones are the people of Israel. They say, ‘Our bones are dried up and our hope is gone; we are cut off.’ 12 Therefore prophesy and say to them: ‘This is what the Sovereign LORD says: My people, I am going to open your graves and bring you up from them; I will bring you back to the land of Israel. 13 Then you, my people, will know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves and bring you up from them. 14 I will put my Spirit in you and you will live, and I will settle you in your own land. Then you will know that I the LORD have spoken, and I have done it, declares the LORD.’”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Ezekiel 36:26.** NIV: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.” LSB: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.”
- **Ezekiel 37:3.** NIV: “Sovereign LORD, you alone know.” LSB: “O Lord Yahweh, You know.” The prophet does not pretend the bones can live by human power.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“Lord, You Know!”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/lord-you-know/) and [“Where God Breathes, Life Follows”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/dry-bones-live-again/) sit in the valley of Ezekiel 37. John Piper’s [“God Created Us for His Glory”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/god-created-us-for-his-glory) and Ask Pastor John [“The God Who Breaks Us with Kindness”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/the-god-who-breaks-us-with-kindness) hear Ezekiel 36: God acts “not for your sake,” but for his holy name. BibleProject’s [Book of Ezekiel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-ezekiel/) holds the two chapters together: a new heart, and bones that live by the Spirit.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been trying to raise dry bones by human effort, or asking God to act merely for your sake? What would it look like to ask him, for his holy name, for a new heart — and to leave the valley’s “can these bones live?” in his hands?

**Lesson 137: Ezekiel: a river from the temple — everything will live where the river flows**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD promised a new heart, and made dry bones live by his Spirit. Today a river comes out from the temple, and everything lives where the river flows. Another, up to the waist. **Lesson 138: Daniel: resolved not to defile himself**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday a river came out from the temple, and everything lived where it flowed. Today the story moves to Babylon, and a young man resolves not to defile himself. In the third year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem. Articles from the temple of God were carried to the temple of his god. Young men from the royal family were taken to be trained for the king’s service, and assigned food and wine from the king’s table. “But Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the royal food and wine, and he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself this way.” God caused the official to show him favor. Daniel asked for a test of ten days: vegetables and water. At the end they looked healthier than the others. “To these four young men God gave knowledge and understanding of all kinds of literature and learning. And Daniel could understand visions and dreams of all kinds.” And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus. BibleProject says, “Daniel and his friends are wise and capable and are soon recruited to serve in the royal palace of Babylon. However, they are also pressured to give up their Jewish identity by living and eating like Babylonians and violating the Jewish food laws found in the Torah. They refuse and instead choose faithfulness to the Torah. This decision puts them in grave danger, but God delivers them, and they go on to be elevated by the king of Babylon.” John Piper, reading Daniel 1:8, hears a man for whom even his food is a God-issue: “Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself.” As a man, husband, and father, Heaven’s rule does not cancel a holy resolve. In a place that is not home, decide beforehand that you will not defile yourself. Ask permission where you can. Trust the God who gives knowledge, and who is not absent from the scene.

**Daniel 1:1–21 (NIV)**
1 In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. 2 And the Lord delivered Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, along with some of the articles from the temple of God. These he carried off to the temple of his god in Babylonia and put in the treasure house of his god. 3 Then the king ordered Ashpenaz, chief of his court officials, to bring into the king’s service some of the Israelites from the royal family and the nobility— 4 young men without any physical defect, handsome, showing aptitude for every kind of learning, well informed, quick to understand, and qualified to serve in the king’s palace. He was to teach them the language and literature of the Babylonians. 5 The king assigned them a daily amount of food and wine from the king’s table. They were to be trained for three years, and after that they were to enter the king’s service. 6 Among those who were chosen were some from Judah: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. 7 The chief official gave them new names: to Daniel, the name Belteshazzar; to Hananiah, Shadrach; to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego. 8 But Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the royal food and wine, and he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself this way. 9 Now God had caused the official to show favor and compassion to Daniel, 10 but the official told Daniel, “I am afraid of my lord the king, who has assigned your food and drink. Why should he see you looking worse than the other young men your age? The king would then have my head because of you.” 11 Daniel then said to the guard whom the chief official had appointed over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, 12 “Please test your servants for ten days: Give us nothing but vegetables to eat and water to drink. 13 Then compare our appearance with that of the young men who eat the royal food, and treat your servants in accordance with what you see.” 14 So he agreed to this and tested them for ten days. 15 At the end of the ten days they looked healthier and better nourished than any of the young men who ate the royal food. 16 So the guard took away their choice food and the wine they were to drink and gave them vegetables instead. 17 To these four young men God gave knowledge and understanding of all kinds of literature and learning. And Daniel could understand visions and dreams of all kinds. 18 At the end of the time set by the king to bring them into his service, the chief official presented them to Nebuchadnezzar. 19 The king talked with them, and he found none equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah; so they entered the king’s service. 20 In every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king questioned them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his whole kingdom. 21 And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Daniel 1:8.** NIV: “But Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the royal food and wine.” LSB: “But Daniel set in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s choice food or with the wine which he drank.” The resolve is in the heart, before the request is on the lips.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“When You Need Courage (Daniel 1)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-you-need-courage-daniel-1/) says Heaven rules does not mean we sit back; Daniel “determined that he would not defile himself.” John Piper’s [“Daniel’s Defiance of Darius in Prayer”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/daniels-defiance-of-darius-in-prayer) also traces the resolve of Daniel 1:8. BibleProject’s [Book of Daniel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-daniel/) says they “refuse and instead choose faithfulness to the Torah.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where is the “royal food and wine” that would defile you — a compromise you have been treating as small, because you live in someone else’s palace? What would a clear resolve, and a humble request, look like this week?

**Lesson 139: Daniel: the fiery furnace — we will not serve your gods**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Daniel resolved not to defile himself, and God gave him favor and understanding. Today his three friends will not bow, even if the furnace is heated seven times hotter. Furious with rage, Nebuchadnezzar summoned Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. The command is plain: worship the image, or be thrown into the blazing furnace. They reply, “If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us from it, and he will deliver us from Your Majesty’s hand. But even if he does not, we want you to know, Your Majesty, that we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up.” The furnace is heated seven times hotter than usual. The men who take them up are killed by the flames. Then the king leaps to his feet: “Look! I see four men walking around in the fire, unbound and unharmed, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods.” They come out. Not a hair is singed; their robes are not scorched; there is no smell of fire on them. The king praises the God who sent his angel and rescued his servants. John Piper says, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego kept their integrity when thrown into the fiery furnace.” He hears their word as civil disobedience on the basis of religious conscience: they would not bow, and they did not resist the sentence. BibleProject says they “refuse to bow down and worship a huge idol statue, which represents the king and his imperial power… God delivers them from death.” As a man, husband, and father, the God we serve is able to deliver. That is enough to keep you from bowing. “Even if he does not” is not unbelief. It is obedience that leaves the outcome in his hands.

**Daniel 3:13–30 (NIV)**
13 Furious with rage, Nebuchadnezzar summoned Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. So these men were brought before the king, 14 and Nebuchadnezzar said to them, “Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the image of gold I have set up? 15 Now when you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe and all kinds of music, if you are ready to fall down and worship the image I made, very good. But if you do not worship it, you will be thrown immediately into a blazing furnace. Then what god will be able to rescue you from my hand?” 16 Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego replied to him, “King Nebuchadnezzar, we do not need to defend ourselves before you in this matter. 17 If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us from it, and he will deliver us from Your Majesty’s hand. 18 But even if he does not, we want you to know, Your Majesty, that we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up.” 19 Then Nebuchadnezzar was furious with Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and his attitude toward them changed. He ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual 20 and commanded some of the strongest soldiers in his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego and throw them into the blazing furnace. 21 So these men, wearing their robes, trousers, turbans and other clothes, were bound and thrown into the blazing furnace. 22 The king’s command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames of the fire killed the soldiers who took up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, 23 and these three men, firmly tied, fell into the blazing furnace. 24 Then King Nebuchadnezzar leaped to his feet in amazement and asked his advisers, “Weren’t there three men that we tied up and threw into the fire?” They replied, “Certainly, Your Majesty.” 25 He said, “Look! I see four men walking around in the fire, unbound and unharmed, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods.” 26 Nebuchadnezzar then approached the opening of the blazing furnace and shouted, “Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out! Come here!” So Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego came out of the fire, 27 and the satraps, prefects, governors and royal advisers crowded around them. They saw that the fire had not harmed their bodies, nor was a hair of their heads singed; their robes were not scorched, and there was no smell of fire on them. 28 Then Nebuchadnezzar said, “Praise be to the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who has sent his angel and rescued his servants! They trusted in him and defied the king’s command and were willing to give up their lives rather than serve or worship any god except their own God. 29 Therefore I decree that the people of any nation or language who say anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego be cut into pieces and their houses be turned into piles of rubble, for no other god can save in this way.” 30 Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Daniel 3:17–18.** NIV: “the God we serve is able to deliver us from it, and he will deliver us from Your Majesty’s hand. But even if he does not… we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up.” LSB: “our God whom we serve is able to save us from the furnace of blazing fire… But if not… we will not worship the golden image that you have set up.” The hope is in his ability. The obedience does not wait on the outcome.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“When Your Faith Is Tested (Daniel 3)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-your-faith-is-tested-daniel-3/) lingers over “even if he does not.” John Piper’s [“Subjection to God and Subjection to the State, Part 3”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/subjection-to-god-and-subjection-to-the-state-part-3) and [“When Your Boss Expects You to Lie”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/when-your-boss-expects-you-to-lie) hear the same integrity. BibleProject’s [Book of Daniel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-daniel/) says the friends “refuse to bow down and worship a huge idol statue… God delivers them from death.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been willing to obey only if God will clearly deliver you on your terms? What would it look like to say, with these three, “the God we serve is able,” and “even if he does not, we will not serve your gods”?

Not a hair is singed; their robes are not scorched; there is no smell of fire on them. The king praises the God who sent his angel and rescued his servants. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth says, “These men did not see God as their servant who was obligated to do what they wanted Him to do. They were God’s servants, and they were committed to do His will, wherever that took them, whatever that cost them.” “They knew their God was able to rescue them; they didn’t know if He would choose to do so, but they were willing to leave their fate in God’s hands.” John Piper says, “Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego kept their integrity when thrown into the fiery furnace.” He hears their word as civil disobedience on the basis of religious conscience: they would not bow, and they did not resist the sentence. BibleProject says they “refuse to bow down and worship a huge idol statue, which represents the king and his imperial power… God delivers them from death.” As a woman, wife, and a mother, the God we serve is able to deliver. That is enough to keep you from bowing. “Even if he does not” is not unbelief. It is obedience that leaves the outcome in his hands.

**Daniel 3:13–30 (NIV)**
13 Furious with rage, Nebuchadnezzar summoned Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. So these men were brought before the king, 14 and Nebuchadnezzar said to them, “Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the image of gold I have set up? 15 Now when you hear the sound of the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipe and all kinds of music, if you are ready to fall down and worship the image I made, very good. But if you do not worship it, you will be thrown immediately into a blazing furnace. Then what god will be able to rescue you from my hand?” 16 Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego replied to him, “King Nebuchadnezzar, we do not need to defend ourselves before you in this matter. 17 If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us from it, and he will deliver us from Your Majesty’s hand. 18 But even if he does not, we want you to know, Your Majesty, that we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up.” 19 Then Nebuchadnezzar was furious with Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and his attitude toward them changed. He ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual 20 and commanded some of the strongest soldiers in his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego and throw them into the blazing furnace. 21 So these men, wearing their robes, trousers, turbans and other clothes, were bound and thrown into the blazing furnace. 22 The king’s command was so urgent and the furnace so hot that the flames of the fire killed the soldiers who took up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, 23 and these three men, firmly tied, fell into the blazing furnace. 24 Then King Nebuchadnezzar leaped to his feet in amazement and asked his advisers, “Weren’t there three men that we tied up and threw into the fire?” They replied, “Certainly, Your Majesty.” 25 He said, “Look! I see four men walking around in the fire, unbound and unharmed, and the fourth looks like a son of the gods.” 26 Nebuchadnezzar then approached the opening of the blazing furnace and shouted, “Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out! Come here!” So Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego came out of the fire, 27 and the satraps, prefects, governors and royal advisers crowded around them. They saw that the fire had not harmed their bodies, nor was a hair of their heads singed; their robes were not scorched, and there was no smell of fire on them. 28 Then Nebuchadnezzar said, “Praise be to the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who has sent his angel and rescued his servants! They trusted in him and defied the king’s command and were willing to give up their lives rather than serve or worship any god except their own God. 29 Therefore I decree that the people of any nation or language who say anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego be cut into pieces and their houses be turned into piles of rubble, for no other god can save in this way.” 30 Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Daniel 3:17–18.** NIV: “the God we serve is able to deliver us from it, and he will deliver us from Your Majesty’s hand. But even if he does not… we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up.” LSB: “our God whom we serve is able to save us from the furnace of blazing fire… But if not… we will not worship the golden image that you have set up.” The hope is in his ability. The obedience does not wait on the outcome.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“When Your Faith Is Tested (Daniel 3)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-your-faith-is-tested-daniel-3/) lingers over “even if he does not.” John Piper’s [“Subjection to God and Subjection to the State, Part 3”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/subjection-to-god-and-subjection-to-the-state-part-3) and [“When Your Boss Expects You to Lie”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/when-your-boss-expects-you-to-lie) hear the same integrity. BibleProject’s [Book of Daniel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-daniel/) says the friends “refuse to bow down and worship a huge idol statue… God delivers them from death.”

**Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where have you been willing to obey only if God will clearly deliver you on your terms? What would it look like to say, with these three, “the God we serve is able,” and “even if he does not, we will not serve your gods”?

**Lesson 140: Daniel: the lion's den — a man who still prays**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday three men would not bow, even if the furnace was heated seven times hotter. Today a man will not stop praying, even if the den of lions is the law. It pleased Darius to appoint 120 satraps, and three administrators over them, one of them Daniel. He so distinguished himself that the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom. The others could find no charge against him, “unless it has something to do with the law of his God.” They trap the king in a decree: for thirty days, no one may pray to any god or human except the king. “Now when Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before.” He is thrown into the lions’ den. The king says, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” At dawn he hurries back. Daniel is alive. “My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions.” “And when Daniel was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.” John Piper says, “prayer is more precious than life.” “Daniel would rather pray than save his life.” “Not praying was a worse prospect to Daniel than being eaten by lions.” “You will have to take my life before you take my prayer.” BibleProject says Daniel “is persecuted because he refuses to pray to and worship the king as a god… God delivers him from the beasts.” As a man, husband, and father, the habit was not invented for a crisis. It was the same prayer, in the open, after the decree. Be a man who still prays — not a new performance, but the same kneeling, the same thanks, when it would be easier to close the window.

**Daniel 6:1–23 (NIV)**
1 It pleased Darius to appoint 120 satraps to rule throughout the kingdom, 2 with three administrators over them, one of whom was Daniel. The satraps were made accountable to them so that the king might not suffer loss. 3 Now Daniel so distinguished himself among the administrators and the satraps by his exceptional qualities that the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom. 4 At this, the administrators and the satraps tried to find grounds for charges against Daniel in his conduct of government affairs, but they were unable to do so. They could find no corruption in him, because he was trustworthy and neither corrupt nor negligent. 5 Finally these men said, “We will never find any basis for charges against this man Daniel unless it has something to do with the law of his God.” 6 So these administrators and satraps went as a group to the king and said: “May King Darius live forever! 7 The royal administrators, prefects, satraps, advisers and governors have all agreed that the king should issue an edict and enforce the decree that anyone who prays to any god or human being during the next thirty days, except to you, Your Majesty, shall be thrown into the lions’ den. 8 Now, Your Majesty, issue the decree and put it in writing so that it cannot be altered—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” 9 So King Darius put the decree in writing. 10 Now when Daniel learned that the decree had been published, he went home to his upstairs room where the windows opened toward Jerusalem. Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before. 11 Then these men went as a group and found Daniel praying and asking God for help. 12 So they went to the king and spoke to him about his royal decree: “Did you not publish a decree that during the next thirty days anyone who prays to any god or human being except to you, Your Majesty, would be thrown into the lions’ den?” The king answered, “The decree stands—in accordance with the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be repealed.” 13 Then they said to the king, “Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, Your Majesty, or to the decree you put in writing. He still prays three times a day.” 14 When the king heard this, he was greatly distressed; he was determined to rescue Daniel and made every effort until sundown to save him. 15 Then the men went as a group to King Darius and said to him, “Remember, Your Majesty, that according to the law of the Medes and Persians no decree or edict that the king issues can be changed.” 16 So the king gave the order, and they brought Daniel and threw him into the lions’ den. The king said to Daniel, “May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!” 17 A stone was brought and placed over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet ring and with the rings of his nobles, so that Daniel’s situation might not be changed. 18 Then the king returned to his palace and spent the night without eating and without any entertainment being brought to him. And he could not sleep. 19 At the first light of dawn, the king got up and hurried to the lions’ den. 20 When he came near the den, he called to Daniel in an anguished voice, “Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?” 21 Daniel answered, “May the king live forever! 22 My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.” 23 The king was overjoyed and gave orders to lift Daniel out of the den. And when Daniel was lifted from the den, no wound was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Daniel 6:10.** NIV: “Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before.” LSB: “he continued kneeling on his knees three times a day, praying and giving thanks before his God, as he had been doing previously.” The habit was not new. It was the same prayer, in the open, after the decree.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“When You Need to Be Rescued (Daniel 6)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-you-need-to-be-rescued-daniel-6/) asks how much our habits would have to change if prayer were made illegal. John Piper’s [“Daniel’s Defiance of Darius in Prayer”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/daniels-defiance-of-darius-in-prayer) says “prayer is more precious than life.” BibleProject’s [Book of Daniel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-daniel/) pairs this chapter with chapter 3: Daniel “refuses to pray to and worship the king as a god… God delivers him from the beasts.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, if prayer were suddenly costly, how much would your habits have to change before anyone would notice? What would it look like this week to pray “just as he had done before” — openly, regularly, with thanks — and to trust the God who shuts the mouths of lions?

**Lesson 141: Daniel: one like a son of man, and a prayer of confession**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Daniel would not close the window. He knelt three times a day, as he had done before, and the LORD shut the mouths of the lions. Today the book turns from the court stories to a night vision, and then to a prayer of confession. Daniel looks, and thrones are set in place, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat. His clothing is white as snow; the hair of his head is white like wool. His throne is flaming with fire. Then, in the vision at night, “there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence.” “He was given authority, glory and sovereign power; all nations and peoples of every language worshiped him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” This is not a slogan. It is a courtroom in heaven, and a human figure who is also more than human, receiving an unending kingdom. John Piper, looking at Daniel 7, says that “the figure of a ‘son of man’ in Daniel 7:13 is both human and far more than human.” It was Jesus’s favorite designation for himself. In Ask Pastor John he puts the two sides together: on the face of it, “Son of Man is an ordinary phrase for ‘human being,’” and in Daniel 7 “the Son of Man is a very exalted figure: not just a human figure but an exalted figure.” Then he walks into Daniel 9 and says, “Daniel spends most of his prayer confessing the sin of the people.” Then the prayer. In the first year of Darius, Daniel understood from the Scriptures, according to the word of the LORD given to Jeremiah, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. So he turned to the Lord God and pleaded with him in prayer and petition, in fasting, and in sackcloth and ashes. He prayed and confessed: “Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps his covenant of love with those who love him and keep his commandments, we have sinned and done wrong.” Nancy notices that he does not confess Babylon’s sins. “He didn’t excuse. He didn’t blame. He didn’t defend. He didn’t rationalize. He just humbly confessed, ‘We have sinned.’” And the plea at the end is not their record: “We do not make requests of you because we are righteous, but because of your great mercy.” “Lord, listen! Lord, forgive! Lord, hear and act! For your sake, my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your Name.” As a man, husband, and father, hold both scenes. The Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom. And under heaven’s rule, you still get on your knees — not to impress the LORD with your righteousness, but to confess, and to ask him to act for his own name.

**Daniel 7:9–14 (NIV)**
9 “As I looked, “thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His clothing was as white as snow; the hair of his head was white like wool. His throne was flaming with fire, and its wheels were all ablaze. 10 A river of fire was flowing, coming out from before him. Thousands upon thousands attended him; ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court was seated, and the books were opened. 11 “Then I continued to watch because of the boastful words the horn was speaking. I kept looking until the beast was slain and its body destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire. 12 (The other beasts had been stripped of their authority, but were allowed to live for a period of time.) 13 “In my vision at night I looked, and there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence. 14 He was given authority, glory and sovereign power; all nations and peoples of every language worshiped him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.

**Daniel 9:1–19 (NIV)**
1 In the first year of Darius son of Xerxes (a Mede by descent), who was made ruler over the Babylonian kingdom— 2 in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the Scriptures, according to the word of the LORD given to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. 3 So I turned to the Lord God and pleaded with him in prayer and petition, in fasting, and in sackcloth and ashes. 4 I prayed to the LORD my God and confessed: “Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps his covenant of love with those who love him and keep his commandments, 5 we have sinned and done wrong. We have been wicked and have rebelled; we have turned away from your commands and laws. 6 We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes and our ancestors, and to all the people of the land. 7 “Lord, you are righteous, but this day we are covered with shame—the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and all Israel, both near and far, in all the countries where you have scattered us because of our unfaithfulness to you. 8 We and our kings, our princes and our ancestors are covered with shame, LORD, because we have sinned against you. 9 The Lord our God is merciful and forgiving, even though we have rebelled against him; 10 we have not obeyed the LORD our God or kept the laws he gave us through his servants the prophets. 11 All Israel has transgressed your law and turned away, refusing to obey you. “Therefore the curses and sworn judgments written in the Law of Moses, the servant of God, have been poured out on us, because we have sinned against you. 12 You have fulfilled the words spoken against us and against our rulers by bringing on us great disaster. Under the whole heaven nothing has ever been done like what has been done to Jerusalem. 13 Just as it is written in the Law of Moses, all this disaster has come on us, yet we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our sins and giving attention to your truth. 14 The LORD did not hesitate to bring the disaster on us, for the LORD our God is righteous in everything he does; yet we have not obeyed him. 15 “Now, Lord our God, who brought your people out of Egypt with a mighty hand and who made for yourself a name that endures to this day, we have sinned, we have done wrong. 16 Lord, in keeping with all your righteous acts, turn away your anger and your wrath from Jerusalem, your city, your holy hill. Our sins and the iniquities of our ancestors have made Jerusalem and your people an object of scorn to all those around us. 17 “Now, our God, hear the prayers and petitions of your servant. For your sake, Lord, look with favor on your desolate sanctuary. 18 Give ear, our God, and hear; open your eyes and see the desolation of the city that bears your Name. We do not make requests of you because we are righteous, but because of your great mercy. 19 Lord, listen! Lord, forgive! Lord, hear and act! For your sake, my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your Name.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Daniel 7:13.** NIV: “one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven.” LSB: “with the clouds of heaven One like a Son of Man was coming.” The vision is of a human figure who is also more than human, approaching the Ancient of Days.
- **Daniel 9:19.** NIV: “For your sake, my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your Name.” LSB: “For Your own sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people are called by Your name.” The plea is not Daniel’s record. It is the LORD’s name.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“When You Are Discouraged (Daniel 7)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-you-are-discouraged-daniel-7/) sits before the Ancient of Days and the one like a son of man: earthly kingdoms are temporary, and “Jesus is given ultimate dominion.” Her [“When You Need Endurance through Difficulties (Daniel 9)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-you-need-endurance-through-difficulties-danie/) then watches Daniel pray: “Heaven rules, yes, but that doesn’t mean there’s nothing for us to do under heaven’s rule.” John Piper’s Ask Pastor John [“Why Is Jesus Called ‘Son of Man’?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-is-jesus-called-son-of-man) and [“Son of God, Son of Man, King of Israel”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/son-of-god-son-of-man-king-of-israel) hear Daniel 7 in the same exaltation. His [“How to Pray for a Desolate Church”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-pray-for-a-desolate-church) walks the confession of Daniel 9:1–23. BibleProject’s [Book of Daniel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-daniel/) sets chapter 7 among the visions that give hope that God will confront evil and deliver his people.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been watching earthly kingdoms as if they were final, and forgetting the one like a son of man? And where do you need to pray Daniel’s prayer — confession first, then a plea “for your sake” — instead of asking the LORD to bless your record?

**Lesson 141: Daniel: one like a son of man, and a prayer of confession**

Good morning. Yesterday Daniel would not close the window. He knelt three times a day, as he had done before, and the LORD shut the mouths of the lions. Today the book turns from the court stories to a night vision, and then to a prayer of confession. Daniel looks, and thrones are set in place, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat. His clothing is white as snow; the hair of his head is white like wool. His throne is flaming with fire. Then, in the vision at night, “there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence.” “He was given authority, glory and sovereign power; all nations and peoples of every language worshiped him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” This is not a slogan. It is a courtroom in heaven, and a human figure who is also more than human, receiving an unending kingdom. Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth, teaching Daniel 7, says, “The kingdoms of earth are temporary, power is given, power is taken away. But here, Jesus is given ultimate dominion over heaven and earth, and He will reign and rule forever. The Son of God became a Son of Man.” Then, in Daniel 9, she will not let “Heaven rules” become an excuse to sit still: “Heaven rules, yes, but that doesn’t mean there’s nothing for us to do under heaven’s rule. God moves in response to the prayers, the humility, and the repentance of His people, to accomplish His purposes in our world.” Then the prayer. In the first year of Darius, Daniel understood from the Scriptures, according to the word of the LORD given to Jeremiah, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. So he turned to the Lord God and pleaded with him in prayer and petition, in fasting, and in sackcloth and ashes. He prayed and confessed: “Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps his covenant of love with those who love him and keep his commandments, we have sinned and done wrong.” Nancy notices that he does not confess Babylon’s sins. “He didn’t excuse. He didn’t blame. He didn’t defend. He didn’t rationalize. He just humbly confessed, ‘We have sinned.’” And the plea at the end is not their record: “We do not make requests of you because we are righteous, but because of your great mercy.” “Lord, listen! Lord, forgive! Lord, hear and act! For your sake, my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your Name.” As a woman, wife, and a mother, hold both scenes. The Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom. And under heaven’s rule, you still get on your knees — not to impress the LORD with your righteousness, but to confess, and to ask him to act for his own name.

**Daniel 7:9–14 (NIV)**
9 “As I looked, “thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His clothing was as white as snow; the hair of his head was white like wool. His throne was flaming with fire, and its wheels were all ablaze. 10 A river of fire was flowing, coming out from before him. Thousands upon thousands attended him; ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court was seated, and the books were opened. 11 “Then I continued to watch because of the boastful words the horn was speaking. I kept looking until the beast was slain and its body destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire. 12 (The other beasts had been stripped of their authority, but were allowed to live for a period of time.) 13 “In my vision at night I looked, and there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence. 14 He was given authority, glory and sovereign power; all nations and peoples of every language worshiped him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.

**Daniel 9:1–19 (NIV)**
1 In the first year of Darius son of Xerxes (a Mede by descent), who was made ruler over the Babylonian kingdom— 2 in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the Scriptures, according to the word of the LORD given to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years. 3 So I turned to the Lord God and pleaded with him in prayer and petition, in fasting, and in sackcloth and ashes. 4 I prayed to the LORD my God and confessed: “Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps his covenant of love with those who love him and keep his commandments, 5 we have sinned and done wrong. We have been wicked and have rebelled; we have turned away from your commands and laws. 6 We have not listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes and our ancestors, and to all the people of the land. 7 “Lord, you are righteous, but this day we are covered with shame—the people of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem and all Israel, both near and far, in all the countries where you have scattered us because of our unfaithfulness to you. 8 We and our kings, our princes and our ancestors are covered with shame, LORD, because we have sinned against you. 9 The Lord our God is merciful and forgiving, even though we have rebelled against him; 10 we have not obeyed the LORD our God or kept the laws he gave us through his servants the prophets. 11 All Israel has transgressed your law and turned away, refusing to obey you. “Therefore the curses and sworn judgments written in the Law of Moses, the servant of God, have been poured out on us, because we have sinned against you. 12 You have fulfilled the words spoken against us and against our rulers by bringing on us great disaster. Under the whole heaven nothing has ever been done like what has been done to Jerusalem. 13 Just as it is written in the Law of Moses, all this disaster has come on us, yet we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our sins and giving attention to your truth. 14 The LORD did not hesitate to bring the disaster on us, for the LORD our God is righteous in everything he does; yet we have not obeyed him. 15 “Now, Lord our God, who brought your people out of Egypt with a mighty hand and who made for yourself a name that endures to this day, we have sinned, we have done wrong. 16 Lord, in keeping with all your righteous acts, turn away your anger and your wrath from Jerusalem, your city, your holy hill. Our sins and the iniquities of our ancestors have made Jerusalem and your people an object of scorn to all those around us. 17 “Now, our God, hear the prayers and petitions of your servant. For your sake, Lord, look with favor on your desolate sanctuary. 18 Give ear, our God, and hear; open your eyes and see the desolation of the city that bears your Name. We do not make requests of you because we are righteous, but because of your great mercy. 19 Lord, listen! Lord, forgive! Lord, hear and act! For your sake, my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your Name.”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Daniel 7:13.** NIV: “one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven.” LSB: “with the clouds of heaven One like a Son of Man was coming.” The vision is of a human figure who is also more than human, approaching the Ancient of Days.
- **Daniel 9:19.** NIV: “For your sake, my God, do not delay, because your city and your people bear your Name.” LSB: “For Your own sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people are called by Your name.” The plea is not Daniel’s record. It is the LORD’s name.

**Go deeper:** Nancy DeMoss Wolgemuth’s [“When You Are Discouraged (Daniel 7)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-you-are-discouraged-daniel-7/) sits before the Ancient of Days and the one like a son of man: earthly kingdoms are temporary, and “Jesus is given ultimate dominion.” Her [“When You Need Endurance through Difficulties (Daniel 9)”](https://www.reviveourhearts.com/podcast/revive-our-hearts/when-you-need-endurance-through-difficulties-danie/) then watches Daniel pray: “Heaven rules, yes, but that doesn’t mean there’s nothing for us to do under heaven’s rule.” John Piper’s Ask Pastor John [“Why Is Jesus Called ‘Son of Man’?”](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-is-jesus-called-son-of-man) and [“Son of God, Son of Man, King of Israel”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/son-of-god-son-of-man-king-of-israel) hear Daniel 7 in the same exaltation. His [“How to Pray for a Desolate Church”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-pray-for-a-desolate-church) walks the confession of Daniel 9:1–23. BibleProject’s [Book of Daniel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-daniel/) sets chapter 7 among the visions that give hope that God will confront evil and deliver his people.

**Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where have you been watching earthly kingdoms as if they were final, and forgetting the one like a son of man? And where do you need to pray Daniel’s prayer — confession first, then a plea “for your sake” — instead of asking the LORD to bless your record?

**Lesson 142: Hosea: a faithful God and an unfaithful people**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Daniel saw one like a son of man given an everlasting kingdom, and then he prayed a prayer of confession for a desolate people. Today the word of the LORD comes to Hosea, in the years leading up to the fall of the northern kingdom, and the LORD tells the truth about an unfaithful people by a marriage and by three names. “Go, marry a promiscuous woman and have children with her, for like an adulterous wife this land is guilty of unfaithfulness to the LORD.” This is not a story to sensationalize. It is a covenant wound. Hosea marries Gomer, and their children’s names tell the truth: Jezreel, because judgment is coming; Lo-Ruhamah, which means “not loved”; Lo-Ammi, which means “not my people,” “for you are not my people, and I am not your God.” That is what unfaithfulness costs. But it is not the last word. “In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘children of the living God.’” Then the LORD himself will allure her, lead her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her. “In that day,” he says, “you will call me ‘my husband’; you will no longer call me ‘my master.’” “I will betroth you to me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in love and compassion. I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will acknowledge the LORD.” “I will show my love to the one I called ‘Not my loved one.’ I will say to those called ‘Not my people,’ ‘You are my people’; and they will say, ‘You are my God.’” John Piper walks Hosea 1–3 and says the point is, “Love God warmly as your husband, don’t just serve him as your Lord.” He hears the promise three times: “I will betroth you; I will betroth you; I will betroth you.” BibleProject says Israel’s rebellion will bring severe consequences, “but God’s own covenant love and mercy are more powerful and will open the way to a new future.” As a man, husband, and father, do not treat the LORD as a master you merely serve. He is a faithful husband to an unfaithful people, and he means to betroth you in faithfulness. Return his love. Let the names that once said “not loved” and “not my people” be reversed in your house.

**Hosea 1:1–11 (NIV)**
1 The word of the LORD that came to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and during the reign of Jeroboam son of Jehoash king of Israel: 2 When the LORD began to speak through Hosea, the LORD said to him, “Go, marry a promiscuous woman and have children with her, for like an adulterous wife this land is guilty of unfaithfulness to the LORD.” 3 So he married Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son. 4 Then the LORD said to Hosea, “Call him Jezreel, because I will soon punish the house of Jehu for the massacre at Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingdom of Israel. 5 In that day I will break Israel’s bow in the Valley of Jezreel.” 6 Gomer conceived again and gave birth to a daughter. Then the LORD said to Hosea, “Call her Lo-Ruhamah (which means “not loved”), for I will no longer show love to Israel, that I should at all forgive them. 7 Yet I will show love to Judah; and I will save them—not by bow, sword or battle, or by horses and horsemen, but I, the LORD their God, will save them.” 8 After she had weaned Lo-Ruhamah, Gomer had another son. 9 Then the LORD said, “Call him Lo-Ammi (which means “not my people”), for you are not my people, and I am not your God. 10 “Yet the Israelites will be like the sand on the seashore, which cannot be measured or counted. In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘children of the living God.’ 11 The people of Judah and the people of Israel will come together; they will appoint one leader and will come up out of the land, for great will be the day of Jezreel.

**Hosea 2:14–23 (NIV)**
14 “Therefore I am now going to allure her; I will lead her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her. 15 There I will give her back her vineyards, and will make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. There she will respond as in the days of her youth, as in the day she came up out of Egypt. 16 “In that day,” declares the LORD, “you will call me ‘my husband’; you will no longer call me ‘my master.’ 17 I will remove the names of the Baals from her lips; no longer will their names be invoked. 18 In that day I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, the birds in the sky and the creatures that move along the ground. Bow and sword and battle I will abolish from the land, so that all may lie down in safety. 19 I will betroth you to me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in love and compassion. 20 I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will acknowledge the LORD. 21 “In that day I will respond,” declares the LORD— “I will respond to the skies, and they will respond to the earth; 22 and the earth will respond to the grain, the new wine and the olive oil, and they will respond to Jezreel. 23 I will plant her for myself in the land; I will show my love to the one I called ‘Not my loved one.’ I will say to those called ‘Not my people,’ ‘You are my people’; and they will say, ‘You are my God.’”

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Hosea 1:6, 9.** NIV gives the names with their meaning: Lo-Ruhamah “not loved,” Lo-Ammi “not my people.” LSB uses “she who has not obtained compassion” and “not My people.” The names tell the truth about the covenant, and chapter 2 will reverse them.
- **Hosea 2:19–20.** NIV: “I will betroth you to me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in love and compassion. I will betroth you in faithfulness, and you will acknowledge the LORD.” LSB: “in righteousness and in justice, In lovingkindness and in compassion… in faithfulness.” The LORD himself will start over with his people.

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s [“Call Me Husband, Not Baal”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/call-me-husband-not-baal) walks Hosea 1–3 and says the point is, “Love God warmly as your husband, don’t just serve him as your Lord.” He hears the threefold promise, “I will betroth you.” BibleProject’s [Book of Hosea guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-hosea/) says Israel’s rebellion will bring severe consequences, “but God’s own covenant love and mercy are more powerful and will open the way to a new future.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been serving the LORD as a master without loving him as a husband? What would it look like today to hear “I will betroth you to me forever” as a real promise, and to come home?

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 143: Hosea: come, let us return to the Lord**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD promised to betroth his unfaithful people to himself forever, and to say to those called “Not my people,” “You are my people.” Today Hosea calls them to return, and the LORD’s own heart is heard. “Come, let us return to the LORD. He has torn us to pieces but he will heal us; he has injured us but he will bind up our wounds.” “Let us acknowledge the LORD; let us press on to acknowledge him.” And then the word that cuts through religion that has no love: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and acknowledgment of God rather than burnt offerings.” The LORD is not a stranger to this people. “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.” “I led them with cords of human kindness, with ties of love. To them I was like one who lifts a little child to the cheek, and I bent down to feed them.” And when they will not come, the Father’s heart breaks open: “How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel? How can I treat you like Admah? How can I make you like Zeboyim? My heart is changed within me; all my compassion is aroused.” So the last call is plain. “Return, Israel, to the LORD your God. Your sins have been your downfall!” “Take words with you and return to the LORD.” And the promise on the other side of return: “I will heal their waywardness and love them freely, for my anger has turned away from them.” BibleProject hears chapters 11 and 14 as hopeful poems about God’s mercy after the accusations. In Hosea 11, “God is emotionally torn apart,” yet he still will not give his son up. Chapter 14 then calls Israel to repent, and the LORD promises to heal. As a man, husband, and father, do not bring the LORD burnt offerings and withhold mercy. Come, return to him. He has loved you since you were a child, and he still asks, “How can I give you up, Ephraim?” He will heal their waywardness and love them freely.

**Hosea 6:1–6 (NIV)**
1 “Come, let us return to the LORD. He has torn us to pieces but he will heal us; he has injured us but he will bind up our wounds. 2 After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will restore us, that we may live in his presence. 3 Let us acknowledge the LORD; let us press on to acknowledge him. As surely as the sun rises, he will appear; he will come to us like the winter rains, like the spring rains that water the earth.” 4 “What can I do with you, Ephraim? What can I do with you, Judah? Your love is like the morning mist, like the early dew that disappears. 5 Therefore I cut you in pieces with my prophets, I killed you with the words of my mouth— then my judgments go forth like the sun. 6 For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and acknowledgment of God rather than burnt offerings.

**Hosea 11:1–11 (NIV)**
1 “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son. 2 But the more they were called, the more they went away from me. They sacrificed to the Baals and they burned incense to images. 3 It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by the arms; but they did not realize it was I who healed them. 4 I led them with cords of human kindness, with ties of love. To them I was like one who lifts a little child to the cheek, and I bent down to feed them. 5 “Will they not return to Egypt and will not Assyria rule over them because they refuse to repent? 6 A sword will flash in their cities; it will devour their false prophets and put an end to their plans. 7 My people are determined to turn from me. Even though they call me God Most High, I will by no means exalt them. 8 “How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel? How can I treat you like Admah? How can I make you like Zeboyim? My heart is changed within me; all my compassion is aroused. 9 I will not carry out my fierce anger, nor will I devastate Ephraim again. For I am God, and not a man— the Holy One among you. I will not come against their cities. 10 They will follow the LORD; he will roar like a lion. When he roars, his children will come trembling from the west. 11 They will come from Egypt, trembling like sparrows, from Assyria, fluttering like doves. I will settle them in their homes,” declares the LORD.

**Hosea 14:1–9 (NIV)**
1 Return, Israel, to the LORD your God. Your sins have been your downfall! 2 Take words with you and return to the LORD. Say to him: “Forgive all our sins and receive us graciously, that we may offer the fruit of our lips. 3 Assyria cannot save us; we will not mount warhorses. We will never again say ‘Our gods’ to what our own hands have made, for in you the fatherless find compassion.” 4 “I will heal their waywardness and love them freely, for my anger has turned away from them. 5 I will be like the dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily. Like a cedar of Lebanon he will send down his roots; 6 his young shoots will grow. His splendor will be like an olive tree, his fragrance like a cedar of Lebanon. 7 People will dwell again in his shade; they will flourish like the grain, they will blossom like the vine— Israel’s fame will be like the wine of Lebanon. 8 Ephraim, what more have I to do with idols? I will answer him and care for him. I am like a flourishing juniper; your fruitfulness comes from me.” 9 Who is wise? Let them realize these things. Who is discerning? Let them understand. The ways of the LORD are right; the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble in them.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Hosea 6:6.** NIV: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and acknowledgment of God rather than burnt offerings.” LSB: “For I delight in lovingkindness rather than sacrifice, And in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.”
- **Hosea 11:8.** NIV: “My heart is changed within me; all my compassion is aroused.” LSB: “My heart is turned over within Me; All My compassions are stirred.”
- **Hosea 14:4.** NIV: “I will heal their waywardness and love them freely, for my anger has turned away from them.” LSB: “I will heal their turning away from Me; I will love them freely, For My anger has turned away from them.”

**Lesson 144: Joel: return to me with all your heart; I will pour out my Spirit**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD said, “Come, let us return to the LORD.” He also promised, “I will heal their waywardness and love them freely, for my anger has turned away from them.” Today Joel speaks in the shadow of locusts and of the day of the LORD, and the call is the same, only deeper: return with all your heart, and the LORD will pour out his Spirit. “Even now,” declares the LORD, “return to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning.” “Rend your heart and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love, and he relents from sending calamity.” This is not a thin slogan, and it is not only a future hope. The locusts have come. The day of the LORD is in view. And still he says, “Even now,” John Piper hears the threat and the open door together: “Even though God has threatened destruction of his own people… yet he holds out the opportunity of repentance and salvation at the eleventh hour. If they will repent, he will repent. If they will rend their hearts, he will cease to rend their land.” BibleProject says, “God longs to show mercy to Israel if they admit and confess their sin,” and that repentance “can’t just be a show you put on to get out of trouble.” Then the promise that looks beyond this return: “And afterward, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions.” “Even on my servants, both men and women, I will pour out my Spirit in those days.” “And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved.” Piper says that from 2:28 on, God “is going to pour out his Spirit far and wide to bless his people.” The church will one day hear this promise kept. Today, stay with Joel: rend your heart, and trust the LORD who pours out his Spirit. As a man, husband, and father, do not tear a garment and leave the heart intact. Return to him with all your heart — even now — and ask him for the Spirit he has promised to pour out.

**Joel 2:12–32 (NIV)**
12 “Even now,” declares the LORD, “return to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning.” 13 Rend your heart and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love, and he relents from sending calamity. 14 Who knows? He may turn and relent and leave behind a blessing— grain offerings and drink offerings for the LORD your God. 15 Blow the trumpet in Zion, declare a holy fast, call a sacred assembly. 16 Gather the people, consecrate the assembly; bring together the elders, gather the children, those nursing at the breast. Let the bridegroom leave his room and the bride her chamber. 17 Let the priests, who minister before the LORD, weep between the portico and the altar. Let them say, “Spare your people, LORD. Do not make your inheritance an object of scorn, a byword among the nations. Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’” 18 Then the LORD was jealous for his land and took pity on his people. 19 The LORD replied to them: “I am sending you grain, new wine and olive oil, enough to satisfy you fully; never again will I make you an object of scorn to the nations. 20 “I will drive the northern horde far from you, pushing it into a parched and barren land; its eastern ranks will drown in the Dead Sea and its western ranks in the Mediterranean Sea. And its stench will go up; its smell will rise.” Surely he has done great things! 21 Do not be afraid, land of Judah; be glad and rejoice. Surely the LORD has done great things! 22 Do not be afraid, you wild animals, for the pastures in the wilderness are becoming green. The trees are bearing their fruit; the fig tree and the vine yield their riches. 23 Be glad, people of Zion, rejoice in the LORD your God, for he has given you the autumn rains because he is faithful. He sends you abundant showers, both autumn and spring rains, as before. 24 The threshing floors will be filled with grain; the vats will overflow with new wine and oil. 25 “I will repay you for the years the locusts have eaten— the great locust and the young locust, the other locusts and the locust swarm— my great army that I sent among you. 26 You will have plenty to eat, until you are full, and you will praise the name of the LORD your God, who has worked wonders for you; never again will my people be shamed. 27 Then you will know that I am in Israel, that I am the LORD your God, and that there is no other; never again will my people be shamed. 28 “And afterward, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions. 29 Even on my servants, both men and women, I will pour out my Spirit in those days. 30 I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and billows of smoke. 31 The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD. 32 And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved; for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the LORD has said, even among the survivors whom the LORD calls.

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Joel 2:13.** NIV: “Rend your heart and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love, and he relents from sending calamity.” LSB: “tear your heart and not your garments… abounding in lovingkindness, And relenting concerning evil.”
- **Joel 2:28.** NIV: “I will pour out my Spirit on all people.” LSB: “I will pour out My Spirit on all mankind.”

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s [“The Locust Horde and the Day of the Lord”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-locust-horde-and-the-day-of-the-lord) reads Joel in two movements: a locust plague and a call to return, then the promise that God “is going to pour out his Spirit far and wide to bless his people.” “If they will rend their hearts, he will cease to rend their land.” BibleProject’s [Book of Joel guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-joel/) says, “God longs to show mercy to Israel if they admit and confess their sin,” and that repentance “can’t just be a show you put on to get out of trouble.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been rending garments — outward sorrow, religious noise — and not your heart? What would “return to me with all your heart” look like today, and how will you wait for the Spirit the LORD has promised to pour out?

sources.label: John Piper, Why Christians Care About Every Injustice (Desiring God)

**Lesson 145: Amos: let justice roll on like a river**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the LORD said, “return to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning,” and promised to pour out his Spirit on all people. Today Amos will not let worship become a cover for injustice. “Seek good, not evil, that you may live. Then the LORD God Almighty will be with you, just as you say he is.” The people already say the LORD is with them. Amos asks whether their life tells the truth. And then the word that will not be made into a thin slogan: “I hate, I despise your religious festivals; your assemblies are a stench to me.” “Even though you bring me burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them.” Music, gatherings, and the name of the LORD cannot hide a life that tramples what is right. So the call lands: “But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!” John Piper, citing this verse, says, “Christians care about all injustice, especially injustice against God.” BibleProject says Amos’s words “are a call to embrace the true worship of God that should always include acts of justice, righteousness, and love for one’s neighbor,” and that he is “constantly exposing the religious hypocrisy” of people who faithfully attend the gatherings while injustice goes on. As a man, husband, and father, do not love the festival and withhold the river. Seek good, not evil. Let justice roll on in your house, your work, and your worship — a never-failing stream, not a performance the LORD despises.

**Amos 5:14–24 (NIV)**
14 Seek good, not evil, that you may live. Then the LORD God Almighty will be with you, just as you say he is. 15 Hate evil, love good; maintain justice in the courts. Perhaps the LORD God Almighty will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph. 16 Therefore this is what the Lord, the LORD God Almighty, says: “There will be wailing in all the streets and cries of anguish in every public square. The farmers will be summoned to weep and the mourners to wail. 17 There will be wailing in all the vineyards, for I will pass through your midst,” says the LORD. 18 Woe to you who long for the day of the LORD! Why do you long for the day of the LORD? That day will be darkness, not light. 19 It will be as though a man fled from a lion only to meet a bear, as though he entered his house and rested his hand on the wall only to have a snake bite him. 20 Will not the day of the LORD be darkness, not light— pitch-dark, without a ray of brightness? 21 “I hate, I despise your religious festivals; your assemblies are a stench to me. 22 Even though you bring me burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them. Though you bring choice fellowship offerings, I will have no regard for them. 23 Away with the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps. 24 But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!

**Translation note (NIV vs. LSB)**
- **Amos 5:21.** NIV: “I hate, I despise your religious festivals; your assemblies are a stench to me.” LSB: “I hate, I reject your feasts, Nor do I delight in your solemn assemblies.”
- **Amos 5:24.** NIV: “But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!” LSB: “But let justice roll down like waters And righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.”

**Go deeper:** John Piper’s [“Why Christians Care About Every Injustice”](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-do-christians-care-about-most/excerpts/why-christians-care-about-every-injustice) cites Amos 5:24 and says, “Christians care about all injustice, especially injustice against God.” BibleProject’s [Book of Amos guide](https://bibleproject.com/guides/book-of-amos/) says Amos’s words “are a call to embrace the true worship of God that should always include acts of justice, righteousness, and love for one’s neighbor,” and that the prophet is “constantly exposing the religious hypocrisy” of people who attend the gatherings while injustice goes on.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have your gatherings, songs, or religious habits gotten ahead of justice and righteousness? What would it look like this week for justice to roll on like a river in one ordinary place you actually have a say — at home, at work, or among the people God has given you?
