lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 188: Acts: in the name of Jesus, we cannot help speaking**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday the Spirit came at Pentecost, and Peter preached that God raised Jesus from the dead. Today that same name walks up to the temple at the time of prayer. A man lame from birth is being carried to the gate called Beautiful, where he begs. Peter says, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.” He helps him up, and the man goes with them into the temple courts, walking and jumping, and praising God. A crowd runs together, and Peter will not take the credit. “By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know was made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through him that has completely healed him, as you can all see.” The leaders have Peter and John brought in, and they ask by what power or what name they have done this. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, says it is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and whom God raised from the dead. “Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.” The leaders see their courage and take note that these men had been with Jesus. They command them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. Peter and John answer, “Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.” John Piper, in “Jesus' Name Made This Man Strong,” preaches this healing as the work of Jesus’ name, not the apostles’ technique. The man they can see and know is made strong by faith in that name. In “There Is Salvation in No One Else,” he takes the next day’s confession as far as it will go: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. The courage to keep speaking comes from having been with Jesus, and from having seen and heard what they cannot now be silent about. BibleProject’s Acts guide hears the same church, filled with the Spirit, unwilling to stop saying the name. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that has been given among men by which we must be saved.” The NIV’s “Salvation is found in no one else” is that same exclusive mercy. The name that made the man walk is the name that saves. They do not have silver or gold, but they have a name, and they cannot help speaking it. As a man, husband, and father, do not be quiet about what you have seen and heard. There is no other name, and that name is enough.

**Acts 3:1–16 (NIV)**
1 One day Peter and John were going up to the temple at the time of prayer—at three in the afternoon. 2 Now a man who was lame from birth was being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those going into the temple courts. 3 When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. 4 Peter looked straight at him, as did John. Then Peter said, “Look at us!” 5 So the man gave them his attention, expecting to get something from them. 6 Then Peter said, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.” 7 Taking him by the right hand, he helped him up, and instantly the man’s feet and ankles became strong. 8 He jumped to his feet and began to walk. Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and jumping, and praising God. 9 When all the people saw him walking and praising God, 10 they recognized him as the same man who used to sit begging at the temple gate called Beautiful, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. 11 While the man held on to Peter and John, all the people were astonished and came running to them in the place called Solomon’s Colonnade. 12 When Peter saw this, he said to them: “Fellow Israelites, why does this surprise you? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk? 13 The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant Jesus. You handed him over to be killed, and you disowned him before Pilate, though he had decided to let him go. 14 You disowned the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you. 15 You killed the author of life, but God raised him from the dead. We are witnesses of this. 16 By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know was made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through him that has completely healed him, as you can all see.

**Acts 4:8–20 (NIV)**
8 Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: “Rulers and elders of the people! 9 If we are being called to account today for an act of kindness shown to a man who was lame and are being asked how he was healed, 10 then know this, you and all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed. 11 Jesus is “‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ 12 Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.” 13 When they saw the courage of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they were astonished and they took note that these men had been with Jesus. 14 But since they could see the man who had been healed standing there with them, there was nothing they could say. 15 So they ordered them to withdraw from the Sanhedrin and then conferred together. 16 “What are we going to do with these men?” they asked. “Everyone living in Jerusalem knows they have performed a notable sign, and we cannot deny it. 17 But to stop this thing from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them to speak no longer to anyone in this name.” 18 Then they called them in again and commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. 19 But Peter and John replied, “Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! 20 As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been tempted to stay quiet about the name of Jesus this week? What would it look like today to give what you do have — that name — and to speak about what you have seen and heard?

**Lesson 188: Acts: in the name of Jesus, we cannot help speaking**

Good morning. Yesterday the Spirit came at Pentecost, and Peter preached that God raised Jesus from the dead. Today that same name walks up to the temple at the time of prayer. A man lame from birth is being carried to the gate called Beautiful, where he begs. Peter says, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.” He helps him up, and the man goes with them into the temple courts, walking and jumping, and praising God. A crowd runs together, and Peter will not take the credit. “By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know was made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through him that has completely healed him, as you can all see.” The leaders have Peter and John brought in, and they ask by what power or what name they have done this. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, says it is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and whom God raised from the dead. “Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.” The leaders see their courage and take note that these men had been with Jesus. They command them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. Peter and John answer, “Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.” John Piper, in “Jesus' Name Made This Man Strong,” preaches this healing as the work of Jesus’ name, not the apostles’ technique. The man they can see and know is made strong by faith in that name. In “There Is Salvation in No One Else,” he takes the next day’s confession as far as it will go: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. The courage to keep speaking comes from having been with Jesus, and from having seen and heard what they cannot now be silent about. BibleProject’s Acts guide hears the same church, filled with the Spirit, unwilling to stop saying the name. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that has been given among men by which we must be saved.” The NIV’s “Salvation is found in no one else” is that same exclusive mercy. The name that made the man walk is the name that saves. They do not have silver or gold, but they have a name, and they cannot help speaking it. As a woman, wife, and a mother, do not be quiet about what you have seen and heard. There is no other name, and that name is enough.

**Acts 3:1–16 (NIV)**
1 One day Peter and John were going up to the temple at the time of prayer—at three in the afternoon. 2 Now a man who was lame from birth was being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those going into the temple courts. 3 When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. 4 Peter looked straight at him, as did John. Then Peter said, “Look at us!” 5 So the man gave them his attention, expecting to get something from them. 6 Then Peter said, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.” 7 Taking him by the right hand, he helped him up, and instantly the man’s feet and ankles became strong. 8 He jumped to his feet and began to walk. Then he went with them into the temple courts, walking and jumping, and praising God. 9 When all the people saw him walking and praising God, 10 they recognized him as the same man who used to sit begging at the temple gate called Beautiful, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. 11 While the man held on to Peter and John, all the people were astonished and came running to them in the place called Solomon’s Colonnade. 12 When Peter saw this, he said to them: “Fellow Israelites, why does this surprise you? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk? 13 The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant Jesus. You handed him over to be killed, and you disowned him before Pilate, though he had decided to let him go. 14 You disowned the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you. 15 You killed the author of life, but God raised him from the dead. We are witnesses of this. 16 By faith in the name of Jesus, this man whom you see and know was made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through him that has completely healed him, as you can all see.

**Acts 4:8–20 (NIV)**
8 Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: “Rulers and elders of the people! 9 If we are being called to account today for an act of kindness shown to a man who was lame and are being asked how he was healed, 10 then know this, you and all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed. 11 Jesus is “‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ 12 Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.” 13 When they saw the courage of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they were astonished and they took note that these men had been with Jesus. 14 But since they could see the man who had been healed standing there with them, there was nothing they could say. 15 So they ordered them to withdraw from the Sanhedrin and then conferred together. 16 “What are we going to do with these men?” they asked. “Everyone living in Jerusalem knows they have performed a notable sign, and we cannot deny it. 17 But to stop this thing from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them to speak no longer to anyone in this name.” 18 Then they called them in again and commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. 19 But Peter and John replied, “Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! 20 As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

**Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where have you been tempted to stay quiet about the name of Jesus this week? What would it look like today to give what you do have — that name — and to speak about what you have seen and heard?

**Lesson 189: Acts: Stephen's witness, and an Ethiopian believes**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Peter and John said they could not help speaking about what they had seen and heard. Today that same courage fills Stephen, and then the good news keeps moving down a desert road. Stephen has told the Sanhedrin that they always resist the Holy Spirit, that their ancestors killed the prophets who predicted the coming of the Righteous One, and that they have now betrayed and murdered him. When they hear this, they are furious. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looks up to heaven and sees the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. “Look,” he says, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” They rush at him, drag him out of the city, and begin to stone him. The witnesses lay their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. While they are stoning him, Stephen prays, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he falls on his knees and cries out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he has said this, he falls asleep. Teach this with quiet dignity. A faithful man dies praying, and Jesus is standing. The word does not stop there. An angel of the Lord tells Philip to go south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. He meets an Ethiopian official, an important man in charge of the treasury of the Kandake, sitting in his chariot reading Isaiah. The Spirit tells Philip to go to that chariot and stay near it. Philip hears him reading and asks if he understands. “How can I,” he says, “unless someone explains it to me?” The passage is about the one led like a sheep to the slaughter, whose life was taken from the earth. The official asks who the prophet is talking about. Philip begins with that very passage and tells him the good news about Jesus. They come to some water, and the official asks what can stand in the way of his being baptized. He gives orders to stop the chariot, and Philip baptizes him. When they come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord takes Philip away, and the official goes on his way rejoicing. John Piper, in “The Death of a Spirit-Filled Man,” stays with Stephen to the end: full of the Holy Spirit, seeing Jesus standing, praying that the Lord Jesus would receive his spirit, and asking that this sin not be held against them. The church loses a faithful witness, and a young man named Saul is watching. In “The Leading of the Lord in Personal Evangelism,” Piper follows Philip onto the desert road, where the Spirit leads one step at a time, “Go to that chariot,” and the timing proves perfect: the official is already reading the very Scripture Jesus fulfilled. BibleProject’s Acts guide hears the same movement: a martyr’s witness in Jerusalem, and then the good news on the way to the ends of the earth. The Legacy Standard Bible has Stephen say, “Behold, I see the heavens opened up and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,” and later, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them!” The NIV’s wording is the one we read today, and the two prayers are the same trust and the same mercy. A faithful witness can fall asleep in Jesus, and the good news can still find a chariot on a desert road. As a man, husband, and father, tell the truth about the Righteous One, and be ready to explain the Scriptures to the person God puts in your path.

**Acts 7:51–60 (NIV)**
51 “You stiff-necked people! Your hearts and ears are still uncircumcised. You are just like your ancestors: You always resist the Holy Spirit! 52 Was there ever a prophet your ancestors did not persecute? They even killed those who predicted the coming of the Righteous One. And now you have betrayed and murdered him— 53 you who have received the law that was given through angels but have not obeyed it.” 54 When the members of the Sanhedrin heard this, they were furious and gnashed their teeth at him. 55 But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. 56 “Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” 57 At this they covered their ears and, yelling at the top of their voices, they all rushed at him, 58 dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile, the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. 59 While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” 60 Then he fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

**Acts 8:26–40 (NIV)**
26 Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Go south to the road—the desert road—that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” 27 So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, an important official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake (which means “queen of the Ethiopians”). This man had gone to Jerusalem to worship, 28 and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the Book of Isaiah the prophet. 29 The Spirit told Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.” 30 Then Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. 31 “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. 32 This is the passage of Scripture the eunuch was reading: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. 33 In his humiliation he was deprived of justice. Who can speak of his descendants? For his life was taken from the earth.” 34 The eunuch asked Philip, “Tell me, please, who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” 35 Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus. 36 As they traveled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?” 38 And he gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water and Philip baptized him. 39 When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. 40 Philip, however, appeared at Azotus and traveled about, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where is God asking you to be faithful like Stephen, or simply to come alongside someone who is already reading and still needs help to see Jesus? What would it look like today to do the next step the Spirit gives you?

sources.label: John Piper, Overflowing Grace for All Who Believe (Desiring God)

**Lesson 190: Acts: Saul meets Jesus on the road**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we saw Stephen’s faithful witness, and then an Ethiopian official believe the good news about Jesus. Today the story turns to the young man who had watched Stephen die. “Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples.” He goes to the high priest for letters, so that if he finds any who belong to the Way, men or women, he may take them as prisoners to Jerusalem. As he nears Damascus, a light from heaven flashes around him. He falls to the ground and hears a voice: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied. Saul is led into Damascus, blind, and for three days he does not eat or drink. In the city a disciple named Ananias is afraid to go, because he has heard how much harm this man has done. But the Lord says, “Go!” This man is his chosen instrument to proclaim his name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. Ananias goes, places his hands on him, and says, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Scales fall from Saul’s eyes. He is baptized, takes food, and regains his strength. At once he begins to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God, and he grows more and more powerful, proving that Jesus is the Messiah. Teach this with quiet dignity. The man who hunted the church is stopped by the one he was hunting, and then he is called brother. John Piper, in “Overflowing Grace for All Who Believe,” lingers over this conversion and the later words in 1 Timothy, where Paul calls himself the chief of sinners. Piper says, “So Paul was breathing threats and murder against Christians. He was even taking his persecution 150 miles north to Damascus and planning to bring Christians back to Jerusalem for punishment.” The light and the voice do not merely slow him down. Jesus names the persecution as persecution of himself. In “Jesus Is the Christ the Son of God,” Piper follows the new preacher into the synagogues, where the same man now proves that Jesus is the Messiah. BibleProject’s Acts guide hears this as the risen Lord claiming an enemy and sending him to the nations. The Legacy Standard Bible has the Lord say, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of Mine, to bear My name before the Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel;” The NIV’s “chosen instrument to proclaim my name” is that same errand. The persecutor is chosen, not discarded. Jesus can stop a man on the road, call him brother, and send him to proclaim the name he once tried to crush. As a man, husband, and father, do not decide that anyone is past hope, including you. The Lord who said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” also said, “Go!”

**Acts 9:1–22 (NIV)**
1 Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples. He went to the high priest 2 and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any there who belonged to the Way, whether men or women, he might take them as prisoners to Jerusalem. 3 As he neared Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. 4 He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” 5 “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied. 6 “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” 7 The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless; they heard the sound but did not see anyone. 8 Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand into Damascus. 9 For three days he was blind, and did not eat or drink anything. 10 In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord called to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Yes, Lord,” he answered. 11 The Lord told him, “Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying. 12 In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.” 13 “Lord,” Ananias answered, “I have heard many reports about this man and all the harm he has done to your holy people in Jerusalem. 14 And he has come here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on your name.” 15 But the Lord said to Ananias, “Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. 16 I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.” 17 Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18 Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized, 19 and after taking some food, he regained his strength. Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus. 20 At once he began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. 21 All those who heard him were astonished and asked, “Isn’t he the man who raised havoc in Jerusalem among those who call on this name? And hasn’t he come here to take them as prisoners to the chief priests?” 22 Yet Saul grew more and more powerful and baffled the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Messiah.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been breathing out certainty against people Jesus loves, or assuming someone is too far gone? What would it look like today to receive this overflowing grace, and to call a former enemy, or a hard case, a person Jesus can still choose?

In Caesarea a centurion named Cornelius, devout and God-fearing, gives generously and prays regularly. He sees an angel and is told to send for Peter. Meanwhile Peter, on a rooftop, sees a vision of a sheet with animals, and a voice says, “Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.” Peter objects. The voice speaks a second time: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” When Cornelius’s men arrive, Peter goes with them, and in the house he says, “God has shown me that I should not call anyone impure or unclean.” Then he begins to speak: “I now realize how true it is that God does not show favoritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right.” While Peter is still speaking the good news, the Holy Spirit comes on all who heard the message. The circumcised believers who had come with Peter are astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit has been poured out even on Gentiles. Peter says, “Surely no one can stand in the way of their being baptized with water. They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have.” So he orders that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. God does not show favoritism. The Spirit falls on Gentiles, and the door that Peter thought was shut is open. John Piper, in “What God Has Cleansed Do Not Call Common,” says this story about Cornelius and Peter “has a lot to say about our natural tendency to think of other ethnic groups besides our own as unclean and common and corrupt.” “It has a lot to say about world missions and our commitment as evangelical Christians to take the gospel of Christ to every ethnic group.” In “Exalting Jesus So the Spirit Falls,” he follows the moment when the Spirit is poured out even on Gentiles, and no one can stand in the way of their baptism. The Legacy Standard Bible has Peter say that “God is not one to show partiality, but in every nation the one who fears Him and does righteousness is welcome to Him.” The NIV’s “God does not show favoritism” is that same confession. The welcome is wider than Peter had imagined. Do not call common what God has made clean, and do not call a nation unreachable that God has already visited. As a man, husband, and father, let this truth unmake your favoritism. The Spirit has been poured out even on the people you were not planning to include.

1 At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion in what was known as the Italian Regiment. 2 He and all his family were devout and God-fearing; he gave generously to those in need and prayed to God regularly. 3 One day at about three in the afternoon he had a vision. He distinctly saw an angel of God, who came to him and said, “Cornelius!” 4 Cornelius stared at him in fear. “What is it, Lord?” he asked. The angel answered, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have come up as a memorial offering before God. 5 Now send men to Joppa to bring back a man named Simon who is called Peter. 6 He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea.” 7 When the angel who spoke to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier who was one of his attendants. 8 He told them everything that had happened and sent them to Joppa. 9 About noon the following day as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray. 10 He became hungry and wanted something to eat, and while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance. 11 He saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet being let down to earth by its four corners. 12 It contained all kinds of four-footed animals, as well as reptiles and birds. 13 Then a voice told him, “Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.” 14 “Surely not, Lord!” Peter replied. “I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.” 15 The voice spoke to him a second time, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” 16 This happened three times, and immediately the sheet was taken back to heaven. 17 While Peter was wondering about the meaning of the vision, the men sent by Cornelius found out where Simon’s house was and stopped at the gate. 18 They called out, asking if Simon who was known as Peter was staying there. 19 While Peter was still thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Simon, three men are looking for you. 20 So get up and go downstairs. Do not hesitate to go with them, for I have sent them.” 21 Peter went down and said to the men, “I’m the one you’re looking for. Why have you come?” 22 The men replied, “We have come from Cornelius the centurion. He is a righteous and God-fearing man, who is respected by all the Jewish people. But God has shown me that I should not call anyone impure or unclean. 29 So when I was sent for, I came without raising any objection. He is a guest in the home of Simon the tanner, who lives by the sea.’ 33 So I sent for you immediately, and it was good of you to come. Now we are all here in the presence of God to listen to everything the Lord has commanded you to tell us.” 34 Then Peter began to speak: “I now realize how true it is that God does not show favoritism 35 but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right.

Then Peter said, 47 “Surely no one can stand in the way of their being baptized with water. They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have.” 48 So he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked Peter to stay with them for a few days.

lessons.title: Acts: the Macedonian call, and a jailer believes

sources.label: John Piper, Treasuring Christ in Planting Churches and Loving the Poor (Desiring God)

lessons.deliveredMarkdown:
**Lesson 192: Acts: the Macedonian call, and a jailer believes**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday God showed no favoritism, and the Spirit fell on Gentiles in Cornelius’s house. Today the gospel is steered west. Paul and his companions are kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching in the province of Asia, and when they try to enter Bithynia, the Spirit of Jesus will not allow them. In the night Paul sees a man of Macedonia standing and begging him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” They conclude that God has called them to preach the gospel there, and they go at once. In Philippi, by the river, the Lord opens the heart of Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth and a worshiper of God, to respond to Paul’s message. She and her household are baptized, and she opens her home. The road is not only a welcome. After a slave girl is set free from a spirit, Paul and Silas are beaten and thrown into prison. Teach this with care, including the jailer’s despair. About midnight they are praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners are listening. A violent earthquake opens the doors and loosens the chains. The jailer, waking and seeing the doors open, draws his sword to harm himself, thinking the prisoners have escaped. Paul shouts, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” The jailer brings them out and asks, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They reply, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” He and his whole household believe, he washes their wounds, they are baptized, and he is filled with joy. The God who called them to Macedonia also met a woman by a river and a jailer in the dark. John Piper, in “Treasuring Christ in Planting Churches and Loving the Poor,” follows this planting work into Philippi: “Philippi is the chief city in Macedonia in northern Greece” and watches God open Lydia’s heart and then bring a jailer to faith in the night. The Macedonian call is not a travel plan they invented. The Spirit closes doors, a vision opens one, and then the gospel makes a church out of a businesswoman and a broken jailer. BibleProject’s Acts guide hears the same movement: the word is being led, not merely carried, into Europe, and households believe. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your house.” The NIV’s “you and your household” is that same wide promise. The help Macedonia asked for is the name of Jesus, for a whole house at a time. When the Spirit says go, go. When a household asks how to be saved, give them Jesus, not a smaller hope. As a man, husband, and father, follow the call you are given, and be ready in the night to say, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” and, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”

**Acts 16:6–34 (NIV)**
6 Paul and his companions traveled throughout the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the word in the province of Asia. 7 When they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them to. 8 So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. 9 During the night Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” 10 After Paul had seen the vision, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. 11 From Troas we put out to sea and sailed straight for Samothrace, and the next day we went on to Neapolis. 12 From there we traveled to Philippi, a Roman colony and the leading city of that district of Macedonia. And we stayed there several days. 13 On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer. We sat down and began to speak to the women who had gathered there. 14 One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. 15 When she and the members of her household were baptized, she invited us to her home. “If you consider me a believer in the Lord,” she said, “come and stay at my house.” And she persuaded us. 16 Once when we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a female slave who had a spirit by which she predicted the future. She earned a great deal of money for her owners by fortune-telling. 17 She followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are telling you the way to be saved.” 18 She kept this up for many days. Finally Paul became so annoyed that he turned around and said to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” At that moment the spirit left her. 19 When her owners realized that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to face the authorities. 20 They brought them before the magistrates and said, “These men are Jews, and are throwing our city into an uproar 21 by advocating customs unlawful for us Romans to accept or practice.” 22 The crowd joined in the attack against Paul and Silas, and the magistrates ordered them to be stripped and beaten with rods. 23 After they had been severely flogged, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer was commanded to guard them carefully. 24 When he received these orders, he put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks. 25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. 26 Suddenly there was such a violent earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose. 27 The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself because he thought the prisoners had escaped. 28 But Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!” 29 The jailer called for lights, rushed in and fell trembling before Paul and Silas. 30 He then brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” 31 They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” 32 Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all the others in his house. 33 At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds; then immediately he and all his household were baptized. 34 The jailer brought them into his house and set a meal before them; he was filled with joy because he had come to believe in God—he and his whole household.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where has the Spirit been closing a door, or opening one you did not choose? What would it look like today to go where you are called, and to offer the jailer’s question a true answer: Believe in the Lord Jesus?

**Lesson 193: Acts: an unknown God, a tearful farewell, and the gospel unhindered**

**Lesson 194: Romans: not ashamed of the gospel**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Acts ended in Rome, with the kingdom proclaimed and the gospel unhindered. Today we open the letter that will help us hear that gospel more clearly. Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God, writes to the saints in Rome. The gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets, and it concerns God’s Son, who as to his earthly life was a descendant of David, and who through the Spirit of holiness was appointed the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord. Paul longs to visit them and to preach the gospel also in Rome. Then comes the sentence that will hold the letter: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile.” In the gospel the righteousness of God is revealed—a righteousness that is by faith from first to last, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.” This is not a small religious improvement. It is God’s power for salvation, for everyone who believes, and it reveals a righteousness that comes by faith. John Piper, in “Not Ashamed of the Gospel,” and in “The Gospel Is the Power of God unto Salvation,” will not let this be a slogan. The gospel is not advice. It is the power of God that actually brings salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Gentile. Paul is not ashamed of it because it can do what no human résumé can do. BibleProject’s Romans guide hears the letter as the announcement of that righteousness, given by faith, for a people made up of Jews and Gentiles together. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.” The NIV’s “brings salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile” is that same power and that same order. Do not be ashamed of a gospel that is the power of God. As a man, husband, and father, believe it, live by faith, and speak it without shrinking, first to whoever is near you, and then as far as it will go.

**Romans 1:1–17 (NIV)**
1 Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God— 2 the gospel he promised beforehand through his prophets in the Holy Scriptures 3 regarding his Son, who as to his earthly life was a descendant of David, 4 and who through the Spirit of holiness was appointed the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord. 5 Through him we received grace and apostleship to call all the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith for his name’s sake. 6 And you also are among those Gentiles who are called to belong to Jesus Christ. 7 To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be his holy people: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ. 8 First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being reported all over the world. 9 God, whom I serve in my spirit in preaching the gospel of his Son, is my witness how constantly I remember you 10 in my prayers at all times; and I pray that now at last by God’s will the way may be opened for me to come to you. 11 I long to see you so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to make you strong— 12 that is, that you and I may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith. 13 I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, that I planned many times to come to you (but have been prevented from doing so until now) in order that I might have a harvest among you, just as I have had among the other Gentiles. 14 I am obligated both to Greeks and non-Greeks, both to the wise and the foolish. 15 That is why I am so eager to preach the gospel also to you who are in Rome. 16 For I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile. 17 For in the gospel the righteousness of God is revealed—a righteousness that is by faith from first to last, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.”

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been quietly ashamed of the gospel this week, or tempted to treat it as less than the power of God? What would it look like today to live by faith, and to speak this good news as salvation for everyone who believes?

**Lesson 195: Romans: all have sinned, and justification by grace**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday Paul said he was not ashamed of the gospel, the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. Today he tells us why that power is needed. “What shall we conclude then? Do we have any advantage? Not at all!” Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin. As it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one;” The law does not declare us righteous in God’s sight. Through the law we become conscious of our sin. “But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been made known, to which the Law and the Prophets testify.” This righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no difference between Jew and Gentile, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, through the shedding of his blood—to be received by faith. He did this to demonstrate his righteousness, and so as to be just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus. The diagnosis is universal, and so is the gift. No one is righteous, and anyone who believes is justified freely by grace. John Piper, in “All Jews and Gentiles Are Under Sin,” hears verse 9 as a summary: Jews are not really any better off before God than others, “for we have already charged that both Jews and Greeks are all under sin.” In “The Most Important Paragraph in the Bible,” and in “The Just and the Justifier,” he takes us to Romans 3:21–26, where God is both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus. The righteousness we could not earn is given, freely, through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. BibleProject’s Romans guide hears the same turning: all have sinned, and justification is by grace. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “being justified as a gift by His grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus;” and, “so that He would be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.” The NIV’s “justified freely by his grace” and “just and the one who justifies” keep the same gift and the same God. There is no one righteous, not even one, and there is a righteousness now made known, received by faith. As a man, husband, and father, stop trying to be the exception. All have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by his grace.

**Romans 3:9–26 (NIV)**
9 What shall we conclude then? Do we have any advantage? Not at all! For we have already made the charge that Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin. 10 As it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one; 11 there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God. 12 All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.” 13 “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.” “The poison of vipers is on their lips.” 14 “Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.” 15 “Their feet are swift to shed blood; 16 ruin and misery mark their ways, 17 and the way of peace they do not know.” 18 “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” 19 Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God. 20 Therefore no one will be declared righteous in God’s sight by the works of the law; rather, through the law we become conscious of our sin. 21 But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been made known, to which the Law and the Prophets testify. 22 This righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no difference between Jew and Gentile, 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. 25 God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, through the shedding of his blood—to be received by faith. He did this to demonstrate his righteousness, because in his forbearance he had left the sins committed beforehand unpunished— 26 he did it to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been quietly claiming an advantage, or trying to be declared righteous by your own works? What would it look like today to confess that you have fallen short, and to receive justification as a free gift through Jesus?

**Lesson 195: Romans: all have sinned, and justification by grace**

Good morning. Yesterday Paul said he was not ashamed of the gospel, the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. Today he tells us why that power is needed. “What shall we conclude then? Do we have any advantage? Not at all!” Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin. As it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one;” The law does not declare us righteous in God’s sight. Through the law we become conscious of our sin. “But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been made known, to which the Law and the Prophets testify.” This righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no difference between Jew and Gentile, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, through the shedding of his blood—to be received by faith. He did this to demonstrate his righteousness, and so as to be just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus. The diagnosis is universal, and so is the gift. No one is righteous, and anyone who believes is justified freely by grace. John Piper, in “All Jews and Gentiles Are Under Sin,” hears verse 9 as a summary: Jews are not really any better off before God than others, “for we have already charged that both Jews and Greeks are all under sin.” In “The Most Important Paragraph in the Bible,” and in “The Just and the Justifier,” he takes us to Romans 3:21–26, where God is both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus. The righteousness we could not earn is given, freely, through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. BibleProject’s Romans guide hears the same turning: all have sinned, and justification is by grace. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “being justified as a gift by His grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus;” and, “so that He would be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.” The NIV’s “justified freely by his grace” and “just and the one who justifies” keep the same gift and the same God. There is no one righteous, not even one, and there is a righteousness now made known, received by faith. As a woman, wife, and a mother, stop trying to be the exception. All have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by his grace.

**Romans 3:9–26 (NIV)**
9 What shall we conclude then? Do we have any advantage? Not at all! For we have already made the charge that Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin. 10 As it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one; 11 there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God. 12 All have turned away, they have together become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.” 13 “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit.” “The poison of vipers is on their lips.” 14 “Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.” 15 “Their feet are swift to shed blood; 16 ruin and misery mark their ways, 17 and the way of peace they do not know.” 18 “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” 19 Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God. 20 Therefore no one will be declared righteous in God’s sight by the works of the law; rather, through the law we become conscious of our sin. 21 But now apart from the law the righteousness of God has been made known, to which the Law and the Prophets testify. 22 This righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no difference between Jew and Gentile, 23 for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, 24 and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus. 25 God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, through the shedding of his blood—to be received by faith. He did this to demonstrate his righteousness, because in his forbearance he had left the sins committed beforehand unpunished— 26 he did it to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus.

**Reflection question:** As a woman, wife, and a mother, where have you been quietly claiming an advantage, or trying to be declared righteous by your own works? What would it look like today to confess that you have fallen short, and to receive justification as a free gift through Jesus?

**Lesson 196: Romans: peace with God, and love poured out**

Good morning, Greg. Yesterday we heard that all have sinned, and that all who believe are justified freely by his grace. Today Paul tells us what that gift gives us. “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,” Through him we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand, and we boast in the hope of the glory of God. We even glory in our sufferings, because suffering produces perseverance, perseverance character, and character hope. “And hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” This love has a time and a cost. At just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die. “But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” Since we have now been justified by his blood, how much more shall we be saved from God’s wrath through him. For if, while we were God’s enemies, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life. We also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. Peace with God is not a mood. It is a reconciliation, made at the cross, poured into our hearts by the Spirit. John Piper, in “Let Us Exult in the Hope of the Glory of God!,” says his aim is that you will exult in that hope, because “it is the will of God for you in Christ Jesus.” In “The Depth of Christ’s Love: Its Undeserving Objects,” he asks how you measure the depth of a love. “If someone performs an act of love toward you, there are four ways that you can see the depth of that love.” One is cost: “If it cost his life, it is another degree of love.” And this love was for the undeserving: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. In “The Love of God Has Been Poured Out Within Our Hearts,” he lingers over the Spirit’s gift, so that hope does not put us to shame. BibleProject’s Romans guide hears this chapter as the fruit of justification: peace, hope, and a love already poured out. The Legacy Standard Bible has, “having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,” and, “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” The NIV’s “justified through faith” and “while we were still sinners” are that same peace and that same love. You have peace with God, and his love has been poured out in your heart. As a man, husband, and father, stand in this grace. Do not live like an enemy when you have been reconciled, and do not treat this love as thin. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

**Romans 5:1–11 (NIV)**
1 Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand. And we boast in the hope of the glory of God. 3 Not only so, but we also glory in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; 4 perseverance, character; and character, hope. 5 And hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. 6 You see, at just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. 7 Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die. 8 But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. 9 Since we have now been justified by his blood, how much more shall we be saved from God’s wrath through him! 10 For if, while we were God’s enemies, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life! 11 Not only is this so, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

**Reflection question:** As a man, husband, and father, where have you been living as if you were still at war with God, or as if his love had not yet been poured out? What would it look like today to stand in this peace, and to boast in God through the Lord Jesus Christ?
